concepts/administrative-despotism.title: Administrative Despotism
concepts/administrative-despotism.content:
Administrative Despotism
Administrative despotism, in the interwar constitutional vocabulary of the Lord Chief Justice of England, was the progressive transfer of legislative and judicial power from Parliament and the ordinary courts to government departments—rule by departmental order and official adjudication instead of by statute and open court. It was not the continental droit administratif with its specialised tribunals and known safeguards, but what its critic called administrative lawlessness: decision without the independence, procedure, or publicity of the judges.
Development
The high-water mark of the practice, held up as the type of the whole evil, was Section 67 of the Rating and Valuation Act 1925. That section empowered the Minister of Health, if any difficulty arose in bringing the Act into operation, to remove the difficulty by order and, for that purpose, to “modify the provisions of this Act” as appeared necessary or expedient. A government department could thus, by its own order, override the very statute that created its power. The same pattern, in varying degrees of boldness, ran through housing, health insurance, pensions, town planning, unemployment insurance, agriculture, and a lengthening list of other fields: statutes that vested final decision in a minister, excluded or narrowed the jurisdiction of the courts, or authorised rules with the force of law made in Whitehall rather than on the floor of the House.
Behind the examples stood a constitutional doctrine drawn from the English tradition of the rule of law. Regular law was to be supreme against arbitrary power; every subject, official or private, was equal before the ordinary courts; the executive was subordinate to judicial control. Continental administrative law—separate courts for disputes involving the state, as in the French Conseil d’État—was treated as foreign to that tradition. What was growing in England, the argument ran, was not a regulated administrative law but the substance of administrative power without the continental machinery of review. Judicial functions were exercised by officials who were not independent, who need not sit in public, and whose decisions might be shielded by statute from certiorari or other common-law remedies.
Delegated legislation was distinguished into prerogative forms and statutory forms. The pressure of parliamentary business and the technical complexity of modern statutes explained why Parliament began to hand rule-making to departments; the indictment was that the hand-over had become indiscriminate, that departments used it to enlarge their own authority, and that the power to “modify” Acts by ministerial order crossed the line between filling in detail and rewriting the law. The independence of the judiciary—secured historically from the Act of Settlement onward—was said to be directly threatened when adjudication moved from courts to departments. Leading cases were collected to show both judicial resistance and judicial surrender: publicity in proceedings, the extent of natural justice in departmental inquiries, and ministerial power to remove difficulties under rating and other Acts.
The remedy proposed was not the abolition of all administration but the restoration of judicial authority and the restriction of departmental adjudication: rights of appeal from official persons, reform of the law relating to the Crown as litigant, and a statute book purged of clauses that put ministers beyond the courts. The polemic of 1929 became a rallying text against “bureaucracy” and administrative discretion and helped to force the question of ministers’ powers onto the public agenda of the early 1930s.

concepts/cabinet-dictatorship.title: Cabinet Dictatorship
concepts/cabinet-dictatorship.content:
Cabinet Dictatorship
Cabinet dictatorship, in the interwar diagnosis of how Britain was actually governed, was the concentration of real power in a Cabinet sustained by rigid party organisation, so that the House of Commons became little more than a registering machine for decisions taken elsewhere. It was not personal tyranny in the continental sense but the practical omnipotence of a party executive over a Parliament that textbooks still described in the language of Bagehot and Mill.
Development
Confidence in representative democracy had been “seriously and progressively undermined” since the war. Newspapers gave little space to parliamentary proceedings; electors took their responsibilities lightly; even in Britain, the original home of the system, the prestige of Parliament had strangely waned. The textbooks still taught a constitution that no longer existed. Seven great changes since the nineteenth century had transformed the working machine: uncontrolled growth of bureaucracy; the rise of Cabinet dictatorship; the rigidity of party organisation; distortion of the electoral system through organised parties in single-member constituencies; the House of Commons’s increasing incapacity to do its work; the reduction of the House of Lords to impotence; and the emergence of extra-constitutional organised interests—trade unions, employers’ associations, the Bank of England—exerting direct pressure on government.
“The Government” was not a single mind but a complex of Cabinet, ministers, departments, and the Prime Minister’s office. It held legislative initiative, financial control, foreign policy, the prerogative of dissolution, and a growing range of delegated legislation. Professional administrators had replaced the old amateur regime; government functions and bureaucratic power had expanded together. Bureaucracy’s characteristic defects—slowness, rigidity, secrecy, and the impulse to enlarge its own authority—were only weakly checked by ministerial responsibility, Treasury oversight, and parliamentary questions.
The Cabinet itself had become a party body overloaded with business, dominated by the Prime Minister, and neglectful of long-term policy and of the coordination of administration. The most important Cabinet functions—strategic planning, supervision, continuous control—were almost or entirely neglected. Party organisation, from Chamberlain’s Birmingham caucus of 1877 through party funds and the Whips, had destroyed the freedom of the old two-party system. The independent member declined; the two-party system broke down under post-war three-party conditions that the single-member constituency could not honestly represent. General elections became a gamble in which the result did not fairly reflect the mind of the nation.
The House of Commons, under this pressure, could not control either the vast powers of the Cabinet or the enormous and growing power of bureaucracy. Procedure was faulty; national accounts were presented in bewildering form; legislative and financial work was rushed. The Lords, cut down by the Parliament Act 1911 and by wholesale creations of undistinguished peers for party purposes, stood in “humiliating impotence.” Because Parliament could not check the executive, outside organisations were almost unnoticed taking up the task of control. Regional and functional devolution were proposed as remedies for excessive centralisation—subordinate legislatures for social services, and effective consultation of industry on measures that affected it.
The root of the evil was held to be the two-party system once parties became elaborately organised: that organisation enabled Cabinet dictatorship and reduced Parliament to impotence. A two-party system was “essentially unnatural in modern conditions.” Proposed cures included a smaller and reorganised Cabinet with a secretariat of real analytical capacity; revised Commons procedure for real control of finance and legislation; a better Second Chamber for revision rather than for blocking revolution; and both regional and functional devolution. The closing warning was sharp: if methods of discussion could not be improved, government by discussion would fall into disrepute—it was already doing so. Representative government was on its trial.

concepts/class-feeling.title: Class Feeling
concepts/class-feeling.content:
Class Feeling
English class, in Orwell’s mid-1930s analysis, was not a simple ladder of incomes. It was a money-stratification interpenetrated by a “shadowy caste-system”—like a jerry-built modern bungalow haunted by medieval ghosts—so that a naval officer and his grocer might share an income and still not be equivalent persons. Class feeling was habits, manners, and physical repugnance as much as rent-rolls; and it was the chief obstacle, he argued, to any Socialism that hoped to unite the working class with the sinking middle.
Development
Orwell placed himself in the lower-upper-middle class: the layer between roughly £300 and £2,000 a year, his own family near the bottom, whose heyday had been the eighties and nineties with Kipling as laureate—a mound of wreckage left when Victorian prosperity receded. Before the Great War one was either a gentleman or not; if a gentleman, one struggled to behave as such whatever the income. Traditions were military, official, and professional rather than commercial. Small boys counted plum stones: Army, Navy, Church, Medicine, Law. At four hundred a year gentility was almost purely theoretical—one knew how to tip servants, order a dinner, shoot and ride, without the means to do any of it properly. India (later Kenya, Nigeria) attracted this layer not mainly for money but because cheap horses, free shooting, and servants made it easy to play at being a gentleman.
People of this kind felt poverty more consciously than working-class families above the dole: rent, clothes, and school bills were an unending nightmare; nearly all income went to keep up appearances. Their political importance was as “shock-absorbers of the bourgeoisie.” The real bourgeoisie, at £2,000 a year and over, had money as padding between themselves and the class they plundered; they met the Lower Orders as employees, servants, and tradesmen. The poor genteel, living middle-class codes on working-class incomes, stood in the middle and absorbed the shocks.
Class in the West, Orwell insisted, involved a physical repugnance—the “class smell”—that no amount of abstract goodwill abolished. Somerset Maugham was cited on smell as a barrier; bourgeois Socialists who idealised the proletariat still kept bourgeois table manners and married inside their own class. Public-school snobbery trained the young early; a scholarship boy among richer boys learned the hierarchy from below. Service in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma then put the dirty work of Empire at close quarters and left a residue of guilt. Deliberately going among the destitute—a common lodging-house as “baptism,” tramping with an Irish tramp—seemed for a moment to drop the class-bar among “the lowest of the low.” Yet making friends with tramps did not solve the class problem: outcasts were no more typical of the working class than literary intellectuals were of the bourgeoisie. Real intimacy with ordinary respectable working people remained extremely hard.
Abolishing class distinctions, therefore, meant abandoning middle-class ideology, not attending summer schools or “levelling up” with fruit-juice and hygiene. Forced class-breaking often intensified antagonism. The middle-class Socialist who recoiled in middle age, seeing that a classless society might mean the death of his own codes and tastes, might flee as far as Fascism. By the closing pages of The Road to Wigan Pier the practical political task was to win the sinking middle class—schoolmasters, journalists, clerks, bankrupt drapers—before Fascism played its trump card, and to invite them to sink into the working class with the parody of the Communist Manifesto: “we have nothing to lose but our aitches.” Class feeling was thus both a social fact of industrial England and the hinge on which the fate of English Socialism, in Orwell’s reading, would turn.

concepts/english-socialism.title: English Socialism
concepts/english-socialism.content:
English Socialism
Socialism, in Orwell’s mid-1930s reckoning, was “common sense”: the world as a raft with provisions enough for all, each to do a fair share of the work and take a fair share of the goods. Yet Socialism was losing ground exactly where empty bellies should have made it gain. Socialists almost everywhere were in retreat before Fascism; in England the idea was less widely accepted than ten years earlier. The average thinking person was not merely not a Socialist but actively hostile. To defend Socialism, Orwell argued, one had first to attack the form in which it was presented.
Development
He went to the coal areas partly to see mass-unemployment at its worst and the typical English working class at close quarters—necessary, he said, before one could be sure of favouring Socialism or take up a definite attitude on class. Part Two of The Road to Wigan Pier was the working-out of that attitude: class-feeling as the barrier; then the “obvious preliminary objections” that drove decent people away; then machine-civilisation and the deeper assumptions that alienated sensitive minds; then a practical programme for a party that could still be built.
The worst advertisement for Socialism was its adherents. In developed form the theory was confined almost entirely to the middle classes. The typical Socialist was not the ferocious working man of tremulous imagination but either a youthful snob-Bolshevik who would soon marry money and turn Catholic, or, still more typically, a prim white-collar man, often teetotal or vegetarian, with Nonconformity behind him and a social position he had no intention of forfeiting. Worse was the prevalence of cranks: fruit-juice drinkers, nudists, sandal-wearers, sex-maniacs, Quakers, Nature Cure quacks, pacifists, and feminists seemed magnetically drawn to the words Socialism and Communism. Two old men in pistachio shirts and khaki shorts boarding a bus at Letchworth—where the I.L.P. held its summer school—made a commercial traveller murmur “Socialists” as who should say “Red Indians.” Summer-school prospectuses that asked whether diet was “ordinary or vegetarian” took crankishness for granted and alienated plenty of decent people whose instinct, Orwell thought, was sound.
A second line of repulsion was jargon and heresy-hunting: “bourgeois ideology,” “proletarian solidarity,” “expropriation of the expropriators,” the sacred sisters thesis-antithesis-synthesis, and the word “Comrade” itself. Orthodox Marxists often treated the movement as an exciting hunt for right-wing deviationists rather than a league of the oppressed against the oppressors. Working-class Socialists, like working-class Catholics, were weak on doctrine and full of heresies but had the heart of the matter: Socialism meant the overthrow of tyranny. The Marseillaise, if translated, would move them more than dialectical materialism. At a moment when Fascist forces were bombarding Madrid and another Fascist country might be added to the list before the book was printed, the movement had no time to be a league of dialectical materialists.
Machine-civilisation raised a further difficulty. Socialism as usually presented was bound up with the cult of the machine—tractors, the Dnieper dam, the latest salmon-canning factory in Moscow—as if mechanical progress were integral to the doctrine. Many people were not in love with machine-civilisation even though they depended on it; that identification drove away people the cause needed, including most of those who could hold a pen. Fascism, conversely, was not to be written off as a mere manoeuvre of the ruling class. Its spiritual side mattered: millions who were not capitalists and had nothing material to gain from Fascism could be stampeded into it when Communism attacked, or seemed to attack, things they cared about. Class mishandling might stampede quantities of potential Socialists the same way. A middle-class Socialist who recoiled in middle age, seeing that a classless society might mean the death of his own codes and tastes, might flee as far as Fascism.
The remedy Orwell offered was intelligent propaganda: less class-jargon and Russian machinery, more justice, liberty, and the plight of the unemployed; the two facts that the interests of all exploited people were the same and that Socialism was compatible with common decency. Essentials need not be sacrificed, but externals must—sandals and pistachio shirts burnt in a pile, vegetarians and teetotallers packed off to Welwyn Garden City if necessary. On class, go easy: no muscular-curate class-breaking; Old School Tie loyalties could be useful if handled; the sinking middle class—private schoolmasters, free-lance journalists, clerks, thrice-bankrupt drapers—must be invited to sink into the working class “where we belong,” with nothing to lose but their aitches. Without an effective Socialist party of genuinely revolutionary intentions and sufficient numbers, there was no chance of righting the conditions of Part One or of saving England from Fascism—probably a slimy Anglicised form, with cultured policemen instead of Nazi gorillas and the lion and unicorn instead of the swastika. If such a party were got, struggle would follow, conceivably physical; classes who fought side by side might then feel differently about one another, and the misery of class-prejudice might fade faster than now seemed thinkable.

concepts/industrial-north.title: The Industrial North
concepts/industrial-north.content:
The Industrial North
The industrial North of England, as Orwell found it in the mid-1930s, was not merely a map of coal and cotton but a whole civilisation of slag-heaps, canals, back-to-back houses, and colliery villages, set against a southern “villa-civilisation” that could still ignore mass unemployment. To go north was to pass into the “real ugliness of industrialism”—and also into the most typical section of the English working class at close quarters.
Development
“Our civilization, pace Chesterton, is founded on coal.” Underground, the coal face meant heat, noise, dust, galleries a yard high, and exhausting “travelling” to and from the face that was not even counted as the miner’s real work. Women had once dragged coal in harness; modern comfort rested on labour the rest of society preferred to forget. Above ground a shift left the pit with pale faces under coal dust and blue scars where dust lay under healed cuts. Output figures of around 280 tons a year for the average mine-worker sat beside accident rates: roughly one miner in nine hundred killed each year, one in six injured, and the “death stoppage” rubber stamp on pay-checks. The miner stood as the type of the invisible manual worker on whom “superior persons” depended.
Housing carried the same weight of neglect. Smoke-blackened rows without hot water; shared yards and w.c.s fifty yards from the door; houses unfit for habitation but kept tenanted because there were no others; Corporation estates only marginally better; caravan colonies along miry canals. In Wigan more than two thousand houses stood condemned for years; whole sections would have been condemned en bloc if replacements existed. Leeds and Sheffield kept scores of thousands of back-to-back houses of a condemned type that would stand for decades. Notebook extracts fixed the scale: one-up-one-down rooms twelve feet by ten; sinks and coppers in the living-room; floors subsiding; water coming in upstairs; ten in a family with eight children and no house to which the Corporation could move them. Landlords good and bad; rents of a few shillings plus rates; people clinging to hovels lest worse befall. Caravan “colonies” in Wigan and Sheffield were not picturesque camps but waste ground with fixed caravans as temporary quarters that had become permanent.
The landscape matched the houses. Travelling north, one left southern villa-civilisation for burning slag-heaps, sulphur flames, canals, and a lunar waste around Wigan—smoke, shale, ice, mud, ashes, and foul water—yet even Wigan could be beautiful in a winter afternoon light. Unemployed men and women risked injury picking coal and “carmel” from dirt trains for a few pence worth of fuel; competition for waste coal was sharp in winter. English North–South myth—cold climate, Nordic virtue, the cult of Scotland—had been twisted by industrialisation into a new antithesis: the North as the place where industrial ugliness was concentrated and unemployment filled whole blocks of cities, the South as the region where unemployment existed but was scattered and queerly unobtrusive, and rural districts where a man out of work was almost unheard-of.
Against that ugliness Orwell set the working-class interior: coal fire, kippers, strong tea—a moment in time that he contrasted both with hygienic Utopian futures and with medieval squalor, and treated as evidence that the age had not been altogether a bad one to live in. The Industrial North was thus at once the foundation of national comfort, the theatre of mass unemployment and bad housing, and the cultural pole against which southern England measured itself.

concepts/means-test.title: The Means Test
concepts/means-test.content:
The Means Test
The Means Test was the household-means enquiry under which unemployed men, once their insurance stamps were exhausted and transitional benefit run out, received outdoor relief from the Public Assistance Committee (P.A.C.) only if their total household resources fell below a strict standard. In the industrial North of the mid-1930s it governed the lives of whole streets; it was enforced by inspection, tale-bearing, and deductions for any other income; and its most notorious social consequence was to drive old people out of their children’s homes.
Development
When a man first lost work he drew “full benefit” while his stamps lasted—seventeen shillings for a single man, nine for a wife, three for each child under fourteen. After stamps were exhausted he received twenty-six weeks’ “transitional benefit” from the Unemployment Assistance Board (U.A.B.), at rates that for a typical family of five might come to about thirty-seven shillings and sixpence a week. Only then was he turned over to the P.A.C. P.A.C. rates were lower still: twelve and six for a single man (sometimes raised by half a crown), twenty-three shillings for man and wife, four for the eldest child, three for any other. In theory P.A.C. money came from the local rates, though backed by a central fund; in practice a quarter of a married man’s dole was treated as rent (with a minimum of seven and six on the U.A.B.), and coal allowances of one and six a week were granted only for a few weeks before and after Christmas.
At every stage the Means Test was “very strictly enforced.” The slightest hint of money from another source could stop or cut relief. Dock-labourers hired by the half-day had to sign on at the Labour Exchange twice daily; if they failed, it was assumed they had been working and the dole was reduced. Evasion existed—young men living with parents would take an accommodation address so as to draw a separate allowance—but in industrial towns, where communal life remained strong and every man had neighbours who knew him, it was harder than in London. Spying and tale-bearing were common. One man was reported for “having a job feeding chickens” because he had been seen feeding a neighbour’s birds while the neighbour was away; he had great difficulty refuting it. A favourite Wigan joke told of a man refused relief for “carting firewood” at night—he had been doing a moonlight flit, and the “firewood” was his furniture.
The cruellest effect, in Orwell’s account, was the breaking up of families. An old-age pensioner who was a widower would normally live with one of his children; his weekly ten shillings went into the household, and he was not usually badly cared for. Under the Means Test he counted as a “lodger.” If he stayed, his children’s dole was docked. So, at seventy or seventy-five, he had to turn out into lodgings, hand his pension to the lodging-house keeper, and exist on the verge of starvation. Cases of this kind were to be seen all over England. In lodging-houses and tripe shops the same pressure appeared in miniature: commercial travellers and unemployed men on the P.A.C. were driven from home by the Test; old people and the landlady’s boarders lived under its shadow; and even petty tradesmen were suspected of dodging it while drawing an allowance.
Diet, rent, and housing were all shaped by the same arithmetic. Family income on the dole commonly averaged about thirty shillings a week, of which a quarter went in rent, leaving six or seven shillings a head for food, clothes, and warmth. Corporation houses and better private dwellings often excluded or deterred people on the dole; rent for those on the P.A.C. was assessed at a quarter of the dole, with extras if actual rent ran higher. The Means Test thus did more than police fraud: it fixed a standard of life for a large fraction of the industrial population and rearranged households so that the aged and the unemployed could not safely share a roof.

concepts/the-heartland.title: The Heartland
concepts/the-heartland.content:
The Heartland
The Heartland was the name given, at the close of the First World War, to the great interior of the Eurasian “World-Island”—the closed land mass of Europe, Asia, and Africa seen as one—whose command was held to decide world power in an age when the Columbian epoch of open oceanic expansion was over. Who ruled East Europe commanded the Heartland; who ruled the Heartland commanded the World-Island; who ruled the World-Island commanded the World. The thesis was a warning for the peace settlement: democratic ideals without geographical reality would leave the way open to a land empire from the Heartland.
Development
The ideas had been sketched in 1904 as the “geographical pivot of history” and in 1905 in the language of man-power as a measure of national and imperial strength. The war of 1914–18 confirmed rather than shook them. The world had become a closed political system. Mere juridical conceptions of a League of Nations, without reckoning with geographical and economic “Going Concerns,” risked a future World-Tyranny. Democracy thought ethically—“no annexations, no indemnities”—while the great organiser thought strategically; the peace had to reckon with both.
From the seaman’s point of view the first geographical reality was the unity of the ocean. River-powers and sea-powers had closed and reopened the Nile and the Mediterranean; the Latin Peninsula had been a sea-base for encompassing the World-Promontory; division within that peninsula had opened opportunity for sea-power from the lesser but insular base of Britain. In the Great War sea-power had again been decisive in its own sphere, yet the ultimate base of sea-power was the World-Island itself—the continuous land mass against which oceanic power operated from the margins.
From the landsman’s point of view the World-Island was seen from within. The Heartland was defined physically by Arctic and inland drainage, the great lowland, and the steppes of Euro-Asia; strategically it was extended to include the Black Sea and Baltic basins—as real a physical fact as the World-Island, and the ultimate citadel of land-power. Mobile riders from the steppes had long pressed on the plowmen; the open access from the Heartland to Arabia and to Europe remained. Railways and air-routes were knitting the World-Island together and increasing the mobility of land-power relative to the old sea-routes.
The rivalry of empires followed the same map. Cossack advance had carried Russia over the Heartland; the Russian Homeland was sharply delimited, but East Europe lay within the Heartland and was fundamentally opposed to West Europe. German and Slav competition in East Europe, the German attempt to control East Europe and the Heartland, and the policy of stimulating man-power to occupy that interior, were set against the seaborne, laissez-faire empire of Britain as two Going Concerns whose clash was inevitable. Trafalgar and the two streams of history—Britain and the Not-Europe on one side, the land struggle of East and West Europe on the other—framed the nineteenth century; the Great War was the German bid for the Heartland.
Victory on the Western Front had not removed the geographical threat. Had Germany won even only on land, a Heartland Empire would have had to be reckoned with. East Europe and the Heartland therefore needed division into three state-systems, not two—a Middle Tier of peoples between Germany and Russia—so that no single power dominated the pivot. A League of Nations was feasible only if that division were made and if there were no predominant partner and a reasonable equality of power among a considerable number of members. Certain strategical positions of world importance had still to be watched; Going Concerns would grow unequally; the ideal was the independent nation of balanced economic development, and, within nations, balanced provinces based on localities rather than on nation-wide classes that led toward international war of classes.
That land-power thesis stood in explicit tension with the older sea-power reading of British greatness. In the generation after Mahan, the strategic debate set naval mastery—command of oceanic communications from an insular base—against the Mackinder claim that railways and massed man-power in the Heartland were beginning to eclipse sea-power. The First World War showed the limits of sea-power in a continental struggle: Jutland was indecisive; the submarine campaign nearly strangled Britain; the blockade required American weight. In the years of decay between the wars, treaty ratios, the Ten-Year Rule, and industrial and financial strain reduced the Royal Navy’s global margin while Japan and the United States built toward treaty limits; the need to cover Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Far East at once with inadequate forces was never resolved. The Second World War was fought with tactical skill at sea, yet the protection of the sea lanes depended on massive American assistance, and by the mid-war years the United States Navy held the dominant oceanic position. The Heartland warning of 1919 and the measured decline of British naval mastery after 1914 were two readings of the same closed-world map: land power at the pivot, sea power no longer able to decide alone from the periphery.

concepts/unemployment-and-the-dole.title: Unemployment and the Dole
concepts/unemployment-and-the-dole.content:
Unemployment and the Dole
“Two millions unemployed” was the figure the papers and politicians repeated; it was also, as Orwell insisted, a misleading measure of who actually lived on the edge of want. Dependants, low-paid full-time workers, old-age pensioners, and the unregistered pushed the underfed population far higher. In the mining and cotton towns of the North, whole blocks of streets lived on the dole and the Public Assistance Committee; a change in the attitude of the submerged working class, compared with the late 1920s, was already visible by the mid-1930s.
Development
Wigan, typical enough of industrial and mining districts, had about 36,000 insured workers (26,000 men and 10,000 women). At the beginning of 1936 some 10,000 were unemployed in winter, when the mines worked full time; in summer the figure might reach 12,000. Multiplied by three for dependants, that meant 30,000 or 36,000 people drawing or living on the dole in a town of a little under 87,000—more than one person in three of the whole population, not merely of registered workers. Among the unemployed stood a steady core of four to five thousand miners continuously out of work for seven years. Sheffield, for all the recent stimulus of “wars and rumours of war,” showed about the same proportion: one in three of registered workers unemployed.
Nationally Orwell argued that if one multiplied Labour Exchange figures by three for dependants and added those on wages too low to feed a family (Lancashire cotton mills with over 40,000 full-time employees under thirty shillings a week), together with pensioners and the destitute, one reached an underfed population of well over ten millions. Sir John Orr put it at twenty millions. Full benefit, transitional benefit, and P.A.C. rates then fixed the money available: a family on the dole commonly averaged about thirty shillings a week, a quarter of it rent, so that each person had six or seven shillings for food, clothes, and fuel.
That money bought a diet of white bread, margarine, sugar, tea, potatoes, and occasional scraps of meat—filling but deficient. Napoleon’s maxim that an army marches on its stomach was turned into a claim that diet shapes history more than dynasties; industrial substitutes and tinned food were linked to a decline in physique; English cookery among the poor was often wasteful even when money was short. People on sixteen shillings a week could not be well nourished if they concentrated only on what filled them; white bread-and-marg and sugared tea did not nourish. Yet cheap luxuries—fish-and-chips, the radio, the cinema, football pools, tinned salmon—softened the surface of misery. Orwell did not treat these as a conscious “bread and circuses” plot by the governing class; he treated them as an unintended buffer that helped avert revolution without restoring work.
The moral and social effects mattered as much as the figures. When Orwell first saw unemployed men at close quarters in 1928, fresh from Burma where unemployment was only a word, what horrified him was that many were ashamed. By the mid-1930s, in streets where nobody had a job and winning fifty pounds in the Football Pool seemed more likely than employment, that shame had lessened. Drawing the dole, though still unpleasant, ceased to be shameful for many who had lived on it for years. In the back streets of Wigan and Barnsley he saw every kind of privation, but also a stubborn refusal of absolute demoralisation: men married on the dole, kept up appearances in small ways, and did not present themselves as the “loafers” of comfortable rhetoric. Occupational centres—boot-mending, sea-grass work, a Y.M.C.A. atmosphere—kept some men busy and, Socialists said, quiet and less likely to read the Daily Worker; Orwell found them ambiguous but better than years of absolute idleness. The deeper fact remained: unless another war broke out, several million men in England would never have a real job this side of the grave.

concepts/versailles-and-reparations.title: Versailles and Reparations
concepts/versailles-and-reparations.content:
Versailles and Reparations
Versailles and reparations, in the economic argument of 1919–20, meant not merely the territorial map of the Treaty of Peace with Germany but the whole apparatus by which the victors proposed to transfer wealth from the defeated Central Powers—merchant fleets and colonies stripped, coal and iron cut away, a reparation bill without a fixed total, and a Commission empowered to take year by year what surplus remained. The settlement was framed as a moral and political act; its critics insisted that it was first of all an economic fact that would decide whether Europe could again feed its towns and clear its exchanges.
Development
Germany laid down her arms under a pre-Armistice engagement: the Fourteen Points as modified by the Allied Note of 5 November 1918, formally communicated as the basis of peace. That engagement limited reparation to “all damage done to the civilian population of the Allies and to their property by the aggression of Germany by land, by sea, and from the air,” and it excluded “contributions” and “punitive damages.” On a strict reading, British claims ran chiefly to civilian damage by air raids, bombardments, and submarine warfare, and to improper treatment of interned civilians—not to the general costs of the war. French and Belgian claims added invasion damage, loot, fines, and forced labour. Aggregate legitimate claims on that basis were guessed in the order of eight to fifteen thousand million dollars; a round ten thousand million, fixed at once and divided by need and equity among the Allies, would have been a statesmanlike settlement within the contract.
What arrived at Paris was another atmosphere. After the Armistice it became clear that unconditional surrender could have been forced. The British Coalition, fighting a December 1918 election, moved from a manifesto that spoke of a just and lasting peace and a League of Nations to platform pledges of hanging the Kaiser, the fullest indemnities, and payment of the costs of the war “up to the limit of capacity.” Sir Eric Geddes’s lemon was to be squeezed “until you can hear the pips squeak.” The new House of Commons was full of hard-faced men who looked as if they had done well out of the war. Lloyd George went to Paris with electoral entanglements; the finance ministers of France and Italy, whose peace budgets made no pretence of balancing without vast enemy receipts, could not face scientific estimates of capacity. Clemenceau’s policy was security by a Carthaginian peace—to set the clock back to 1870 by curtailing German population and destroying the fabric of iron, coal, and transport on which German strength had grown—while Klotz needed the pretence of an indemnity large enough to save French finance. The two demands were incompatible: a permanently crippled Germany could not also pay huge annual transfers.
The Council of Four settled the text. Article 231 affirmed German responsibility for all loss and damage; Article 232 admitted that resources were inadequate for complete reparation yet required compensation for civilian damage “and in general all damage as defined in Annex I.” Annex I, by including separation allowances and combatants’ pensions computed on French scales, roughly doubled the bill and brought the total claim, on one careful guess, near forty thousand million dollars. No definitive sum was named in the Treaty. Before 1 May 1921 Germany was to pay five thousand million dollars (with abatements for armies of occupation and essential food and raw materials); bearer bonds for further tens of thousands of millions, interest deferred then compounding at five per cent, could roll the debt up so that even substantial annual payments left the capital larger than before. Until the Treaty was altered, Germany had in effect engaged to hand over the whole of her surplus production in perpetuity.
Capacity to pay was a different question from legal entitlement. Immediately transferable wealth—gold, ships, foreign securities—was limited. Annual transfer required a German export surplus in foreign currencies while the Treaty had already taken merchant marine, colonies, foreign investments, Saar coal under French control, Upper Silesian hard coal subject to plebiscite, and deliveries of coal to France, Belgium, and Italy, and had disordered transport and tariffs. Maximum annual payment was put near five hundred million dollars on a capital of about ten thousand million—far below the machinery of the Reparation Chapter. The transfer problem was compounded by Allied tariffs and by the deliberate impoverishment of the very productive capacity from which payment was expected.
Europe after the Treaty was a continent of dense industrial populations dependent on coal, iron, transport, and imported food and materials. The settlement made no provision for economic rehabilitation of the Central Empires, for stabilising new states, for reclaiming Russia, or for a compact of solidarity among the Allies. Coal production for Europe as a whole was estimated down by some thirty per cent; German soil productivity and livestock quality had fallen heavily; railway and currency systems were broken; fifteen million families were said to be on unemployment allowances paid largely by inflation. Currency debauch—notes printed against deficits—confiscated wealth arbitrarily, disordered the relation of debtor and creditor, and bred hatred of “profiteers” who were the consequence, not the cause, of rising prices. French and Italian budgets rested on expected German receipts that their own officials knew to be baseless.
The programme of remedy was fourfold: revision of the Treaty (a fixed reparation of about ten thousand million dollars, with ships, cables, war material, and state property in ceded territory reckoned as a lump two and a half thousand million, plus relief on coal and iron and on tariffs); settlement of inter-Allied indebtedness by general cancellation; an international loan and currency reform to stabilise exchanges and supply working capital; and the opening of relations between Central Europe and Russia so that production and trade might revive. The Council of Four could not be expected to undo its own work; new leadership and, if the League were used, a public opinion strong enough to overcome the Covenant’s bias toward unanimity and the territorial status quo were the political conditions of any such salvage.

entities/andrew-bonar-law.title: Andrew Bonar Law (1858–1923)
entities/andrew-bonar-law.content:
Andrew Bonar Law (1858–1923)
Unionist leader · Coalition lieutenant under Lloyd George · Prime Minister, October 1922–May 1923

Coalition years
Through the last years of the First World War and the peace that followed, Bonar Law stood as the principal Unionist colleague of David Lloyd George. In the War Cabinet and Imperial War Cabinet he appears in Hankey’s record among the handful of ministers who sat at the centre of business; in the peacetime Coalition he remained Lord Privy Seal and Leader of the House until his resignation from that office in 1920, recorded in the Annual Register. He was not the political father of the Cabinet Office—that was Lloyd George’s December 1916 creation, with Maurice Hankey as Secretary—but he was present at its wartime workings and later decisive for its peacetime survival.
The conference era of 1919–22 found him often representing Britain when Lloyd George was elsewhere, and as a steadying force at home while Ireland, reparations, and unemployment pressed. Chanak in September 1922—the Turkish advance toward the British position after the burning of Smyrna, Cabinet talk of war, Dominion and domestic protest, and the Convention of Mudania—broke open Conservative discontent that had long simmered against Coalition rule.

Carlton Club and the premiership
On 19 October 1922 Conservative MPs at the Carlton Club voted to fight the next election as an independent party. Austen Chamberlain had defended the Coalition; Bonar Law led the secession. Lloyd George’s government fell. Bonar Law formed a Conservative ministry and went to the country. The party’s election pledge treated the Cabinet Secretariat as a Lloyd George inheritance to be abolished. Wilson records that Bonar Law’s government nevertheless “provisionally” approved Hankey’s Instructions to the Secretary. Roskill’s second volume opens the Bonar Law chapter as “The Fight for the Cabinet Secretariat”: the office survived, reorganised but intact, under the man who had seemed its most dangerous political master.
Short premiership followed. In January 1923 Bonar Law visited Paris seeking a settlement of German reparations; his proposals broke down, and the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr began on 11 January. Britain adopted a policy of “benevolent neutrality,” refusing to join the occupation. At home, Stanley Baldwin negotiated the funding of the British war debt to the United States. Ill health forced Bonar Law’s resignation in May 1923. Stanley Baldwin succeeded him as Prime Minister. The Annual Register for 1923 closes the brief chapter: from Ruhr and debt settlement to the succession that would shape the rest of the decade.

Place in the machine
Hankey’s diary and Roskill’s narrative place Bonar Law less as innovator of procedure than as the bridge between Coalition and pure Conservative rule. He kept the secretariat that the Carlton Club generation had attacked; he handed the premiership to Baldwin when his strength failed. The wiki’s sources fix him for 1919–23 as Coalition lieutenant, destroyer of that Coalition, and brief first minister under whom the modern Cabinet Office learned that it could outlive its creator.

entities/arthur-henderson.title: Arthur Henderson (1863–1935)
entities/arthur-henderson.content:
Arthur Henderson (1863–1935)
Labour leader and Foreign Secretary · President of the World Disarmament Conference · Principal colleague of MacDonald and Snowden in the first Labour ministries

Labour leadership and the first governments
Hankey’s assessment of the first Labour government of 1924, recorded in Roskill’s second volume, places Arthur Henderson with Ramsay MacDonald and Philip Snowden as the trio by which the permanent officials measured the new administration. Henderson had long been a central figure of the Labour Party—organiser, party secretary, wartime minister under the Coalition—and in 1924 he sat among the principal ministers of MacDonald’s minority. The Annual Register frames that year around MacDonald’s dual role as Premier and Foreign Secretary, Snowden’s Budget, housing and reparations work, and the fall over Campbell and the Zinoviev letter; Henderson’s place in the sources is as one of the experienced Labour hands who made the experiment of office possible.
In the second Labour government of 1929 Henderson took the Foreign Office. The Annual Register for 1929 notes the new spirit of the government: MacDonald’s meeting with General Dawes on Anglo-American relations and naval disarmament, resumption of diplomatic threads, and the programme of an early approach to President Hoover. Henderson’s Foreign Secretaryship ran through the London Naval Conference of 1930 and the first sessions of the Indian Round Table process, with Hankey as Secretary-General of the great conferences. The volume closes on the economic deterioration that would destroy the government in 1931.

1931 and the break with MacDonald
When the May Report and the run on the pound split the Labour Cabinet in August 1931, Henderson stood with the bulk of the party against the economies that MacDonald and Snowden accepted in forming the National Government. He did not follow MacDonald into the National ministry. Thereafter he remained a principal figure of Labour in opposition while MacDonald headed the National Government through the election of October 1931.

Disarmament Conference
Hankey’s third volume places Henderson in the international disarmament machinery of the early 1930s: president of the World Disarmament Conference at Geneva, touring to converse with Hitler and Mussolini, reporting results to Eden, and declaring at moments of crisis his refusal “to contemplate even the” resort to force that the conference was meant to make unnecessary. The conference adjourned without achieving general disarmament; Germany left the League; Henderson’s presidency became a symbol of the effort that the Annual Register and Hankey’s narrative both record as overtaken by rearmament and the revisionist powers.
The wiki’s sources fix Henderson less as continuous domestic premier-maker than as Labour’s organisational and foreign-policy heavyweight of the first two Labour governments and as the public face of Geneva disarmament after 1931—bound, in the Hankey record, to MacDonald and Snowden as the measure of Labour in office, and then to the failure of the Disarmament Conference as Europe rearmed.

entities/cabinet-office.title: Cabinet Office (1916–1945)
entities/cabinet-office.content:
Cabinet Office (1916–1945)
Permanent secretariat to the Cabinet and War Cabinet · Record of ministerial decision · Centre of British high administration from Lloyd George to Churchill

Creation, December 1916
The Cabinet Office was created in December 1916 as the secretarial equipment required to record and notify the decisions of Lloyd George’s small War Cabinet. Its nucleus was the existing staff of the Committee of Imperial Defence, already organised under Maurice Hankey. Before 1917 the Cabinet had been an informal meeting of the Sovereign’s principal ministers without agenda or secretary; the Prime Minister’s letters to the Sovereign had been the sole continuous record. Wilson’s handbook presents the new Office as the answer to that procedural void under the pressure of total war: locked-box circulation of memoranda, an agenda prepared by the Prime Minister through the Secretary, recorded Conclusions, and a web of committees.
Hankey’s Instructions to the Secretary, first circulated in January 1917 and later revised, fixed the working rules. From August 1919 fuller Minutes gave way to Conclusions. Confidential annexes covered matters of special secrecy. A weekly report went to the Sovereign. Document symbols, registered files, and security arrangements turned the Cabinet’s business into an archive—the collection Wilson later ranked among the most valuable single series of modern official sources for British political history, while warning that the papers were made for administration, not for historians.

War Cabinet, 1916–1919, and the Lloyd George peace Cabinet
Under the five-member War Cabinet the Office handled a flood of GT and early CP papers, new wartime ministries (Shipping, Labour, Food, Pensions, National Service, Air), and specialised committees—War Policy, War Priorities, Eastern Committee, Economic Defence and Development, Home Affairs, Demobilisation. It served the Imperial War Cabinet and War Conference and the Peace Conference of 1919. In November 1919 government returned toward a peacetime Cabinet of about twenty members; the Haldane Report on the Machinery of Government framed contemporary debate on how far the wartime machine should survive. Political criticism of the secretariat as Lloyd George’s instrument hardened into a Conservative election pledge in 1922 to abolish it.

Survival and interwar routine, 1922–1939
After the Conservatives’ victory Bonar Law’s government “provisionally” approved the Instructions to the Secretary; the Office lived. Warren Fisher’s Treasury minute addressed the propriety of a permanent secretariat; a five-day rule for circulating memoranda, press communiqués from 1924, anxiety over leakage, and rules on custody of Cabinet papers defined interwar practice. Access rules for the public later moved from a fifty-year toward a thirty-year regime. The committee system grew; subjects of Cabinet business widened; staff changed; physical location moved between 2 Whitehall Gardens and Great George Street. Hankey retired in 1938; Edward Bridges succeeded him as Secretary. Parallel to ordinary Cabinet work, the Office provided the United Kingdom secretariat for imperial and international conferences from the wartime Supreme War Council through Washington, Genoa, Imperial Conferences, the London Naval Conference, Ottawa, and Lausanne.

War again, 1939–1945
Hankey’s 1928 and 1938 papers to the C.I.D. had already set out options for supreme control in a future war. Chamberlain’s nine-member War Cabinet of September 1939 and Churchill’s five-member coalition War Cabinet of May 1940 (with a Caretaker Cabinet in May–July 1945) again made the Office the clerical heart of national direction. Procedure—agenda, memoranda, meetings, minutes, conclusions, confidential annexes—remained recognisable, though Wilson contrasts Chamberlain’s orderly administration with Churchill’s more erratic methods. The committee structure thickened: Defence Committee (Operations), Defence Committee (Supply), Chiefs of Staff Committee (thousands of meetings), Military Co-ordination, Combined Chiefs of Staff, Battle of the Atlantic, Night Air Defence, Tank Parliament, Lord President’s Committee, Import and Production Executives, Manpower, Economic Section, Central Statistical Office, Ministry of Reconstruction. Staff lists for 1945 and statistical tables of meetings form the quantitative skeleton of Wilson’s annexes. The Historical Section, tracing back to Esher’s recommendation under the C.I.D., produced official (and later non-”Official”) military and civil histories under Cabinet Office aegis.

Relation to the C.I.D.
From the start the Cabinet Office and the C.I.D. secretariat were closely joined in persons and method. Hankey held both secretaryships for most of the interwar years. The C.I.D.’s revival after 1918, the ten-year assumption, rearmament after 1935, and the Minister for Co-ordination of Defence (1936) are therefore not separate from the Office’s story but the defence half of the same secretarial world.

entities/committee-of-imperial-defence.title: Committee of Imperial Defence (1902–1939)
entities/committee-of-imperial-defence.content:
Committee of Imperial Defence (1902–1939)
Standing committee of the Prime Minister for imperial and national defence · Home of the War Book and the peacetime defence secretariat · Twin to the Cabinet Office

Origins and Hankey’s secretaryship before 1914
The Committee of Imperial Defence grew from the recognition, after the South African War and the Esher Report of 1904, that defence questions needed systematic attention beyond the informal Cabinet. Under Balfour it became the forum where ministers and service chiefs could plan without the full Cabinet’s day-to-day press of business. Maurice Hankey joined its staff, became Assistant Secretary (1908–1912) under Sir Charles Ottley, and Secretary from 1912. The Ballard–Hankey work on economic pressure against Germany, the invasion debates, and above all the War Book prepared the United Kingdom’s mobilisation for a European war. In July–August 1914 that preparation was put to the test; the C.I.D. staff and method passed into wartime machinery and, in December 1916, into the new Cabinet Office.

War and after: Standing Defence Sub-Committee to full revival
During the First World War the functions of high defence co-ordination were absorbed by War Cabinet and Allied organs; after 1918 the C.I.D. revived, at first through a Standing Defence Sub-Committee (1920–23) that handled the Singapore base, the Washington Conference, and the future of the Royal Air Force. Through the 1920s the full Committee met monthly; early-1930s activity declined before a marked increase after 1935. Hankey remained Secretary of the C.I.D. alongside the Cabinet secretaryship—the personal and institutional link that made the defence machine and the Cabinet machine one secretarial world.

The ten-year assumption and the Singapore problem
Interwar C.I.D. work was shaped by the “ten-year assumption”—the planning rule that no major war need be expected within ten years—and by the hard choices of imperial overstretch: the Singapore naval base, naval treaty renewal after Washington, and the balance among Navy, Army, and Air Force under tight estimates. Roskill’s second volume places Hankey’s “Essentials of Defence” years (1926–29) against the General Strike emergency machinery, the Kellogg–Briand Pact, and his growing anxiety about British unpreparedness. Dominion liaison and Imperial Conference business kept the “imperial” in the Committee’s name alive even as European and Far Eastern threats multiplied.

Rearmament, triple threat, and the Minister for Co-ordination of Defence
From 1933–34, after Hitler’s accession, Hankey as C.I.D. Secretary worked behind the scenes for rearmament against Treasury economy and public disarmament feeling; the Defence Requirements Committee framed early programmes. An Empire tour in the mid-1930s tested dominion capacity. Abyssinia, Mediterranean risk, Rhineland remilitarisation, and the alignment of Germany, Italy, and Japan filled C.I.D. agendas. After 1935 rearmament accelerated; in 1936 a Minister for Co-ordination of Defence (Inskip, later Chatfield) was created to sit above the service departments within the C.I.D. system. Wilson records the rise in meeting frequency and the Committee’s work on grand strategy, organisation for defence planning, and relations with the Dominions through the Imperial Conference of 1937.

End of the peacetime form
Hankey retired from the C.I.D. secretaryship with the Cabinet secretaryship in 1938. On the outbreak of war in 1939 supreme control again shifted into War Cabinet and Chiefs of Staff machinery described in Wilson’s war chapter; the peacetime C.I.D. as a distinct monthly organ of imperial defence planning closed its interwar chapter. Its methods—agenda, papers, sub-committees, permanent secretary—had already been exported to the Cabinet Office and would shape wartime defence committees.

entities/david-lloyd-george.title: David Lloyd George (1863–1945)
entities/david-lloyd-george.content:
David Lloyd George (1863–1945)
Prime Minister of the Coalition, 1916–1922 · Creator of the War Cabinet secretariat · Principal British negotiator of the peace of 1919

From Munitions to the War Cabinet
During the First World War Lloyd George rose from the Ministry of Munitions under Asquith’s first Coalition to the centre of the political crisis of late 1916. Hankey’s diary and Roskill’s first volume place him as the rising force against Asquith’s leadership after the Dardanelles, the Somme, and mounting frustration with the conduct of the war. In December 1916 Asquith fell; Lloyd George formed a small five-member War Cabinet and appointed Maurice Hankey its Secretary. That act created the modern Cabinet Office: agenda, circulated papers, recorded conclusions, and an elaborate committee system (War Policy, War Priorities, Eastern Committee, and the rest). Wilson notes also the “Garden Suburb”—Lloyd George’s personal advisers in temporary buildings—alongside the new wartime ministries of Shipping, Labour, Food, Pensions, National Service, and Air.
Through 1917–18 he directed the war from that machine: the U-boat crisis and convoy, the Imperial War Cabinet, the Supreme War Council, conflict with the soldiers in the spring of 1918, and the final offensives to the Armistice of 11 November 1918. Hankey mediated between Prime Minister and high command; the permanent official’s vantage is the principal continuous witness in this wiki’s sources for Lloyd George’s wartime method.

Peace conference and the conference years
At Paris in 1919 Lloyd George sat with Clemenceau, Wilson, and Orlando as the Council of Four, with Hankey as sole secretary recording their private discussions and the drafting of Versailles. Reparations, war guilt, the Rhineland, and the League filled the months to the signature of 28 June 1919 and the lesser treaties that followed. Returning to London, he oversaw the end of the War Cabinet and the return toward a peacetime Cabinet of about twenty, while Hankey fought to keep the secretariat that critics already branded as Lloyd George’s personal instrument.
The early 1920s were the era of conferences—San Remo, Hythe, Boulogne, Spa, Lympne, London on reparations, Genoa—of which Hankey was often Secretary-General. At home stood Ireland: the Government of Ireland Act, the Anglo-Irish War, the negotiations that produced the Treaty of December 1921, and the subsequent Irish Civil War recorded in the Annual Register. Abroad, the Washington Naval Conference limited capital ships; Genoa collapsed into the Russo-German Treaty of Rapallo. Economic difficulty and unemployment pressed at home even as the Coalition clung to power.

Chanak and the fall, 1922
In September 1922 Turkish nationalist forces under Mustafa Kemal pressed toward the British position at Chanak after the burning of Smyrna. The Cabinet contemplated war; Dominion and domestic protest rose; the Convention of Mudania averted fighting. Unionist discontent, long simmering against Coalition rule, came to a head at the Carlton Club meeting of 19 October 1922: Conservative MPs voted to fight the next election as an independent party. Austen Chamberlain had defended the Coalition; Bonar Law led the secession. Lloyd George’s government fell. Hankey’s record of the Cabinet deliberations and his assessment of the fall close the Coalition chapter in Roskill’s second volume.
The Conservative election pledge to abolish the Cabinet Secretariat treated that office as a Lloyd George inheritance. Bonar Law’s government nevertheless “provisionally” kept Hankey’s Instructions; the machine outlived its creator’s premiership.

After office
In opposition and on the Liberal wing Lloyd George remained a public force—critic of foreign policy, author of schemes for unemployment (noted in the Register’s 1929 campaign coverage)—but he never returned to the premiership. The wiki’s sources for 1919–45 fix him chiefly as wartime and Coalition premier, peace negotiator, and the political father of the permanent Cabinet secretariat rather than as a continuous interwar minister.

entities/george-orwell.title: George Orwell (1903–1950)
entities/george-orwell.content:
George Orwell (1903–1950)
Author of The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) · Reportage of industrial England · Critic of class and of Socialist presentation

Self-description and class position
In The Road to Wigan Pier Orwell described himself as born into the lower-upper-middle class—the layer of society between roughly £300 and £2,000 a year, his own family near the bottom. Before the Great War that class still felt sure of itself: one was either a gentleman or not, and traditions were military, official, and professional rather than commercial. At incomes as low as four hundred a year gentility was almost purely theoretical. He treated his own position as typical enough of the sub-caste to have symptomatic importance for the class question.
He was educated into public-school snobbery and served in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma, where he came to feel himself part of the machinery of despotism and developed an “indescribable loathing” of the whole machinery of so-called justice. After return to England he deliberately went among the destitute: a common lodging-house as a kind of baptism; tramping with an Irish tramp on the northern outskirts of London; months in common lodging-houses from choice or necessity. He later described much of that experience in Down and Out in Paris and London, rearranging but not inventing the incidents. Among tramps the class-bar seemed for a moment to be down; he later insisted that tramps were no more typical of the working class than literary intellectuals of the bourgeoisie, and that intimacy with ordinary respectable working people remained extremely hard.

The road from Mandalay to Wigan
He first became aware of unemployment as a close problem in 1928, after Burma, where unemployment had been only a word. What then horrified him was that many unemployed men were ashamed. By the mid-1930s he went to the coal areas of Lancashire and Yorkshire partly to see mass-unemployment at its worst and the most typical section of the English working class at close quarters—necessary, he said, as part of his approach to Socialism, before one could decide whether present conditions were tolerable and take up a definite attitude on class. Part One of The Road to Wigan Pier recorded lodging-houses, the coal face, housing, the Means Test and the dole, diet, coal-picking, and the industrial landscape; Part Two turned that experience into autobiography of class and a critique of English Socialism’s presentation.
He admired the men of the National Unemployed Workers’ Movement who kept the organisation going on pennies from the unemployed themselves, and he treated Wigan as typical enough of the industrial and mining districts—more than one person in three of the whole population living on the dole, a core of miners continuously unemployed for seven years. He did not present himself as a proletarian convert who had simply “solved” class by goodwill. He remained explicit about middle-class codes of taste and smell, about the difficulty of class-breaking, and about the political need to win the sinking middle class—schoolmasters, free-lance journalists, clerks, bankrupt drapers—before Fascism played its trump card.

Socialism as argued in 1936–37
Writing while Spanish Fascist forces bombarded Madrid, he held that Socialism was common sense yet was visibly going back before Fascism. He argued as advocatus diaboli against the form in which Socialism was offered: middle-class confinement of the theory, the prevalence of cranks, Marxist jargon and heresy-hunting, the cult of the machine and of Russian industrial showpieces. He wanted less “class consciousness” jargon and more justice, liberty, and the plight of the unemployed; the two facts that the interests of all exploited people were the same and that Socialism was compatible with common decency. Without an effective Socialist party of revolutionary intentions and sufficient numbers, England risked a slimy Anglicised Fascism. With such a party, the widely separate classes who would form it might, after struggle, feel differently about one another—and the sinking middle class might sink into the working class with nothing to lose but their aitches.
The book was issued by the Left Book Club in 1937; Victor Gollancz’s unease with Part Two is part of the publication history of the source, not of Orwell’s self-account within the text itself.

entities/left-book-club.title: Left Book Club
entities/left-book-club.content:
Left Book Club
Victor Gollancz subscription series · Issuer of The Road to Wigan Pier (1937)

Relation to this source
The Road to Wigan Pier was published in 1937 by Victor Gollancz Ltd and issued to members of the Left Book Club. The Club was a subscription scheme that distributed left-wing books at low prices to a mass membership, binding reportage and argument to a defined political public. Orwell’s book—Part One on industrial poverty, Part Two on class and the obstacles to English Socialism—thus entered circulation not only as a commercial monograph but as a Club selection aimed at readers already leaning toward Socialism or anti-Fascism.
The text of the book itself does not narrate the Club’s internal history. What the source supplies is the political moment into which the Club published: Socialism losing ground before Fascism; Madrid under bombardment as Orwell wrote; the need, in his view, for propaganda that spoke of justice, liberty, and the unemployed rather than of fruit-juice cranks and Russian dams. The Club’s audience was precisely the middle-class and white-collar public whose capture or loss Orwell treated as decisive—the same public that might, if mishandled on class, stampede toward an Anglicised Fascism rather than toward a league of the oppressed.
For this knowledge base the Left Book Club therefore stands as the organisational channel of the Wigan Pier source: the means by which a lower-upper-middle-class writer’s report from Wigan and his advocatus diaboli critique of Socialist presentation were put into thousands of left-leaning hands in 1937.

entities/maurice-hankey.title: Maurice Hankey (1877–1963)
entities/maurice-hankey.content:
Maurice Hankey (1877–1963)
Secretary of the Committee of Imperial Defence and of the Cabinet · Architect of the modern Cabinet secretariat · Later peer and wartime minister

Formation and the Committee of Imperial Defence
Maurice Hankey was born in 1877 into a family tradition of public service; childhood in Adelaide and Brighton and schooling at Rugby preceded entry to the Royal Marine Artillery. Service in the Mediterranean Fleet and work in the Naval Intelligence Department brought him into strategic planning. Under Balfour’s Committee of Imperial Defence he moved from staff officer to Assistant Secretary (1908–1912) under Sir Charles Ottley, then succeeded Ottley as Secretary of the C.I.D. (1912–1914). In those years he helped develop the War Book and imperial defence planning, and built the small permanent staff that would later become the nucleus of the Cabinet Office.

War Cabinet Secretary, 1916–1918
With the outbreak of war the C.I.D. machinery was mobilised; Hankey became the standing channel between services and ministers through Asquith’s first Coalition, the Dardanelles disaster, Jutland, and the growing crisis of 1916. When Lloyd George’s War Cabinet replaced the Asquith coalition in December 1916, Hankey became its Secretary. He introduced the secretariat system—agenda control, circulation of papers, and recorded conclusions—that transformed an informal body of ministers into a machine capable of running total war. He was present at the great strategic debates of 1917–18: convoy, Imperial War Cabinet, Supreme War Council, manpower, and the final offensives leading to the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

Peace, conferences, and the fight for the Secretariat, 1919–1931
After the Armistice Hankey served the British delegation at the Paris Peace Conference, including as sole secretary to the Council of Four during the drafting of Versailles. He then fought to preserve the peacetime Cabinet Secretariat against critics who saw it as Lloyd George’s personal instrument. As Secretary to the Cabinet, to the C.I.D., and as Clerk of the Privy Council, he became Secretary-General of a long chain of international and imperial conferences—San Remo, Lympne, Washington naval limitation, Genoa, Locarno-era work, and the machinery of dominion relations. He recorded the Chanak crisis and the fall of Lloyd George (October 1922), survived Bonar Law’s provisional confirmation of the Secretary’s Instructions despite the Conservatives’ election pledge to abolish the secretariat, and adjusted to Baldwin and then to the first Labour government under MacDonald. Through the General Strike emergency machinery, the Ten-Year Rule debates, Singapore, and the second Labour government, he remained the permanent official at the centre. Volume II of Roskill’s biography closes on the financial crisis of August–September 1931: the collapse of Labour, the National Government, departure from gold, and Hankey’s diary of that turning point.

Rearmament, retirement, and wartime minister, 1931–1942
After 1931 he managed National Government business while, as C.I.D. Secretary, pressing the case for rearmament against economy and disarmament opinion—the Defence Requirements Committee, the fight after Hitler’s rise, the Empire defence tour of the mid-1930s, Abyssinia and the Mediterranean, the multiplication of German, Italian, and Japanese threats, and the Imperial Conference of 1937. He retired as Cabinet Secretary and C.I.D. Secretary in 1938; Edward Bridges succeeded him; Hankey was raised to the peerage as Baron Hankey of The Chart. Outside office he observed Munich and the last months of peace. On the outbreak of war in September 1939 Chamberlain brought him into the War Cabinet as Minister without Portfolio. When Churchill formed the small coalition War Cabinet in May 1940, Hankey was kept as a minister outside that five-member body (Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, later Paymaster-General), then further sidelined, and finally dismissed in 1942 after policy and personal friction with Churchill. He continued as a constructive critic on shipping, convoy, and post-war questions until 1945, and lived as writer and elder statesman until his death in 1963.

Place in the machinery
Wilson’s handbook on the Cabinet Office treats Hankey’s January 1917 Instructions to the Secretary, the locked-box circulation of memoranda, Conclusions in place of full Minutes after August 1919, the weekly report to the Sovereign, and the long dual secretaryship of Cabinet and C.I.D. as the formative practice of the Office. Hankey’s career is thus inseparable from the institutions he staffed: the Committee of Imperial Defence before 1914 and after 1918, and the Cabinet Office from December 1916 to 1938.

entities/national-unemployed-workers-mov.title: National Unemployed Workers' Movement
entities/national-unemployed-workers-mov.content:
National Unemployed Workers’ Movement
N.U.W.M. · Revolutionary organisation of the unemployed · Built from the pennies of the unemployed themselves

Character and aims
In The Road to Wigan Pier Orwell judged that by far the best work for the unemployed was being done by the National Unemployed Workers’ Movement. He described it as a revolutionary organisation intended to hold the unemployed together, stop them blacklegging during strikes, and give them legal advice against the Means Test. It had been built out of nothing by the pennies and efforts of the unemployed themselves—not by external philanthropy or official occupational schemes.

Practice in the industrial towns
Orwell had seen a good deal of the N.U.W.M. and greatly admired the men, ragged and underfed like the rest, who kept the organisation going. Still more he admired their tact and patience: it was not easy to coax even a penny-a-week subscription out of people on the Public Assistance Committee. He linked that success to a wider English working-class talent for organisation—visible in the trade-union movement and in the excellent working-men’s clubs of Yorkshire, “really a sort of glorified cooperative pub”—even while he held that the English working class showed less capacity for leadership.
In many towns the N.U.W.M. had shelters and arranged speeches by Communist speakers. Even at those shelters, however, the men who went there often did nothing but sit round the stove and occasionally play dominoes. Orwell’s constructive wish was that the movement might be combined with something along the lines of the occupational centres—boot-mending, furniture-making for the home—without the “nasty Y.M.C.A. atmosphere” of official or semi-official schemes that Socialists denounced as devices to keep the unemployed quiet and less likely to read the Daily Worker. The N.U.W.M. stood, in his account, for solidarity and legal defence under the Means Test; the occupational centres stood for activity that risked demobilising political anger. He wanted both skill used and political organisation kept alive, in a world where several million men might never have a real job again unless another war broke out.

entities/neville-chamberlain.title: Neville Chamberlain (1869–1940)
entities/neville-chamberlain.content:
Neville Chamberlain (1869–1940)
Chancellor of the Exchequer under the National Government · Prime Minister, 1937–1940 · Architect of the Munich settlement · Head of the nine-member War Cabinet, September 1939–May 1940

From health and local government to the Exchequer
Neville Chamberlain entered the first rank of national politics in the interwar Conservative and National ministries. Hankey’s third volume and the Annual Register place him at the Exchequer after the crisis of 1931: when the National Government, returned with an overwhelming majority in October, enlarged the Cabinet under MacDonald, Chamberlain took the Treasury from Snowden (who moved to the Privy Seal). The Register for 1931 records the first steps in protection—the Abnormal Importations Bill, horticultural duties, the Needs Test—and the path to Ottawa. In 1932 Chamberlain went with Baldwin to the Imperial Economic Conference; the bilateral agreements granting imperial preference split the Free Trade ministers from the Cabinet and confirmed Chamberlain as the fiscal driver of the National Government’s tariff turn.
Through the mid-1930s he presented Budgets under MacDonald and then Baldwin, while Hankey as C.I.D. Secretary pressed rearmament against Treasury economy. Roskill records Chamberlain’s dominance in Cabinet on arms and embargo questions, his correspondence with Hankey on defence requirements, and the tension between the Treasury’s desire for economy and the services’ needs after Hitler’s accession and the Defence Requirements Committee reports. The Register for 1935 notes his Budget in the year of Stresa, the Silver Jubilee, and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement.

Premiership, 1937–1939
Baldwin retired after the Coronation of 1937; Chamberlain succeeded as Prime Minister. The Annual Register for 1937 records the Ministers of the Crown Bill, the Coronation, the Imperial Conference, and the National Defence Contribution—a graduated tax on business profits that alarmed the City and had to be revised. Foreign policy defined the premiership. In February 1938 a fundamental difference over policy toward Italy led to the resignation of Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden; Chamberlain overrode him and opened conversations with Mussolini; Lord Halifax succeeded at the Foreign Office. The Anglo-Italian Agreement of 16 April was conditional on a settlement in Spain.
The central crisis of 1938 was Czechoslovakia. Lord Runciman’s mediation mission to Prague failed to reconcile the Sudeten Germans and the Czechoslovak Government. As German military pressure intensified, Chamberlain made three flights to Germany—Berchtesgaden (15 September), Godesberg (22 September), and Munich (29 September)—where Hitler, Mussolini, Daladier, and Chamberlain agreed to the cession of the Sudetenland. An Anglo-German Declaration was signed. Duff Cooper resigned as First Lord of the Admiralty in protest. Parliament debated the settlement amid deep division; Labour moved censure, but the Government won a large majority. Hankey, by then retired from the secretaryship and elevated to the peerage, observed the last months of peace from outside and later re-entered government under Chamberlain.

End of appeasement and war
In March 1939 Germany occupied the rump Czecho-Slovak state and established the Protectorate of Bohemia-Moravia. The Annual Register for 1939 records Britain’s reaction: abandonment of the Munich line, peacetime conscription, and guarantees to Poland (31 March, formalised 6 April), then to Greece, Romania, and Turkey. Anglo-French negotiations with the Soviet Union for a military alliance proved fruitless; the Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August cleared the way for Germany’s invasion of Poland on 1 September. Britain declared war on 3 September.
Wilson describes Chamberlain’s nine-member War Cabinet of September 1939 and contrasts its orderly administration with Churchill’s later methods. Hankey returned as Minister without Portfolio in that War Cabinet, with responsibilities including petrol rationing, the Ministry of Information, and coordination of home-front and economic-warfare matters through the “Phoney War.” After the Norwegian campaign of spring 1940, Chamberlain’s position collapsed; on 10 May Winston Churchill formed a five-member coalition War Cabinet. Chamberlain remained briefly in the new structure before leaving office; he died later in 1940.
The wiki’s sources fix him as National Government Chancellor of protection and Ottawa, Baldwin’s successor, the Premier of Eden’s resignation and the three flights to Germany, and the first wartime Prime Minister of the nine-member War Cabinet—bound in Hankey and Wilson to the machinery of Cabinet and C.I.D. as much as to diplomacy.
