sources/annual-register-1926.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1926
sources/annual-register-1926.content:
The Annual Register 1926
Part I — English History
Chapter I — THE ECONOMY CAMPAIGN
The political and economic situation was dominated by the Government’s economy campaign. Departmental economies were pressed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Mr. Churchill and the Premier spoke on the need for economy. The Italian debt settlement was concluded, with Sir A. Chamberlain and Signor Mussolini reaching agreement. Negotiations with Turkey proceeded. Evidence of widespread industrial distress was presented. A Trade Union Bill was proposed. Sir Alfred Mond called for industrial peace. The Coal Commission under Sir Herbert Samuel began its inquiry into the mining industry. The Budget reduced expenditure and taxation. Unemployment remained high. The Government prepared emergency measures for a possible coal stoppage.
The Soviet Union’s trade relations with Britain remained tense.
Chapter II — THE GENERAL STRIKE
The Samuel Coal Commission reported in March, recommending wage reductions and reorganisation but rejecting the owners’ demands for longer hours and larger cuts. The Government, owners, and miners assumed entrenched positions. Negotiations between the owners and the Miners’ Federation broke down. The Trade Union Congress supported the miners. The Government declared a state of emergency. On May 1 the owners locked out the miners. On May 3 the TUC called a General Strike in support of the miners. Essential services were maintained by volunteers and the military. The Government used the BBC and the British Gazette to communicate its position. After nine days, on May 12, the TUC called off the General Strike unconditionally, having achieved nothing. The miners remained on strike.
The Strike was the most serious industrial confrontation in British history, involving three million workers.
Chapter III — THE COAL STOPPAGE
The coal stoppage continued after the collapse of the General Strike. The Premier made new proposals for a settlement. Both the owners and the miners rejected them. The Government decided to stand firm. Peace moves emerged among the miners, but the executive held out. The French Minister of Finance visited London for debt talks. The Budget was debated, and the second reading of the Electricity Bill proceeded. Emergency regulations remained in force. The King appealed for peace in the mining industry. The coal dispute caused severe hardship in mining districts, with Poor Law authorities providing relief. The Samuel Committee’s proposals were revived but failed to bridge the gap.
The Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Bill was foreshadowed by the Government.
Chapter IV — THE RETURN TO WORK
The miners’ leaders interviewed Mr. Churchill. Mr. Cook, the miners’ secretary, advised against surrender but the rank and file began to drift back. Emergency regulations were renewed. Labour leaders met the miners’ executive to urge a settlement. A Commons debate on the coal situation was held. Mr. Lloyd George appealed to Mr. Churchill to intervene. Mr. Churchill replied, defending the Government’s position. The miners decided to return to work on the owners’ terms, having been starved into submission. The stoppage ended after seven months in December. The Coal Bill was introduced, implementing the Government’s own mining policy. The Trade Disputes Bill was promised for the next session.
The year’s events permanently weakened the trade union movement.
Chapter V — END OF THE COAL STOPPAGE
Parliament reassembled after the summer recess. The Electricity Bill received its third reading. The Government and the BBC faced questions on political impartiality. Lord Cecil spoke on disarmament. A grant for rural housing was approved. A supplementary vote for poor relief in mining areas was passed. The resumed coal negotiations finally produced a settlement on the owners’ terms. The miners’ conference accepted the terms by a narrow majority. The year’s industrial struggles left deep scars. The Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Bill was introduced, making general strikes illegal and restricting trade union political funds. The Bill aroused intense opposition from Labour.
The Imperial Conference defined Dominion status in the Balfour Report.
Foreign and Imperial History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
Germany admitted to the League as a permanent Council member; the League’s seventh Assembly; the work of the Preparatory Commission for the Disarmament Conference; the Sino-Belgian treaty dispute.
Chapter II — Ireland
The Irish Free State under Cosgrave: the Army mutiny settled; the passage of the Electoral Amendment Act; the continuing work of the Boundary Commission and the final border agreement.
Chapter III — France and Italy
France’s financial crisis and the Poincaré government’s return to stabilise the franc; Italy’s Fascist regime: the consolidation of the corporate state, the suppression of opposition, and the pacification of Libya.
Chapter IV — Germany and Austria
Stresemann’s continued diplomacy under Locarno, the Berlin Treaty with the USSR; Germany’s entry into the League; the referendum on expropriating the former ruling houses; Austria’s economic improvement and the continuing Pan-German debate.
Chapter V — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
Stalin’s decisive move against Trotsky and the Zinoviev-Kamenev opposition; Soviet industrialisation planning; Poland’s Pilsudski coup in May; Czecho-Slovakia’s political stability; Rumania’s land reform; Yugoslavia’s centralisation; Greece’s republican consolidation under Pangalos then Kondylis.
Chapter VI — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium’s language legislation and Flemish-Walloon tensions; Dutch colonial governance; Switzerland’s League participation; Spain’s Primo de Rivera dictatorship continuing; Portugal’s financial recovery; Scandinavia’s social democratic governance and the Nordic Labour Congress.
Chapter VII — The Middle East and India
The Syrian rebellion crushed by the French; Iraq’s treaty with Britain and the end of the mandate; Palestine under increasing Arab-Jewish tension; India’s Simon Commission announced, causing widespread Indian protest; the Bengal criminal law continuing.
Chapter VIII — The Far East: China – Japan
The Northern Expedition launched by Chiang Kai-shek, the Kuomintang-CCP split deepening; the Canton and Shanghai uprisings; Japan’s Shōwa era beginning with Emperor Hirohito’s accession; Japanese economic expansion.
Chapter IX — The United States and Latin America
The US prosperity peak; the passage of the Revenue Act; the Kellogg-Briand Pact proposed; Mexico’s Cristero War; Brazil’s continued political transition; the Pan-American Conference in Havana.
Chronicle of Events in 1926
A day-by-day chronology of the principal political, diplomatic, military, industrial, and social events of the year, arranged by month. Covers domestic British developments and major international occurrences, including cabinet changes, parliamentary debates, strikes, treaties, elections, and notable public occasions.

sources/annual-register-1927.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1927
sources/annual-register-1927.content:
The Annual Register 1927
Part I — English History
Chapter I — PEACE IN INDUSTRY
The industrial atmosphere improved after the traumatic events of 1926. Export trade in 1926 had been severely affected by the strikes. The Trade Unions faced financial difficulty and declining membership. A return to normal conditions was the Government’s watchword. The public strongly favoured peace in industry. Opposing forces within the labour movement — between the TUC leadership and the left wing — became more apparent. Party cleavages hardened, and the Liberal Party continued its decline. Anti-British outbreaks in China, particularly in Hankow and Shanghai, raised foreign policy questions. The Government announced the dispatch of troops to Shanghai to protect British interests.
The Budget reduced income tax and addressed the deficit.
Chapter II — THE TRADE UNION BILL
The Budget was introduced by Mr. Churchill, showing a deficit carried over from 1926. The effects of the previous year’s strikes were evident in the public finances. The Budget analysis showed reduced revenue and increased unemployment costs. The sinking fund was reduced. Mr. Churchill’s Budget speech was a major political event. The Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Bill was debated intensely, making general strikes illegal, restricting picketing, and requiring trade union members to ‘contract in’ for political levies. The Bill passed and became law. Votes for women at 21 was debated, and the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill was introduced. The I.L.P. opposed the Government’s trade union policy.
Sir Austen Chamberlain pursued the Locarno policy in Europe.
Chapter III — THE GENEVA NAVAL CONFERENCE
The Government and disarmament dominated the summer. The Geneva Naval Conference opened in June, bringing together Britain, the United States, Japan, France, and Italy to limit naval armaments. British proposals for cruiser limitation clashed with American demands for parity. The Conference broke down in August without agreement, the British and American positions on cruisers proving irreconcilable. Mr. Bridgeman, the First Lord of the Admiralty, defended the British position. The American reply was published. Sir A. Chamberlain made a statement in the Commons. Meanwhile, the British position in China was regularised through the Chen-O’Malley agreement. The Government announced the appointment of the Simon Commission on Indian constitutional reform.
The Naval Conference failure marked a setback for Anglo-American relations.
Chapter IV — CLOSE OF THE SESSION
The Government’s position remained strong as the session closed. The programme included the rating and valuation proposals. The announcement of the Indian Statutory Commission under Sir John Simon was made, with Labour refusing to serve. The amendment of the Indian Reforms Act was debated. Lord Birkenhead made a statement on India. Commons debate followed, with Labour opposing the Commission’s exclusively British composition. The Prime Minister defended the Government’s record. The session’s legislation included the Trade Disputes Act, the Rating and Valuation Act, and the Cinematograph Films Act. Mr. Churchill’s Budget surplus was announced. Unemployment remained over one million. The Dominion status issue was clarified by the Imperial Conference decisions of 1926.
The year ended with the Government secure and the Labour Party reorganising.
Foreign and Imperial History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League’s eighth Assembly; the failure of the Preparatory Commission for the Disarmament Conference; the Polish-Lithuanian dispute over Vilna; the work of the Mandates Commission on the Middle East.
Chapter II — Ireland
The Irish Free State’s continued consolidation: the Electricity Supply Board established; the Shannon hydroelectric scheme; the assassination of Kevin O’Higgins; the Electoral Amendment Act and the continuing political dominance of Cumann na nGaedheal.
Chapter III — France and Italy
France’s currency stabilisation under Poincaré; the franc stabilised de facto; Italy under Mussolini: the Charter of Labour enacted, the corporate state’s institutions established, the Lateran Treaty preliminary negotiations.
Chapter IV — Germany and Austria
Germany’s continued integration into the League, the economic boom under the Dawes Plan; the Thälmann leadership of the Communist Party; Austria’s political crisis, the Schattendorf incident and the July revolt in Vienna.
Chapter V — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
Stalin’s triumph over the Left Opposition, Trotsky and Zinoviev expelled from the Party; the crash of Soviet grain procurement and the beginnings of forced collectivisation; Pilsudski’s Poland consolidating; the Little Entente’s military convention; Balkan stability.
Chapter VI — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium’s Flemish-Walloon equilibrium; Dutch colonial policy and the rise of Indonesian nationalism; Spain under Primo de Rivera; Portugal’s financial stability; Scandinavia’s social democratic governance and Nordic solidarity.
Chapter VII — The Middle East and India
Iraq’s full independence treaty; Syria’s pacification under the French mandate; the Wailing Wall dispute in Palestine; India’s Simon Commission boycott and the development of the All-India Congress campaign; the appointment of the Butler Committee on Indian princely states.
Chapter VIII — The Far East: China – Japan
The Kuomintang’s Shanghai massacre of Communists; the Northern Expedition continuing; the establishment of the Nationalist government in Nanking; Japan’s first Shōwa financial crisis; the Japanese expedition to Shantung.
Chapter IX — The United States and Latin America
US Coolidge prosperity continuing; the execution of Sacco and Vanzetti; the Kellogg-Briand Pact signed; Mexico’s Cristero War continuing; US intervention in Nicaragua; the Pan-American Conference.
Chronicle of Events in 1927
A day-by-day chronology of the principal political, diplomatic, military, industrial, and social events of the year, arranged by month. Covers domestic British developments and major international occurrences, including cabinet changes, parliamentary debates, strikes, treaties, elections, and notable public occasions.

sources/annual-register-1928.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1928
sources/annual-register-1928.content:
The Annual Register 1928
Part I — English History
Chapter I — THE STATE OF INDUSTRY
The year opened with the disastrous London flood on January 7, when the Thames burst its banks, drowning fourteen people and causing extensive damage. The 1927 trade balance showed modest improvement. The Mond Conference — a series of meetings between leading employers and trade union leaders — held its inaugural meeting, marking a new spirit of cooperation in industry. Committees were formed to examine industrial reorganisation. The Lancashire cotton industry held its first conference on rationalisation. The Government published a memorandum on security and arbitration. Lord Cecil criticised the Government’s disarmament policy. Ministerial speeches addressed unemployment and the need for industrial efficiency. The Budget discussion began.
The Anglo-French naval compromise was initiated in preliminary discussions.
Chapter II — THE BUDGET AND THE RELIEF OF INDUSTRY
A surplus for the year was announced. The death penalty in the army was debated. The Women’s Franchise Bill — the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill — was carried, giving women the vote on equal terms with men at 21. Lord Birkenhead and the press were in controversy. The Premier visited the South Wales coalfield. Mr. Churchill’s Budget introduced the de-rating scheme, relieving industry and agriculture of three-quarters of local rates. The scheme’s reception was mixed, with Labour criticising it as a gift to property. The Budget reduced income tax and the tea duty. The Local Government Bill was announced, aimed at reforming the rating system and reorganising local authority areas.
The Franchise Bill added five million women to the electorate.
Chapter III — THE ANGLO-FRENCH NAVAL COMPROMISE
Sir A. Chamberlain fell ill. The unemployed were recruited for the Canadian harvest. A settlement with China was reached on tariff autonomy. A Commission on Police Powers was appointed. Air manoeuvres were held. The Premier appealed to employers to increase production. New rating valuation lists were published. The Trades Union Congress debated the Mond-Turner talks. The Anglo-French naval compromise was negotiated, proposing to limit cruisers and submarines. The agreement provoked strong American protests, as it appeared to favour the European naval powers. The Government defended the proposal in Parliament. The Simon Commission arrived in India. The Kellogg Pact renouncing war was signed in Paris.
The compromise damaged Anglo-American relations.
Chapter IV — THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL
Parliament reassembled. The King’s Speech announced the Local Government Bill and the de-rating scheme. Mr. MacDonald criticised the Government’s proposals. The Premier replied, defending the reforms. Private members’ time was restricted. The Lords debated the Address. A Labour amendment on unemployment was defeated. Mr. Churchill outlined the Government’s plans. The Local Government Bill passed, abolishing the Poor Law unions, reorganising county and county borough administration, and introducing block grants. The Bill was the most significant reform of local government since 1888. The Representation of the People Bill received Royal Assent, making women eligible to sit in the House of Lords. The year closed with a general election expected in 1929.
The Government’s majority remained secure, but industrial depression persisted.
Foreign and Imperial History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League’s ninth Assembly; the signature of the Kellogg-Briand Pact (Pact of Paris) renouncing war; the continuing Preparatory Commission for the Disarmament Conference; the Greco-Bulgarian dispute settled.
Chapter II — Ireland
The Irish Free State’s seventh year: the Juries Protection Bill; the appointment of the Tariff Commission; the continuing dominance of the Cosgrave government; Northern Ireland’s stability under Lord Craigavon.
Chapter III — France and Italy
France’s financial stability under Poincaré, the Law of 1928 stabilising the franc de jure; Italy’s corporate state fully established, the Grand Council becoming a constitutional organ, the Italian population increase campaign.
Chapter IV — Germany and Austria
Germany’s economic expansion, the Reichstag election of 1928 with Social Democratic gains; the building of the first pocket battleship; Austria’s political polarisation between Christian Socials and Social Democrats; the Heimwehr movement’s rise.
Chapter V — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
Stalin’s First Five-Year Plan launched, the grain crisis leading to forced requisitioning and dekulakisation beginning; the Shakhty show trial; Poland’s authoritarian consolidation; the Little Entente’s continuing diplomatic co-operation; Balkan stability; Turkey’s secular reforms accelerating.
Chapter VI — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium’s language policy and the Flemish University question at Ghent; Dutch colonial governance and the Indonesian nationalist trials; Spain under Primo de Rivera; Portugal’s Estado Novo beginning; Scandinavia’s social legislation and the Nordic economic agreement.
Chapter VII — The Middle East and India
Iraq’s full independence under the new treaty; the Syrian constituent assembly; increasing Arab-Jewish tension in Palestine; India’s Simon Commission boycotted, the Nehru Report proposing Dominion status, the All-Parties Conference.
Chapter VIII — The Far East: China – Japan
The Kuomintang’s Northern Expedition reaching Peking, the Nationalist government recognised by the US; the Chinese Eastern Railway dispute; Japan’s Shōwa depression and the Yamagata-Aritomo influence; the assassination of Chang Tso-lin in the Huanggutun incident.
Chapter IX — The United States and Latin America
US presidential election: Hoover’s victory; the Kellogg-Briand Pact ratified; the US stock market boom; Mexico’s Obregón re-election and assassination; continuing US intervention in Nicaragua; the Pan-American Conference.
Chronicle of Events in 1928
A day-by-day chronology of the principal political, diplomatic, military, industrial, and social events of the year, arranged by month. Covers domestic British developments and major international occurrences, including cabinet changes, parliamentary debates, strikes, treaties, elections, and notable public occasions.
Retrospect of Literature, Science, and Art in 1928
A survey of the year’s contributions to literature (including notable books, poetry, and essays), the biological and physical sciences, art exhibitions and movements, drama and theatre, cinema, and music. Written by specialist contributors including W. T. Whitley (Art), Ernest Kuhe (Drama), Robin H. Legge (Music), and W. B. Brierley (Biological Sciences).
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1928
Short biographical notices of notable British and foreign figures who died during the year, including statesmen, soldiers, writers, scientists, artists, and public benefactors. The notices are drawn principally from The Times obituary columns.

sources/annual-register-1929.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1929
sources/annual-register-1929.content:
The Annual Register 1929
Part I — English History
Chapter I — PREPARATIONS FOR THE GENERAL ELECTION
The Government and the question of dissolution dominated the opening months. The economic outlook was gloomy, with unemployment rising above 1.4 million. The King made a slow recovery from a serious illness. ‘Rationalisation’ was the watchword in trade and industry, particularly in coal, iron and steel. The iron and steel industry pressed for safeguarding duties. Farmers demanded protection against the ‘dumping’ of German wheat. Changes in the Local Government Bill were introduced. The Budget continued de-rating. The Simon Commission visited India. Mr. Baldwin’s Government prepared for a general election on the slogan of ‘Safety First’. The Liberal Party, reunited under Lloyd George, published ‘We Can Conquer Unemployment’, a bold programme of public works.
The election was fixed for May 30.
Chapter II — THE BUDGET AND THE GENERAL ELECTION
The BBC allowed party leaders to broadcast. The Liberal position strengthened, with Sir H. Samuel touring the country. The Budget: Mr. Churchill delivered his fifth Budget, a personal apologia reviewing the financial results of his tenure and forecasting a balanced position. Criticism of Mr. Lloyd George’s unemployment scheme featured in the Budget debate. The election campaign began. The Conservatives campaigned on the record of the Baldwin Government; Labour promised socialism and peace; the Liberals offered a constructive programme of national development. The result on May 30 was a hung Parliament: Labour 287, Conservatives 260, Liberals 59. Mr. Baldwin resigned. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald formed his second Labour Government, again a minority administration dependent on Liberal support.
The election saw the first use of the equal franchise with the ‘flapper vote’.
Chapter III — LABOUR IN OFFICE
A new spirit pervaded the Government. Mr. MacDonald met General Dawes to discuss Anglo-American relations and disarmament. Both made statements on naval disarmament. Labour’s victory celebration was held. Liberal and Conservative attitudes to the new Government were initially cautious. The election of the Speaker proceeded. Mr. Jowitt’s by-election at Preston was contested. The Government announced its programme: an early meeting with President Hoover on disarmament, resumption of diplomatic relations with Russia, the Coal Mines Bill, the Agricultural Land (Utilisation) Bill, and the Development (Loan Guarantees and Grants) Bill to implement unemployment relief. Mr. Snowden’s Budget reduced taxation and removed the McKenna Duties.
Mr. MacDonald visited President Hoover at Rapidan Camp, securing agreement in principle on naval limitation.
Chapter IV — LABOUR’S ‘FIRST INSTALMENTS’
The programme of the session unfolded. The liquidation of ex-enemy property was debated. The Government addressed wheat ‘dumping’. Coast erosion was discussed. The Widows’, Orphans’ and Old Age Contributory Pensions Bill was passed, extending pensions to seven million more people. The Prime Minister returned from his American visit. Unemployment relief works were announced under the Development Act. The Government’s Coal Mines Bill proposed a seven-and-a-half-hour day, a national marketing scheme, and the establishment of a Mine National Council. Acceptance by the Lords was secured after a constitutional confrontation. The Agricultural Land (Utilisation) Bill promoted smallholdings. The London Naval Conference was prepared for 1930. The year ended with the Labour Government established but facing rising unemployment.
The Government restored diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League’s tenth Assembly; the continuing Preparatory Commission for the Disarmament Conference; the settlement of the Bulgarian-Greek reparations dispute; the Optional Clause of the Permanent Court signed by many Powers.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France’s Poincaré government ending, Briand continuing foreign policy; the evacuation of the Rhineland agreed; Italy’s Concordat with the Vatican: the Lateran Treaty signed in February establishing Vatican City sovereignty.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
The Young Plan negotiated to replace the Dawes Plan, reducing total reparations; Germany’s acceptance of the new schedule; the Reichstag ratification debate and nationalist opposition; Austria’s Heimwehr radicalisation and the continuing political polarisation.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
Stalin’s consolidation of absolute power: Trotsky exiled, the First Five-Year Plan in full force, forced collectivisation and dekulakisation intensifying; the Polish-Lithuanian dispute; the Little Entente; Yugoslavia’s King Alexander’s dictatorship established in January; Turkey’s continuing secularisation under Kemal.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium’s Flemish-Walloon cultural compromise; the Dutch East Indies’ nationalist movement; Spain’s Primo de Rivera dictatorship ending, the fall of the dictator; Portugal’s Salazar stabilisation; Scandinavia’s social democratic progress and the Nordic economic conference.
Chapter VI — The Middle East and India
The Palestine mandate continuing: the 1929 Wailing Wall riots, the Hebron massacre, and the British Shaw Commission investigation; Iraq’s independence consolidated; India: Lord Irwin’s Declaration (the Irwin Declaration) proposing Dominion status, the Congress Lahore session demanding Purna Swaraj.
Chapter VII — The Far East: China – Japan
The Kuomintang’s Northern Expedition complete, the Nanking government recognised internationally; the Sino-Soviet conflict over the Chinese Eastern Railway; Japan’s Hamaguchi government and the Gold Embargo decision; the Wall Street Crash’s impact on Japan.
Chapter VIII — The United States and Latin America
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 and the beginning of the Great Depression; President Hoover’s initial responses; the Kellogg-Briand Pact in effect; Mexico’s Maximato period under Calles; the end of US intervention in Nicaragua.
Chronicle of Events in 1929
A day-by-day chronology of the principal political, diplomatic, military, industrial, and social events of the year, arranged by month. Covers domestic British developments and major international occurrences, including cabinet changes, parliamentary debates, strikes, treaties, elections, and notable public occasions.
Retrospect of Literature, Science, and Art in 1929
A survey of the year’s contributions to literature (including notable books, poetry, and essays), the biological and physical sciences, art exhibitions and movements, drama and theatre, cinema, and music. Written by specialist contributors including W. T. Whitley (Art), Ernest Kuhe (Drama), Robin H. Legge (Music), and W. B. Brierley (Biological Sciences).
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1929
Short biographical notices of notable British and foreign figures who died during the year, including statesmen, soldiers, writers, scientists, artists, and public benefactors. The notices are drawn principally from The Times obituary columns.

sources/annual-register-1930.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1930
sources/annual-register-1930.content:
The Annual Register 1930
Part I — English History
Chapter I — THE COAL BILL AND THE NAVAL CONFERENCE
The close of the 1929 session had left the Labour Government in a precarious position, its fate bound up with the Coal Bill. The attack on the second reading had been warded off but the measure’s future remained uncertain. Meanwhile the London Naval Conference opened in January, with the Government seeking an agreement on cruiser ratios, culminating in the London Naval Treaty of April 22. The chapter covers the parliamentary struggle over the Coal Bill, the course of the naval negotiations, Lord Grey’s attack on Mr. Lloyd George, the state of trade, and Mr. Thomas’s attempts to secure bank credit for industry.
Chapter II — THE NEW TAXATION
The accounts for 1929-30 showed a deficit of £14.5 million. Mr. Snowden’s Budget of April 14 raised income tax to 4s 6d and increased surtax and estate duties, provoking strong criticism from Mr. Churchill and Mr. Lloyd George. The chapter covers the Budget debate, the Coal Bill’s passage through the House of Lords after a three-party compromise on hours and quotas, the Consumers’ Council Bill, the Commercial Agreement with Soviet Russia, and the I.L.P. conference.
Chapter III — FISCAL POLICY AND THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE
The parliamentary recess saw speeches by Mr. Baldwin and Mr. Neville Chamberlain attacking Lord Beaverbrook’s ‘Empire Free Trade’ policy. The Imperial Conference opened in October, dominated by economic questions: imperial preference, the Ottawa system, and the depression in trade. The chapter covers Conservative fiscal policy, the Free Trade Manifesto, the T.U.C. Congress, the Bishops and Birth Control debate, the Mandates Commission report on Palestine, and the collapse of the Naval Treaty negotiations between Britain, the US, and France.
Chapter IV — THE LABOUR-LIBERAL CONTACT
Parliament reassembled on October 28 with a crowded programme. The Conservative vote of censure, the deepening internal split in the Liberal Party, the publication of the Liberal Memorandum on Unemployment, and the help extended to the iron and shipbuilding industries are covered. The King’s Speech included measures on education, factories, and transport. Sir Oswald Mosley’s resignation from the Government, the Liberal-Labour tension over electoral reform, and the Wreck of the R101 airship in October dominate the closing months of the year.
The Empire
Chapter I — IRELAND
Northern Ireland’s Parliament opened in March; the legislative programme included the Unemployment Insurance Bill and the Education Bill. The Irish Free State faced economic difficulties and continued political consolidation under the Cosgrave Government.
Chapter II — CANADA
The year’s two outstanding events were the General Election, which reversed political trends when R. B. Bennett’s Conservatives defeated Mackenzie King’s Liberals, and the Western wheat marketing crisis, which overshadowed the economic situation throughout the year.
Chapter III — THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
South Africa was less affected than many countries by the world depression, though the collapse of the diamond and wool markets caused concern. The Native Economic Commission and the continuing operation of the mandate over South-West Africa were prominent.
Chapter IV — AUSTRALASIA
Australia faced severe economic perplexities, with falling export prices and rising unemployment. The Labour Government under Mr. Scullin struggled with the depression. New Zealand also experienced economic contraction and industrial unrest.
Chapter V — INDIA
The year was momentous: the civil disobedience movement organised by the National Congress led to widespread tumult and dislocation of trade. In June the Report of the Statutory Commission (the Simon Report) was published, recommending constitutional reforms. The Round Table Conference opened in London in November.
Foreign History
Chapter I — THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS
The tenth anniversary of the League’s foundation gave rise to a realisation of remarkable progress, but a far less confident spirit prevailed as the year went on. The Preparatory Commission for the Disarmament Conference continued its work; the Permanent Mandates Commission dealt with Palestine and Iraq; the economic depression cast its shadow over the League’s activities.
Chapter II — FRANCE AND ITALY
France participated in the Second Hague Conference on reparations and the London Naval Conference. The Briand Memorandum for a European Federal Union was circulated. In Italy, Mussolini’s Fascist regime consolidated further, with the corporative state taking shape and the Lateran Treaty ratified.
Chapter III — GERMANY AND AUSTRIA
The Müller coalition government fell over the question of unemployment insurance contributions. Chancellor Brüning took office in March, governing by emergency decree. The Young Plan was ratified by the Reichstag. In Austria, political polarisation continued with the Heimwehr movement gaining strength and the Creditanstalt crisis looming.
Chapter IV — SOVIET RUSSIA AND EASTERN EUROPE
Stalin’s First Five-Year Plan continued at full intensity, with forced collectivisation and rapid industrialisation. The trial of the ‘Industrial Party’ in Moscow signalled a new wave of purges. Poland and Romania maintained their anti-Soviet alliance; the Little Entente continued; Yugoslavia under King Alexander’s dictatorship faced Croat opposition; Turkey under Kemal advanced secularisation; Greece and Bulgaria remained unsettled.
Chapter V — LESSER STATES OF WESTERN AND NORTHERN EUROPE
Belgium faced internal tension over the language question. The Netherlands contended with economic depression and the nationalist movement in the Dutch East Indies. Spain’s Primo de Rivera dictatorship ended and the Berenguer government prepared for elections. Switzerland, the Scandinavian states, and Finland experienced varying degrees of economic difficulty.
Chapter VI — THE MIDDLE EAST
Persia under Reza Shah continued modernisation. Afghanistan stabilised after the civil war. Iraq’s treaty relationship with Britain was renegotiated. Palestine saw the continuing aftermath of the 1929 riots and the Hope Simpson Report on land settlement. Syria remained under French mandate.
Chapter VII — THE FAR EAST
China continued under the Nanking Government of Chiang Kai-shek, contending with northern secessionists, the Kuominchun, and Communist insurgency. Japan felt the impact of the world depression, and the Hamaguchi Government struggled to maintain liberal policies. The Dutch East Indies experienced nationalist agitation.
Chapter VIII — MOROCCO AND EGYPT
France took energetic steps to establish security in south-eastern Morocco near Bu Denib. Egypt continued under parliamentary government, with the Anglo-Egyptian treaty negotiations stalled and the Wafd Party in opposition.
Chapter IX — AMERICA
The year was marked by complete prostration of business and widespread unemployment in the United States, as the Great Depression deepened. President Hoover’s efforts to revive confidence included the Smoot-Hawley Tariff (enacted June 17), which provoked international retaliation. Latin American states including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico all suffered severely from collapsing commodity prices.
Chronicle of Events in 1930
A day-by-day chronology of the principal political, diplomatic, military, industrial, and social events of the year, arranged by month. Covers domestic British developments and major international occurrences, including cabinet changes, parliamentary debates, the London Naval Conference, the R101 airship disaster, elections, treaties, and notable public occasions.
Retrospect of Literature, Science, and Art in 1930
A survey of the year’s contributions to literature (including notable books, poetry, and essays), art (by W. T. Whitley), drama (by Ernest Kuhe), the cinema (by Monica Ewer), music (by Ernest Kuhe), the biological sciences (by W. B. Brierley), and the physical sciences. Written by specialist contributors.
Public Documents
The texts of important state papers and official documents of 1930, including treaties, declarations, and diplomatic correspondence relating to the London Naval Treaty, the Imperial Conference, and other significant international engagements.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1930
Short biographical notices of notable British and foreign figures who died during the year, including statesmen, soldiers, writers, scientists, artists, and public benefactors. The notices are drawn principally from The Times obituary columns.

sources/annual-register-1931.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1931
sources/annual-register-1931.content:
The Annual Register 1931
Part I — English History
Chapter I — INDUSTRIAL UNREST AND PARTY DISAFFECTION
The year opened inauspiciously with serious Labour disputes: nearly 150,000 South Wales miners struck on January 1, followed by a lock-out of 200,000 Lancashire weavers in the ‘more-looms-per-weaver’ dispute. The parliamentary session was overshadowed by the Economy Campaign, the India Round Table Conference, and the slow disintegration of the Government’s parliamentary position. The chapter covers the industrial troubles, the Education Bill, debate on India, Mr. Churchill’s secession over the India policy, the Electoral Reform Bill, the Agricultural Marketing Bill, the Lords and Russian timber imports, and the growing uneasiness within the Labour-Liberal coalition.
Chapter II — THE BUDGET AND THE LAND TAXES
When Parliament reassembled after Easter, political circles spoke of an impending crisis. Mr. Snowden’s Budget of April 27 raised no new direct taxation but introduced controversial proposals for land valuation and taxation. The chapter covers the Government and housing question, the Town and Country Planning Bill, the Budget debate and criticism, the Liberal demand for electoral reform, the Plural Voting Bill, the growing demand for tariff protection, the Macmillan Report on Finance and Industry, the campaign for Free Trade, and the first political crisis of the summer.
Chapter III — THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND THE CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT
The publication of the May Report on national expenditure precipitated a financial crisis. The Bank of England was in distress, and the Labour Cabinet split over economy proposals. On August 24 Mr. MacDonald resigned, but immediately formed a ‘National’ Government with Conservative and Liberal support. The chapter covers the collapse of the Labour Government, the formation of the National Government, the Bank of England’s difficulties, President Hoover’s moratorium on war debts, the German financial crisis, the emergency Budget borrowing of £50 million, the departure from the gold standard on September 21, and the General Election of October 27.
Chapter IV — FIRST STEPS IN PROTECTION
The National Government, returned with 554 supporters against 52 Labour and 56 Independent Liberals, moved decisively towards fiscal protection. The chapter covers the enlargement of the Cabinet under Mr. MacDonald, Mr. Neville Chamberlain at the Exchequer, the Abnormal Importations Bill and the first protective orders, the Horticultural Imports Bill, the Statute of Westminster debates, the Ottawa Conference agreement, the introduction of the ‘Needs Test’ for unemployment relief, the India Round Table Conference, the Burma Round-Table Conference, the suspension of work on the Cunard liner, and the appointment of Indian constitutional committees.
Imperial History
Chapter I — IRELAND
The outstanding event in Northern Ireland was the repercussion of an attempt by the Irish Republican Army to suppress an Orange meeting in County Cavan, leading to serious anti-Catholic riots in Armagh, Lisburn, Portadown, and Belfast in August, with sixty to seventy persons injured. The year also saw the destruction by fire of the steamer Bermuda while in dock at Belfast. In the Irish Free State, Mr. de Valera campaigned against the Oath of Allegiance and the land annuities, while the Dáil and Senate continued normal business.
Chapter II — CANADA
Although the world economic depression was felt throughout the Dominion, Canada’s banking institutions remained sound. The grave wheat situation in the Prairie Provinces caused anxiety. Mr. Bennett, the Prime Minister, visited Washington to confer with President Hoover on the St. Lawrence waterways and cross-border restrictions. The Imperial Conference in London, the Unemployment Relief Acts, and the deepening crisis in wheat exports dominated the year.
Chapter III — THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA — SOUTH-WEST PROTECTORATE — SOUTHERN RHODESIA — NORTHERN RHODESIA
South Africa entered 1931 with a degree of optimism, but gradually felt the world slump in commodity prices. The Parliament opened by the Governor-General, the Earl of Clarendon, in January. The Customs Agreement, the Imperial Conference discussions, and the continuing mandate over South-West Africa were prominent. The Native Economic Commission and the Copperbelt developments in Northern Rhodesia were also covered.
Chapter IV — AUSTRALASIA
The history of Australia in 1931 was markedly like that of Great Britain: both faced drastic curtailment of imports and urgent cutting of national expenditure. The year opened with a Labour Government in power and closed with a National Coalition Government after an exciting General Election. New Zealand experienced the same pattern of deflation, falling incomes, and political upheaval, with industrial disturbances and the collapse of export prices for wool and dairy produce.
Chapter V — INDIA
India suffered a full measure of the world’s financial and economic ills, together with internal unrest. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March brought a cessation of civil disobedience and enabled Gandhi to attend the second session of the Round Table Conference in London. The chapter covers the first session of the Round Table Conference closing in January, the release of Congress leaders, the Delhi Pact, the second session of the Round Table Conference in September, the appointment of the Federal Structure Committee, and the threatened renewal of civil disobedience under Lord Willingdon’s Government.
Foreign History
Chapter I — THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS
Few human institutions were sorry to part company with 1931, the most perplexing year since the Great War. The League’s activities were overshadowed by the world-wide economic and financial crisis. The chapter covers the League’s attention to the financial troubles of individual states, the work of the Economic and Financial Organisation, the Disarmament Conference preparations, the problem of the Sino-Japanese dispute, and the League’s efforts to maintain peace in the face of the deepening international crisis.
Chapter II — FRANCE AND ITALY
French politics were dominated throughout the year by Pierre Laval, who introduced a firmer policy. The Steeg Cabinet fell in January; subsequent ministries struggled with the economic crisis, the German reparations question, and Franco-American differences. The chapter covers the Hoover Moratorium and its reception in Paris, the visit of the German Chancellor Brüning, and Franco-Italian relations. Italy under Mussolini consolidated the corporative state, with the Grand Council assuming greater importance in the constitutional structure.
Chapter III — GERMANY AND AUSTRIA
The effects of the world economic crisis were felt in Germany with especial severity. The Brüning Cabinet ruled increasingly by emergency decree as the National Socialist Party grew in strength. The Austrian Creditanstalt collapsed in May, triggering a financial crisis across Central Europe. The chapter covers the German emergency decrees, the Hoover Moratorium, the proposed Austro-German Customs Union, the banking crisis, and the deepening depression that created fertile ground for political extremism.
Chapter IV — SOVIET RUSSIA — ESTONIA — LATVIA — LITHUANIA — POLAND — DANZIG — CZECHOSLOVAKIA — HUNGARY — RUMANIA — YUGOSLAVIA — TURKEY — GREECE — BULGARIA — ALBANIA
Stalin’s position grew stronger, with all energies concentrated on the Five-Year Plan. Stalin warned against the perils of too-hasty accomplishment, while economic progress in industry was undeniable. Eastern Europe was gripped by the agricultural depression, with falling prices affecting Poland, the Balkan states, and the Baltic republics. Yugoslavia continued under King Alexander’s dictatorship. Turkey consolidated the Kemalist reforms. Greece and Bulgaria remained in economic difficulty.
Chapter V — LESSER STATES OF WESTERN AND NORTHERN EUROPE: BELGIUM — NETHERLANDS — SWITZERLAND — SPAIN — PORTUGAL — DENMARK — SWEDEN — NORWAY — FINLAND
Belgian politics were dominated by the question of national defence and military credits for fortifications. The Netherlands contended with economic depression and colonial questions. Spain was the scene of the most dramatic change: the fall of the monarchy, the flight of King Alfonso XIII in April, and the establishment of the Second Spanish Republic. Switzerland, the Scandinavian countries, and Finland all experienced the effects of the world economic crisis.
Chapter VI — THE MIDDLE EAST: PERSIA — AFGHANISTAN — IRAQ — PALESTINE — SYRIA — ARABIA
Persia was free from internal rebellion for the first time since the Shah’s accession, with Sartip Khan surrendering in March. A Bill compelled foreigners owning agricultural land to sell it within three months. Iraq’s treaty relationship with Britain was renegotiated. Palestine faced continued tension between Arab and Jewish communities. Syria remained under French mandate. Afghanistan stabilised under King Nadir Shah.
Chapter VII — THE FAR EAST: CHINA — JAPAN — THE DUTCH EAST INDIES
A cleavage appeared between the sections led by Chiang Kai-shek and Hu Han-min. The People’s Convention in May adopted a provisional Constitution. The most momentous event was the Mukden Incident of September 18, when Japanese forces seized Mukden, initiating the conquest of Manchuria. Japan’s Government came under military dominance. The League of Nations was unable to halt the aggression. The Dutch East Indies experienced nationalist agitation and economic difficulties.
Chapter VIII — MOROCCO AND EGYPT
Military operations on a considerable scale were carried out by the French in the Middle Atlas to keep nomad tribes in check. The Budget for Morocco showed an increase. In Egypt, the Sidqi Government continued in power, with the Wafd in opposition. Anglo-Egyptian negotiations made no progress. The Egyptian Parliament was prorogued and a new electoral law was introduced, restricting the franchise and strengthening executive control.
Chapter IX — AMERICA: THE UNITED STATES — ARGENTINA — BOLIVIA — BRAZIL — CHILE — MEXICO — PERU — OTHER AMERICAN STATES
Colonel Ayres described 1931 as marking the trough of a depression paralleled only twice in American history. The United States experienced unprecedented unemployment, bank failures, and the collapse of commodity prices. President Hoover struggled to revive confidence. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff’s effects deepened the crisis. In Latin America, the fall in raw material prices caused severe economic and political instability, with revolutions in several states.
Chronicle of Events in 1931
A day-by-day chronology of the principal political, diplomatic, military, industrial, and social events of the year, arranged by month. Covers domestic British developments and major international occurrences, including the Indian Round Table Conference, the Spanish Revolution (April 14), the German financial crisis, the Hoover Moratorium (June 20), the departure from the gold standard (September 21), the British General Election (October 27), and the Sino-Japanese conflict in Manchuria.
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1931
A survey of the year’s contributions to literature (including the death of Arnold Bennett and the notable books of the year), art (featuring the Persian Exhibition at Burlington House, by W. T. Whitley), drama (highlighting Noël Coward’s ‘Cavalcade’ at Drury Lane, by Ernest Kuhe), the cinema (the rapid expansion of sound cinemas, by Monica Ewer), music (by Ernest Kuhe), the biological sciences (including the discovery of Peking man artefacts, by W. B. Brierley), and the physical sciences (the centenary of the British Association and the commemoration of Faraday’s discoveries).
Finance and Commerce in 1931
The most tumultuous economic crisis the modern world had witnessed. The breakdown followed the collapse of the Austrian Creditanstalt, the German banking crisis, and the suspension of the gold standard in Britain. The chapter covers the Hoover Moratorium, the abandonment of free trade, the rise of protectionist tariffs, the decline in world commodity prices, the shrinkage of shipping and shipbuilding, the crisis in the cotton and coal trades, the fall in Bank Rate from 4½ to 2½ per cent after leaving gold, and the general paralysis of commercial confidence.
Law in 1931
Except for the repercussions of the political upheaval, the year was comparatively uneventful in the legal world. The constitutional Statute of Westminster was the outstanding piece of legislation. In case law there was an unusually large number of decisions on the interpretation of the Finance Acts and the Rating and Valuation Acts. The chapter also covers the decisions of the House of Lords and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Public Documents
The text of the Constitution of the Spanish Republic (December 9, 1931), together with other significant official documents of the year, including treaties, diplomatic correspondence, and the final communiqués of the Imperial Conference and the Indian Round Table Conference.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1931
Short biographical notices of notable British and foreign figures who died during the year. A selection includes: Thomas Edison (inventor), Arnold Bennett (novelist), Arthur Wing Pinero (dramatist), Vachel Lindsay (poet), Lord Glenavy (Lord Chancellor of Ireland), John Redmond’s brother William Redmond (Nationalist MP), Sir William Mitchell Ramsay (historian), and many other figures from the worlds of science, literature, law, politics, and public affairs. The notices are drawn principally from The Times obituary columns.
Sources

sources/annual-register-1932.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1932
sources/annual-register-1932.content:
The Annual Register for 1932
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The General Tariff
The year opened with the supreme question of whether the national accounts would balance by March 31; the Budget of October 1931, balanced on paper, depended heavily on income-tax revenue. The public’s extraordinary response to an appeal for prompt tax payments averted a feared collapse of the currency. The Government introduced its General Tariff, with the Import Duties Bill imposing a general ad valorem duty of 10 per cent. on foreign manufactured goods, marking Britain’s historic break with free trade. The Bill passed after fierce debate, with the Liberal ministers — Sir Herbert Samuel and his colleagues — deeply divided, ultimately adopting an “agreement to differ” that allowed them to remain in the National Government while opposing protection.
Chapter II — The Budget and the Conversion Loan
Parliament resumed after Easter with the Wheat Bill’s passage and continued debates on the means test and transitional payments for the unemployed. On April 19, the Chancellor presented a Budget that increased the standard rate of income tax to 5s. in the pound and raised surtax, while the House debated the new tariff scheme. The great event of the chapter was the launching of the Conversion Loan — the conversion of £2,000,000,000 of 5 per cent. War Loan to 3½ per cent. — which succeeded beyond expectation, with 92 per cent. of holders accepting the terms, saving the Exchequer over £23,000,000 annually. Relations with Ireland deteriorated sharply over the oath and land annuities, with Mr. de Valera’s government withholding payments.
Chapter III — The Ottawa Agreements
The British delegation, led by Mr. Baldwin and Mr. Chamberlain, departed for the Imperial Economic Conference at Ottawa in July. The Conference produced a series of bilateral trade agreements granting帝国 preferences, with Britain agreeing to maintain or impose duties on foreign foodstuffs in exchange for preferential treatment from the Dominions. The agreements split the Cabinet: the Free Trade ministers — Sir Herbert Samuel, Sir Archibald Sinclair, and Lord Snowden — resigned rather than accept the protectionist policy, while Mr. MacDonald remained as Prime Minister of a reconstructed National Government. The Ottawa Agreements Bill passed through Parliament, formally committing Britain to a new direction in imperial trade policy.
Chapter IV — The American Debt Payment
As winter approached, the vast army of unemployed faced deepening hardship, with protests against the means test culminating in the “Hunger March” and outbreaks of violence. The Government introduced supplementary estimates for unemployment and debated relief for farmers hit by the sharp decline in agricultural prices. The chapter centres on the war debt question: with the Hoover Moratorium expiring, Britain made a $95,000,000 payment to the United States — described as a “transfer” rather than a “payment” — after an acrimonious exchange of notes. The payment was made on December 15, but the episode left Anglo-American relations strained and the principle of debt revision unresolved.
Imperial History
Chapter I — Ireland
The outstanding event was the opening of the new Parliament Buildings at Stormont, Belfast, by the Prince of Wales on November 16. Northern Ireland passed several industrial Bills but faced growing nationalist protests; Nationalist members walked out of the House of Commons in May over restrictions on debating Imperial questions. In the Irish Free State, Mr. de Valera’s government pursued its constitutional course, withholding the land annuities and removing the oath of allegiance, deepening the rift with Britain.
Chapter II — Canada
The Bennett Conservative Administration opened its third session in February, with the Governor-General’s Speech emphasising rigid economy despite universal economic disturbance. Canada’s trade balance held favourable, and a National Service Loan was oversubscribed. The Ottawa Conference loomed large in Canadian calculations, with the government seeking secure markets for its wheat, timber, and other primary products. Canada’s departure from the gold standard in the spring created a new currency alignment with sterling.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa
The Union Government found itself increasingly embarrassed by the economic crisis, with General Smuts warning of the alternatives of “gold bankruptcy or sterling.” The year was dominated by the decision to abandon the gold standard in December, following Australia and New Zealand. To counteract the effects of exchange depreciation, the government increased export subsidies for agricultural products. The debate over gold versus sterling became entangled with racial politics, as moderates of both white races despaired at the intensification of national ambitions amidst general financial distress.
Chapter IV — Australasia
In Australia, a National Coalition under Mr. Lyons took office following the decisive defeat of Mr. Scullin at the December 1931 election, and was responsible for the Commonwealth’s representation at Ottawa. The chapter details Australia’s tariff negotiations with Britain and the resignation of two ministers — Mr. Fenton and Mr. Hawker — over disagreements on trade and expenditure policy. New Zealand faced similar economic pressures, with falling export prices for wool and dairy products forcing stringent economies.
Chapter V — India
Persistence was the keynote of 1932: persistence of the third civil disobedience campaign renewed by Congress at the beginning of the year, and persistence of the Government in pushing forward constitutional reform. Mr. Gandhi was arrested in January under a Bombay Regulation of 1827, and the Congress Working Committee was declared an unlawful association. Despite the unrest, the Round Table Conference process continued, with the Communal Award published in August, granting separate electorates to minorities, and the third session of the Round Table Conference meeting in London in November.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The year 1932 became the annus terribilis for the League, as the economic blizzard intensified and international trade declined to less than half its 1929 volume. The League’s Disarmament Conference opened in Geneva in February but made little progress, overshadowed by the deepening depression and the rise of nationalist economic policies. The Lytton Commission’s report on the Manchurian crisis was published in October, condemning Japan’s actions but failing to produce effective international action.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France faced the triple problems of reparations, debts, and disarmament. The death of M. Maginot in January led to a Cabinet reconstruction under M. Laval, with M. Tardieu succeeding to the War Ministry. The chapter covers France’s strained budgetary position, the Lausanne Conference on reparations, and the growing political instability. Italy under Mussolini maintained its fascist corporative system, with the economy strained by the world slump and the government’s emphasis on autarky and public works.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
The most significant feature of Germany’s internal history was the spread of political extremism: Hitler’s National Socialists became by far the largest single party. President von Hindenburg was re-elected in the spring after a bitter contest against Hitler, but a rapid succession of Chancellors — Brüning, von Papen, and von Schleicher — weakened the authority of the State. The July elections gave the Nazis 230 seats, but Hindenburg refused to appoint Hitler as Chancellor. The Lausanne Conference effectively ended German reparations. Austria struggled with the aftermath of the Creditanstalt collapse and growing Nazi agitation.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
The Soviet Five-Year Plan made indifferent progress: oil, electric, and machine-building industries were ahead of schedule, but coal, steel, and pig-iron were considerably behindhand, and transport remained unsatisfactory. A second Five-Year Plan was launched amidst increasing qualitative defects in production. The chapter covers the economies of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Rumania, Yugoslavia, Turkey, Greece, and the Baltic states, all grappling with the depression and the collapse of agricultural prices.
Chapter V — Western and Northern Europe
Financial anxieties weighed heavily on Belgium, whose franc weathered a serious crisis but faced a budget deficit of a milliard francs. The chapter follows the economic difficulties of the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain (under its new republican constitution), Portugal, and the Scandinavian states — Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Finland — all of which experienced severe trade contraction and rising unemployment.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
The chapter covers Persia’s frontier rectification with Turkey, the state visit of King Feisal of Iraq to Teheran, ongoing developments in Palestine under the British Mandate (including Jewish immigration and Arab opposition), French administration in Syria, and the consolidation of Ibn Saud’s position in Arabia.
Chapter VII — The Far East
The year was notable for Japan’s deepening involvement in Manchuria following the Mukden Incident of 1931, and the Shanghai hostilities of January–March, in which Japanese forces bombarded the Chinese city. The League’s Lytton Report, while condemning Japan, failed to halt its advance. China experienced somewhat greater political stability under Chiang Kai-shek, who returned to power, but the civilian government remained feeble against military despotism.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
French operations in the High Atlas were crowned with success, the Tafilet oases being occupied in January. In Egypt, the Wafd government under Sidky Pasha continued to grapple with economic difficulties, while the question of Anglo-Egyptian relations — particularly the status of the Sudan and the Capitulations — remained unresolved.
Chapter IX — America
The “economic blizzard” continued at hurricane force through the first half of 1932. Wholesale prices fell to their lowest levels since 1908; wheat touched 41½ cents a bushel — below the tariff. Unemployment was estimated at over 12,000,000. The presidential election in November resulted in a landslide victory for Franklin D. Roosevelt over President Hoover. The chapter also covers the Chaco War between Bolivia and Paraguay and the economic difficulties of Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico.
Part II — Chronicle of Events in 1932
A day-by-day chronicle of notable events throughout the year, covering Britain and the wider world. January opened with the New Year Honours and Princess Mary being granted the title of Princess Royal; the first regular air-mail service between London and Cape Town began on January 20. The year included the opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge in March, the disappearance of Mr. and Mrs. Mollison in April (they were later found safe), and President von Hindenburg’s re-election in April. The “Hunger March” of the unemployed reached London in October, and November saw Roosevelt’s election victory and the opening of the Ottawa buildings.
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1932
Literature: [by J. Isaacs] The year’s notable publications included John Galsworthy winning the Nobel Prize for Literature, Leon Trotsky’s History of the Russian Revolution, and a wide range of historical and biographical works covering Georgian history, Roman Britain, and European social history.
Art: [by W. T. Whitley] The art world saw major exhibitions at the Royal Academy and elsewhere, with continued interest in modern movements as well as traditional British painting.
Drama: [by Ernest Kuhe] The London stage premiered significant new works, with the theatre showing resilience despite economic pressures.
The Cinema: [by Monica Ewer] The film industry continued its expansion, with the advent of talking pictures fully established and British studios producing an increasing number of feature films.
Music: [by Ernest Kuhe] The musical season included notable performances at Covent Garden and the Proms, with both classical and contemporary composers represented.
The Biological Sciences: [by W. B. Brierley] Advances in genetics, biochemistry, and agricultural science were recorded, with continued research into plant and animal breeding.
The Physical Sciences: Key developments in physics and chemistry were noted, building on the foundations of quantum mechanics and nuclear research.
Finance and Commerce in 1932
The world economic crisis became more intense, but exceptional success attended British efforts, and the prestige of Great Britain stood higher than that of any other leading nation at the close of the year. Britain’s departure from the gold standard in September 1931, combined with the new General Tariff, gave British industry an estimated 70 per cent. advantage over gold-standard competitors. The Conversion of the War Loan from 5 to 3½ per cent. saved £23,000,000 annually. The visible adverse balance of trade was drastically reduced, and there was a marked increase in factory building. The chapter covers the Ottawa Agreements’ financial provisions, the Exchange Equalisation Account, and the continuing difficulty of international debt settlement.
Law in 1932
The year saw important reports from the Gregory Committee on Unemployment Insurance (recommending reconstitution on bona fide insurance lines) and the Rent Restriction Committee. The Committee on Departmental Powers reviewed the delegation of legislative authority, recommending a Standing Committee of the House of Commons to scrutinise such delegations. In criminal law, the Persistent Offenders Committee recommended prolonged detention for habitual criminals. Notable legal cases included the protracted disputes arising from the means test administration and the constitutional questions surrounding the “agreement to differ” in the National Government.
Public Documents
Three major documents are reproduced: (I) The Imperial Economic Conference at Ottawa — Summary of Conclusions, covering the bilateral trade agreements, Empire content requirements, and monetary policy resolutions; (II) The British Note to the United States Government relating to the War Debt payment of December 1932, setting out Britain’s position that the payment was a “transfer” made under protest; (III) The Non-Aggression Pact between the U.S.S.R. and France, signed in November 1932.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1932
Notable figures who died in 1932 included: Aristide Briand, the former French Premier and Nobel Peace Prize winner; Albert, King of the Belgians (in a climbing accident on February 17); M. Maginot, the French Minister of War; Lord Balfour, the British statesman and author of the Balfour Declaration; M. Doumer, President of France (assassinated); John Galsworthy, the novelist and Nobel laureate; Henry George, the American economist; and Sir William Osler, the renowned physician.

Sources

Epstein, M. (ed.), The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1932, Longmans, Green and Co., London, 1933. New Series.

sources/annual-register-1933.content:
The Annual Register for 1933 (Vol. 175)
Part I — English History
Chapter I — Preparations for the World Economic Conference
As 1933 opened, the National Government under Ramsay MacDonald still commanded an overwhelming majority, having outlived the currency-crisis task for which it was formed. The centre of political interest shifted from internal to external affairs: the American debt settlement, a general adjustment of world economic conditions, and the Disarmament Conference now dominated. Chapter covers trade in 1932, the Totalisator problem, Waterloo Bridge decision, imprisonment of Tom Mann, British disarmament proposals, the Anglo-Persian Oil Company dispute, Kenya native rights, the London Passenger Transport Bill, the White Paper on India, the Anglo-Russian crisis (Metro-Vickers trial), and the Prime Minister’s visit to Washington.
Chapter II — The World Economic Conference
Opens with the Budget speech (April 25), showing a deficit from tariff revenue falling short of estimates, beer revenue at a thirteen-year low, and surtax down 16 million pounds reflecting a great decline in personal incomes. Covers trade pacts with Denmark, Germany, and Argentina; the Road and Rail Traffic Bill; taxation of co-operative societies; the London Police reorganisation; Herr Rosenberg’s visit; the Four-Power Pact initialled; and the World Economic Conference itself — Mr. MacDonald’s address, Mr. Roosevelt’s “bombshell” message that shattered currency stabilisation hopes, the effective failure of the Conference, and the stimulus to group action between nations.
Chapter III — The Disarmament Problem
Covers the summer recess and political calm, with modest trade improvement and falling unemployment. The plight of livestock farmers and the Moyne Committee report on housing. The Empire Marketing Board closed. Trade Union Congress and Labour Party conference debates. Mr. Baldwin on armaments. The growing crisis over Germany’s demands: Sir John Simon’s Geneva speech, the Premier’s appeal to Germany, debates on disarmament in both Houses. The Archbishop of Canterbury’s deputation. The new cruiser programme. Relations with the Irish Free State deteriorate. Liberals decide to go into opposition. Parliament prorogued.
Chapter IV — Trade Improvement
Parliament reassembles in November for its third full session. Sir H. Samuel and about thirty Liberals leave the cross-benches for the Opposition. Conservative backbench revolt against the Government’s Indian policy and growing discontent with its armament policy. The King’s Speech stresses disarmament and the League of Nations. The Unemployment Insurance Bill, slum clearance, and new trade agreements (especially cotton and coal) are the legislative programme. The chapter also covers the Newfoundland crisis and the long-running debate on House of Lords reform.
Imperial History
Chapter I — Ireland
Northern Ireland’s General Election fought on a single issue — the Union or a Republican all-Ireland — returned Lord Craigavon with a fresh mandate. In the Irish Free State, de Valera’s government continued its policy of dismantling the Treaty settlement, including the removal of the oath of allegiance and the withholding of land annuity payments, deepening the Anglo-Irish economic war.
Chapter II — Canada
Canada faced the deepening effects of the Great Depression, with widespread unemployment and provincial relief crises. The Imperial Economic Conference at Ottawa had raised expectations but the benefits were slow to materialise. The Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF) emerged as a new political force advocating social reform.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa
South Africa faced economic pressures from falling export prices and the continued gold standard debate. General Hertzog’s government struggled with the Afrikaner nationalist challenge and the question of South Africa’s relationship with the Crown and Empire.
Chapter IV — Australasia
Australia: The Lyons Ministry reaped the rewards of financial reorganisation — higher wool prices, improved trade balance, a recovery budget with a surplus, and unemployment falling from 30% to 25.7%. New Zealand faced continued economic strain with falling export incomes.
Chapter V — India
The Round Table Conference process continued with the publication of the White Paper on Indian constitutional reform, proposing a federal structure with responsible government at the provincial level. The Joint Select Committee was appointed to examine the proposals in detail, provoking fierce debate in Britain between Conservative imperialists and reform advocates.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
A critical and crowded year for the League. The Disarmament Conference stalled despite the British Plan (MacDonald’s draft convention of March 16). On October 14, Germany announced its withdrawal from both the Disarmament Conference and the League itself, a devastating blow. The League’s prestige was further eroded by the Far East crisis.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France: Four governments in one year, all grappling with a massive budgetary deficit of twelve milliard francs. Disarmament and security remained central — France demanded compensating guarantees for any German rearmament. Italy: Mussolini promoted the Four-Power Pact as a mechanism for Great Power management of European affairs, arousing suspicion among smaller states.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
Germany: The year of Hitler’s assumption of power. The collapse of Schleicher’s chancellorship, the intrigues of Hugenberg and Papen with Hitler, and on January 28 Hindenburg’s decision to appoint Hitler Chancellor. The Reichstag fire, the Enabling Act, the destruction of trade unions and political parties, and the beginnings of systematic anti-Jewish persecution. Austria: The suppression of the Socialist movement and Dollfuss’s authoritarian turn.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
Soviet Russia: A notable change in foreign orientation as the rise of Hitler and Japanese expansion in Manchuria drove Moscow to seek new friendships. Co-operation with France, Poland, and the League increased. The Soviet Union participated fully in the World Economic Conference. Eastern Europe: Poland’s non-aggression pact with Germany alarmed France and the Little Entente. Czechoslovakia, Rumania, and Yugoslavia faced internal strains exacerbated by the Depression. Turkey, Greece, and the Balkan states attempted regional consolidation.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland: Neutral states anxious about the German revival. Spain: The Republic faced growing instability as anarchist and socialist unrest challenged the left-wing government; the elections of November swung the country to the Right. Portugal: Salazar’s Estado Novo consolidated. Scandinavia: Denmark, Sweden, and Norway pursued co-operative trade policies and maintained political stability.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
Persia: Negotiations for a new oil concession following the cancellation of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company agreement. Iraq: The kingdom approached independence from the Mandate, joining the League of Nations in 1932. Palestine: Rising tensions between Jewish immigrants and Arab population under the British Mandate. Syria and Arabia remained quiet but restive under French and British influence.
Chapter VII — The Far East
China and Japan: Japan consolidated its hold on Manchuria, establishing the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Lytton Report’s condemnation was ignored. China struggled with internal Communist-Nationalist conflict. The League’s non-recognition policy had no practical effect. The Netherlands East Indies remained under Dutch control.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
Morocco: French and Spanish zones remained pacified under colonial administration. Egypt: The Wafd government faced economic difficulties and the continued presence of British forces under the 1922 treaty provisions. The Anglo-Egyptian treaty negotiations made no progress.
Chapter IX — America
United States: The year of Roosevelt’s inauguration and the New Deal. The banking crisis of March, the Hundred Days, the National Recovery Administration (NRA), Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA), and the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). Roosevelt’s decision to take the dollar off gold and torpedo the World Economic Conference’s currency stabilisation plans. Latin America: The Chaco War between Bolivia and Paraguay continued; the Good Neighbour policy was inaugurated.
Part II
Chronicle of Events in 1933
Day-by-day record of notable events, including Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor (January 30), the Reichstag fire (February 27), the German General Election and Enabling Act (March), the opening of the World Economic Conference (June), Germany’s withdrawal from the League (October), and Roosevelt’s inauguration (March 4).
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science
Literature: A notable year featuring the publication of H.G. Wells’s The Shape of Things to Come, Vera Brittain’s Testament of Youth, and James Hilton’s Lost Horizon. George Bernard Shaw’s The Adventures of the Black Girl in Her Search for God provoked controversy. Art: The Royal Academy exhibition showed a conservative trend; the modernists gained ground at the Leicester Galleries. Drama: The London stage featured new works by J.B. Priestley and Noël Coward. Cinema: 1933 was a landmark year for British cinema with The Private Life of Henry VIII (starring Charles Laughton) achieving international success. Music: The Proms continued under Sir Henry Wood; contemporary composers faced a divided public. Biological Sciences: Progress in genetics and microbiology. Physical Sciences: Advances in atomic physics and the continuing development of quantum mechanics.
Finance and Commerce in 1933
The year saw continued recovery from the 1931 crisis. The conversion of the War Loan to a lower coupon had strengthened government finances. The Exchange Equalisation Account managed sterling fluctuations. Trade showed modest improvement with unemployment falling from 23% to 18%. The failure of the World Economic Conference was a disappointment, but the Ottawa imperial preference system provided a framework for intra-Empire trade expansion.
Law in 1933
Notable legal developments included judgments on the legality of totalisator clubs, the Married Women’s Disabilities Bill, and the continuing application of the Statute of Westminster. The House of Lords delivered important rulings on landlord and tenant law.
Public Documents
I. Statute of the Little Entente — formalising the alliance between Czechoslovakia, Rumania, and Yugoslavia. II. The Four-Power Pact — signed June 7 by Britain, France, Italy, and Germany, intended to maintain peace. III. The Soviet Pact (London Convention) — defining aggression between the USSR and its neighbours. IV. Monetary and Economic Conference — Final Act of the London World Economic Conference. V. Final Act of the Wheat Conference — an international agreement to regulate wheat production and exports.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1933
Notable deaths included John Galsworthy (Nobel Prize-winning novelist), Lord Curzon (former Viceroy and Foreign Secretary), Sir Edward Grey (the pre-war Foreign Secretary), and Adeline, Lady Asquith (widow of the former Prime Minister).

sources/annual-register-1934.title: Annual Register 1934
sources/annual-register-1934.content:
The Annual Register for 1934
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The Question of Rearmament
The year opened with a confident New Year message from Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, who noted that Britain’s exports had maintained their level despite shrinking world trade and that unemployment was falling. However, two factors forbade complacency: the absence of any revival of world trade and the precarious condition of the Disarmament Conference. The Government’s attention was divided between disarmament negotiations, domestic reforms, and the growing need for rearmament. Mr. Eden was given a new post, Sir J. Simon reported on the Disarmament Conference, and a new German note on armaments prompted a British memorandum. Trade negotiations with France began, Anglo-Japanese textile conversations took place, and the T.U.C. declared against war policy. The Government supported Austrian independence and concluded an Anglo-German debt agreement. An Unemployment Bill was in committee, and the “March of the Unemployed” to London drew parliamentary attention. Anxiety over Fascist movements grew following the Olympia “Blackshirt brutality” incident. The National Government campaign and questions of Cabinet reconstruction featured prominently. Civil, Navy, and Army estimates were presented; slum clearance and overcrowding policy were debated.
Chapter II — The Increase in Air Armament
Parliament reassembled after Easter on April 10, and the Minister of Transport moved the second reading of the new Road Traffic Bill. The Budget was presented by the Chancellor, showing a surplus and its proposed application. The Unemployment Bill reached its concluding discussions. A Cabinet reconstruction took place. The Tithe Bill was introduced and later withdrawn, the Petroleum Bill passed through the Lords, and the Betting Bill was debated. The Iron and Steel industry faced reorganisation, and wage agreements were legislated. The Government responded to Japanese textile competition and the New Zealand tariff offer. A Milk Subsidy was introduced. Lord Salisbury’s House of Lords Bill sparked demands for Lords reform. The Palestine Loan was guaranteed. French notes on “guarantees of execution” and German rearmament prompted Cabinet deliberations, with Signor Suvich visiting London. A British reminder was sent to Japan.
