The Lords debated the Government’s foreign policy. Peace declarations came from the Labour Movement and the Archbishop of Canterbury. The Finance Bill passed, repealing the Land Value Tax. The “Blackshirt brutality” at Olympia was discussed in the Commons. Reports on housing and the Most-Favoured Nation clause were presented. The dispute over Waterloo Bridge continued. An Anglo-French Trade Agreement was finally reached, and Germany suspended debt payments, leading to a British protest and ultimately a clearing agreement.
Chapter III — The India Report
Parliament rose on July 31 for the summer vacation. The period was marked by concern over a sharp increase in motor accidents on the roads, leading to the Minister of Transport issuing new orders. A railway wage agreement was reached. Lancashire’s trade concerns with both Germany and Australia were aired. The Labour Party published a report on Fascism; the Trades Union Congress debated the issue, and Fascist and anti-Fascist demonstrations clashed in Hyde Park. A report on migration policy was issued. The Queen Mary was launched. A threatened coal strike in South Wales was averted. The Liberal Party announced its election decision. The Labour Party Conference showed hostility to Communists, and Sir Stafford Cripps and the Socialist League suffered defeats. The India Report dominated political discussion, with the future of Indian constitutional reform at the centre of the Government’s programme. The Joint Select Committee on India concluded its work, preparing the ground for the Government of India Bill.
Chapter IV — Help for the Depressed Areas
Parliament reassembled for a new session on November 20. The King’s Speech outlined an unusually large programme of legislation, foremost being proposals for the future government of India. Other major measures included Bills for assisting the tramp shipping industry, preventing overcrowding, and promoting recovery in the depressed areas. The Electricity Supply Act of 1926 was to be amended, and steps were taken for the further development of imperial air communications. The Government also announced plans to assist the depressed areas, addressing the persistent unemployment and social distress in regions like South Wales, Lancashire, and the industrial North-East.
The Empire
Ireland
The Parliament of Northern Ireland passed important legislation, with special attention to agricultural interests and the alleviation of unemployment. The Minister of Finance introduced a Budget estimating expenditure of £11,756,000 for the year.
Canada
Canada made steady progress towards recovery from the economic depression, though hampered by a burdensome railway system and the disposal of accumulated grain crops. A severe drought in the West reduced the aggregate yield of crops, but compensation from better prices helped.
The Union of South Africa
The year opened with the prospect of party fusion brightly in the ascendant. Long-standing causes of schism and suspicion were cleared away, and the result, as General Smuts described it, was the birth of a nation.
Australasia
The Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand continued their economic recovery, with trade relations with Britain featuring prominently in political debate.
India
The year 1934 in India was one of recovery, adjustment, and preparation for the great constitutional advance for which legislative proposals were being shaped. Civil disobedience, which had been ebbing since 1933, continued to decline, and the “greater quietude” of the previous year was maintained and advanced.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The year 1934 reflected the alternation of fear, suspense, relief, and hope which characterised the political history of the world. For Europe it was a year of violent shocks and alarms, intensified by bloodshed in many countries, with the ever-present threat that internal unrest might overflow into international anarchy.
Chapter II — France and Italy
In the closing days of December 1933, a financial fraud involving the Municipal Loan Office of Bayonne and an adventurer named Stavisky was discovered. Stavisky’s violent death and the subsequent revelations shook the French Third Republic, leading to the far-right riots of February 6, 1934, the fall of the Daladier government, and the formation of a national unity government under Gaston Doumergue.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
In 1933 the totalitarian state was established in Germany. In 1934 the tensions within the Nazi Party itself became intense, culminating in the Night of the Long Knives (June 30), when Hitler purged the SA leadership including Ernst Röhm. In Austria, Chancellor Dollfuss was assassinated in a failed Nazi coup (July 25), but the putsch collapsed. President Hindenburg died on August 2, and Hitler assumed the powers of the presidency, becoming Führer and Reich Chancellor.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia — Estonia — Latvia — Lithuania — Poland — Danzig — Czechoslovakia — Hungary — Rumania — Yugoslavia — Turkey — Greece — Bulgaria
The Soviet Union pressed forward with its Five-Year Plan and collective farming. The Baltic states consolidated their positions. Poland signed a non-aggression pact with Germany. The Little Entente (Czechoslovakia, Rumania, Yugoslavia) faced growing pressure from revisionist powers. Turkey, Greece, and the Balkan states pursued rapprochement through the Balkan Pact.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Iceland, Sweden, Norway, and Finland each contended with the pressures of economic recovery and the rising tension between the Great Powers. Spain remained under the conservative government of the bienio negro, with increasing polarisation.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
Persia (Iran), Afghanistan, Iraq, Palestine, Syria, and Arabia pursued their separate paths. The Shah of Persia paid a state visit abroad for the first time. Tensions in Palestine between Jewish immigrants and the Arab population continued. Iraq moved towards greater independence from British mandate oversight.
Chapter VII — The Far East
China continued to face Japanese encroachment in Manchuria and north China. Japan consolidated its position in Manchukuo and pushed for greater influence. The Netherlands East Indies remained under Dutch colonial administration.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
In Morocco, the French completed their campaign of pacification in the south. Egypt continued to negotiate with Britain over the terms of its independence and the status of the Suez Canal.
Chapter IX — America
The United States, under President Franklin D. Roosevelt, pushed forward with the New Deal. The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act was passed, and relations with Latin America were shaped by the Good Neighbor Policy. The Chaco War between Bolivia and Paraguay continued. Brazil, Chile, Cuba, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay each faced domestic challenges.
Part II
Chronicle of Events in 1934
A day-by-day record of notable events throughout the year, from January to December.
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science
Literature, Art, Drama, the Cinema, Music, and the Sciences were surveyed. The year saw notable works by H.G. Wells, Winifred Holtby, and others; in science, the discovery of artificial radioactivity by Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie was a landmark.
Public Documents
I. The Baltic Pact — Treaty of Agreement and Collaboration between Lithuania, Estonia, and Latvia (September 12, 1934), establishing co-operation among the three Baltic states.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1934
Included: Jakob Wassermann (novelist), Marie Curie (scientist), King Albert I of the Belgians (killed in a climbing accident), Paul von Hindenburg (German President), Engelbert Dollfuss (Austrian Chancellor), Sir Edward Elgar (composer), Sir James Barrie (playwright), and Kurt von Schleicher (killed in the Night of the Long Knives).

Sources

The Annual Register for 1934, edited by M. Epstein, M.A., Ph.D. Longmans, Green and Co., 1935. OCR text extracted via PyMuPDF from the Internet Archive copy (annualregisterre0000mede).

sources/annual-register-1935.title: Annual Register, 1935
sources/annual-register-1935.content:
The Annual Register for 1935 (Vol. 177)
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The Means Test Muddle and Increased Arms Expenditure
The year opened with the National Government still firmly in power but facing growing discontent over the Means Test and unemployment policy. Mr. Lloyd George launched his “New Deal” proposals at Bangor on January 17, calling for a Statutory Council to prepare reconstruction schemes, but the Government remained cautious. The White Paper on Defence (March) provoked German anger, while conscription was announced in Germany and Britain protested. The civil and military estimates reflected growing rearmament, and a Labour vote of censure over the Means Test was defeated. A new Housing Bill and the Government of India Bill advanced through Parliament.
Chapter II — The Silver Jubilee
The Stresa Conference (April 12) brought Britain, France and Italy together to consider relations with Germany following Hitler’s announcement of conscription. Sir John Simon and Mr. Eden reported on their European tours. The Budget was presented by Neville Chamberlain. The Silver Jubilee of King George V was celebrated with great enthusiasm across the country in May, with loyal addresses and national festivities. The Anglo-German Naval Agreement (June) permitted Germany to build up to 35% of British tonnage, causing resentment in France and Italy. Mr. Baldwin succeeded Ramsay MacDonald as Prime Minister on June 7. The Government of India Bill passed the Lords. The Peace Ballot results showed strong public support for the League of Nations.
Chapter III — Britain’s Lead to the League of Nations
Italy’s breach with the League over Abyssinia dominated the second half of the year. Britain took the lead at Geneva, with Sir Samuel Hoare and Mr. Eden advocating collective security and sanctions against Italy. The Cabinet recalled Parliament and the British fleet was strengthened in the Mediterranean. The Labour Party Conference and the Trades Union Congress supported the League. A General Election was held in November, resulting in a decisive victory for the National Government (Baldwin’s majority of 247). Sanctions against Italy commenced on November 18.
Chapter IV — The Government’s Volte-Face
Following the election, Mr. Baldwin reshuffled his Cabinet but retained its balance. Lord Londonderry was replaced by Lord Halifax. The Hoare-Laval proposals (December) — which offered Italy substantial territorial concessions in Abyssinia in exchange for peace — provoked a storm of public indignation when leaked to the press. Sir Samuel Hoare resigned as Foreign Secretary and was replaced by Mr. Eden. The Government reasserted its commitment to the League. The coal crisis loomed with a miners’ strike ballot. The Naval Conference in London opened with Japanese proposals.
Part I — Imperial History
Chapter I — Ireland: Northern Ireland
Northern Ireland’s finances improved through a revised Re-insurance Agreement under the Unemployment Acts. The Budget showed revenue of £12,552,000 against expenditure of £12,534,000. Sectarian rioting broke out in Belfast in May and July, the worst in many years, with nine persons shot dead and hundreds driven from their homes. The Transport Bill established the most complete road-rail co-ordination scheme yet devised. The Summary Jurisdiction Bill transferred judicial administration from JPs to Resident Magistrates.
Chapter II — Canada
Canada faced the deepening Depression. The new Prime Minister, Mr. R. B. Bennett, pursued protectionist policies and trade agreements with the United States. The Bank of Canada was established. Unemployment remained severe, and the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF) gained ground as a political force.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa
General Hertzog’s government continued its policy of domestic consolidation. The gold standard was maintained. South Africa celebrated the Silver Jubilee. Tensions between the British and Afrikaner communities persisted over the country’s constitutional status and the question of participation in imperial defence.
Chapter IV — Australasia: Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand
Australia’s economy showed signs of recovery under the Lyons government, with improved wool and wheat prices. New Zealand continued under the Coalition government of Mr. Forbes, with economic conditions gradually improving. Both dominions participated in the Silver Jubilee celebrations and maintained close ties with the imperial government.
Chapter V — India
The Government of India Bill, providing for provincial autonomy and a federal structure, completed its passage through Parliament. Debates were intense, with Mr. Churchill leading the opposition. The princes’ objections were addressed through amendments. The bill established the framework for elected provincial governments with responsible ministers, while reserving defence and foreign affairs to the Viceroy.
Part II — Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League faced its gravest crisis yet as Italy prepared to invade Abyssinia. Britain took the lead in pushing for collective action under the Covenant. The Council met in September and declared Italy the aggressor. Sanctions were imposed in November, though oil was excluded. The League’s authority and credibility hung in the balance.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France experienced four changes of government (Flandin, Bouisson, Laval), with a 12-billion-franc deficit and political instability. Pierre Laval pursued conciliation with Italy and sought to mediate the Abyssinian dispute. Italy under Mussolini rejected League arbitration, mobilised for the invasion of Abyssinia, and faced sanctions with defiance.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
Germany under Hitler announced universal military conscription (March 16), repudiating the military clauses of Versailles. The Anglo-German Naval Agreement (June 18) was a major diplomatic coup for Berlin. The Nuremberg Laws institutionalised anti-Semitism. In Austria, Chancellor Schuschnigg struggled to maintain independence against Nazi pressure, with Italy distracted by Abyssinia.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
The Soviet Union signed a mutual assistance pact with France (May 2) and pursued collective security through the League, which it had joined in 1934. Stalin’s purges began to take shape. Poland maintained a delicate balancing act between Germany and the Soviet Union. The Little Entente (Czechoslovakia, Rumania, Yugoslavia) faced internal strains.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium restored conscription in response to German rearmament. The Netherlands and Switzerland maintained neutrality. Spain saw the Lerroux government face increasing instability, with the Left gaining ground. The Nordic states co-operated closely on economic and foreign policy.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
Iran changed its name from Persia (formally requested in March). Iraq achieved a new Anglo-Iraqi treaty strengthening its sovereignty. Palestine experienced renewed Arab-Jewish tensions over land purchases and immigration. Syria remained under French mandate with nationalist agitation. Saudi Arabia consolidated under Ibn Saud.
Chapter VII — The Far East: China and Japan
Japan continued its domination of Manchuria and pressed for further concessions in North China. China under the Kuomintang struggled to present a united front against Japanese encroachment. The Soviet-Japanese tension over border issues persisted.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
Morocco remained under French and Spanish administration with nationalist stirrings. Egypt, nominally independent under the 1930 constitution, faced Anglo-Egyptian treaty negotiations over the status of the Sudan and British military presence. The Wafd party pressed for full sovereignty.
Chapter IX — America: The United States and Latin America
The United States under President Roosevelt continued the New Deal. The Works Progress Administration (WPA) was created, and the Social Security Act and Wagner Act were passed. The US remained isolationist but co-operated on the Stresa front and naval limitation. In Latin America, the Chaco War between Bolivia and Paraguay concluded. Brazil experienced political unrest.
Part II — Chronicle of Events in 1935
Day-by-day record of notable events throughout the year, including the Silver Jubilee celebrations, the Stresa Conference, the Anglo-German Naval Agreement, the General Election, the Italo-Abyssinian crisis, the Hoare-Laval proposals, and key parliamentary debates.
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1935
Literature (by J. Isaacs): Notable works included T.S. Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral, Vera Brittain’s Testament of Youth, and James Hilton’s Lost Horizon. Art (by W.T. Whitley): The Royal Academy exhibition and developments in British painting. Drama (by Ernest Kuhe): The London stage saw new works by Bernard Shaw, J.B. Priestley, and others. The Cinema (by Monica Ewer): The 39 Steps, Mutiny on the Bounty, and British film’s growing reputation. Music (by Ernest Kuhe): The Proms season, new compositions by Vaughan Williams and Walton. Biological Sciences (by W.B. Brierley): Advances in genetics and biochemistry. Physical Sciences: Developments in nuclear physics and astronomy.
Finance and Commerce in 1935
A review of the economic year: trade improved, unemployment fell from 2.2 million to 1.8 million. The Budget showed a surplus of £7.5 million. Road transport expanded. The building industry boomed. Agricultural prices recovered modestly. The Stock Exchange rallied.
Law in 1935
Important legal decisions and legislation, including the Housing Act, the Restriction of Ribbon Development Act, and the Government of India Act. The Law of Property reforms continued.
Public Documents
I. Hitler’s Statement Announcing Universal Military Conscription in Germany (March 16) — repudiation of Part V of the Versailles Treaty.
II. The British Ambassador’s Note to the German Government — protest against German rearmament.
III. French Note Protesting against German Military Moves.
IV. French Note to the League — referral of German violations to the Council.
V. Italy’s Note to Berlin — response to German conscription.
VI. Soviet-French Treaty of Mutual Assistance (May 2) — collective security pact.
VII. Mr. James G. McDonald’s Letter of Resignation as League High Commissioner for Refugees — citing the failure of states to respond to the German refugee crisis.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1935
Notable deaths included King George V’s cousin Prince Arthur of Connaught, the statesman Lord Balfour, the composer Sir Edward Elgar, the explorer Sir Francis Younghusband, and the writer Sir James Barrie. Obituaries covered figures from politics, science, literature and the arts.

sources/annual-register-1936.title: Annual Register, 1936
sources/annual-register-1936.content:
The Annual Register for 1936 (Vol. 178)
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The New Reign
The year opened with the fight of Ramsay MacDonald and his son Malcolm to re-enter Parliament after losing their seats in the 1935 election. Japan withdrew from the Naval Conference on January 16. A coal strike was narrowly averted. On January 20 King George V died at Sandringham, aged 70, after 26 years on the throne. King Edward VIII was proclaimed, and the nation united in mourning. The funeral was at Windsor. The new King broadcast a moving tribute. The rearmament White Paper was published (March), the Rhineland crisis erupted (March 7), and Sir Thomas Inskip was appointed Minister for the Co-ordination of Defence. The naval conference concluded without Japan.
Chapter II — The Failure of Sanctions
Mr. Eden protested at Geneva against Italy’s use of poison gas in Abyssinia. Mr. Baldwin defined Britain’s position: sanctions were slow and lost force without the ultimate threat of blockade. The Budget brought increased taxation. Defence loan was foreshadowed. Sanctions were debated intensely as Italy’s victory in Abyssinia became inevitable. The League of Nations Union sent a deputation. Labour moved a vote of censure. By June, the Government decided to abandon sanctions; Mr. Eden defended the decision. By-elections were lost by the Government. Resignation of Mr. J. H. Thomas; Sir Samuel Hoare became First Lord of the Admiralty. The Budget leakage tribunal reported. Parliament passed the Education Bill and the Tithe Bill. Emperor Haile Selassie arrived in London as an exile.
Chapter III — Britain and the Conflict in Spain
The Spanish Civil War erupted in July. France proposed a non-intervention agreement, which Britain welcomed and extended to Germany, Italy and Portugal. The Non-Intervention Committee was set up in London. Public opinion was deeply divided: Labour and Liberals saw the struggle as democracy against Fascism and pressed for aid to the Spanish Government. The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty was signed (August). Troops were sent to Palestine to quell Arab unrest. The Trades Union Congress rejected a United Front with Communists. The franc devalued; Britain supported it. Conservatives at their conference debated rearmament. Fascist-Communist street violence in London’s East End led to the Public Order Bill.
Chapter IV — Abdication of Edward VIII
Parliament met on November 3 with the King’s Speech setting out a programme including rearmament, non-intervention in Spain, and League reform. The Jarrow March arrived in London. The King toured South Wales’ distressed areas. In December the crisis broke: King Edward VIII wished to marry Mrs. Wallis Simpson, an American divorcée. The Cabinet, led by Mr. Baldwin, rejected the proposal for a morganatic marriage. The Dominions were consulted and concurred. The King chose to abdicate rather than abandon the marriage. On December 10, the Instrument of Abdication was signed, and Parliament passed His Majesty’s Declaration of Abdication Act. Prince Albert succeeded as King George VI. The ex-King broadcast to the nation and left for France. Mr. Eden defended non-intervention as the year closed.
Part I — Imperial History
Chapter I — Ireland (Northern Ireland and Irish Free State)
Northern Ireland enjoyed a year of peaceful progress, with Lord Craigavon beginning his fifteenth year as Prime Minister. The Budget balanced with a surplus. Sectarian disorder did not recur. The Irish Free State saw Ministerial changes. An air route agreement was signed between the UK, Irish Free State, Canada and Newfoundland. The Fianna Fáil party gained by-elections but lost Dublin municipal seats.
Chapter II — Canada
Canada experienced continued economic recovery under Mr. Mackenzie King, who returned as Prime Minister in October 1935. The Dominion faced trade negotiations with the United States. The Bank of Canada commenced operations. Parliament debated imperial preference and defence contributions. The Canadian pilgrimage to London for the King’s funeral was a notable event.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa
General Hertzog’s government pursued the Representation of Natives Bill, removing the Cape native franchise and substituting communal representation by whites. The Bill aroused fierce controversy. Dr. Malan’s Nationalist Party opposed it as inadequate; the Dominion Party also resisted. South Africa remained on the gold standard. The question of the country’s constitutional status vis-à-vis the Crown continued to simmer.
Chapter IV — Australasia: Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand
Australia under Mr. Lyons saw economic improvement with rising wool and wheat prices. The government pursued trade diversion policies to protect local industry. New Zealand under the new Labour government of Mr. Michael Joseph Savage began an ambitious programme of social reform, including the forty-hour week, state housing, and guaranteed prices for dairy farmers. The Statute of Westminster was adopted.
Chapter V — India
The Government of India Act of 1935 came into partial operation, with provincial autonomy being prepared. Elections were held for the new provincial legislatures. Congress Party participation remained uncertain. Debates continued on safeguards, the princes’ position in the federal scheme, and communal representation.
Part II — Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League faced the gravest crisis in its history. The Italo-Abyssinian war became a test case for collective security — and the League failed it. Sanctions were abandoned in June. The Abyssinian question was dropped from the Council agenda. The League’s prestige fell worldwide. Germany’s remilitarization of the Rhineland in March further undermined the post-war settlement. The League remained powerless to restrain the Great Powers.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France experienced continuing political instability under the Popular Front government of Léon Blum, elected in May. The Matignon Agreements brought major social reforms: forty-hour week, paid holidays, collective bargaining. The franc came under pressure and was eventually devalued in September. Italy completed its conquest of Abyssinia in May (the fall of Addis Ababa), proclaimed the empire, and King Victor Emmanuel III was named Emperor. Italy grew closer to Germany.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
Germany under Hitler remilitarised the Rhineland on March 7, tearing up the Locarno Treaties. British and French protests were ineffective. Hitler’s peace proposals were evasive. The Nuremberg Rally was held as usual. The Four-Year Plan was announced for economic autarky. The Berlin-Rome Axis began to take shape. In Austria, Schuschnigg’s government faced intensifying Nazi pressure, isolated after the Italo-Abyssinian war weakened Italy’s protection.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
The USSR under Stalin adopted a new Constitution (the “Stalin Constitution”) in November, nominally democratic but consolidating one-party rule. The purges intensified, with the first great show trial (Zinoviev-Kamenev) in August. The Soviet-French mutual assistance pact remained unratified by France. Poland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia, and the Balkan states sought to balance between Germany and the USSR. Turkey secured the Montreux Convention restoring full sovereignty over the Straits.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium renounced its military alliance with France (October) and adopted a policy of “independent” neutrality. The Netherlands and Switzerland maintained strict neutrality. In Spain, the Civil War raged after the July military rising led by General Franco. Portugal under Salazar supported the Nationalists. The Nordic states continued their policy of co-operation and neutrality.
Chapter VI — The Middle East: Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Palestine, Syria
Iran (formerly Persia) consolidated under Reza Shah. Iraq made progress toward independence. Palestine experienced renewed Arab rebellion against Jewish immigration and land purchases, prompted by the large influx from Germany; British troops were sent to restore order. Syria remained under French mandate with nationalist agitation. The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty (August) regulated the status of the Sudan and British military basing rights, granting Egypt fuller sovereignty.
Chapter VII — The Far East: China, Japan, Netherlands Indies
Japan continued its domination of Manchuria and pressed into North China. The Anti-Comintern Pact was signed between Germany and Japan in November. China under Chiang Kai-shek faced both Japanese encroachment and the continued Communist insurgency. The Netherlands Indies maintained neutrality.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
Morocco remained under French and Spanish control. Egypt achieved a new Treaty of Alliance with Britain (signed August 26), regularising the status of the Sudan, British military occupation of the Canal Zone, and Egyptian sovereignty. The treaty was widely welcomed in Egypt.
Chapter IX — America: The United States and Latin America
President Roosevelt campaigned for re-election on the New Deal record and won a landslide victory over Alf Landon in November (46 of 48 states). The US remained isolationist, passing the Neutrality Acts. The Pan-American Conference at Buenos Aires strengthened hemispheric solidarity. In Latin America, the Chaco War between Bolivia and Paraguay formally ended. Brazil under Vargas continued centralisation.
Part II — Chronicle of Events in 1936
Day-by-day record of the year’s notable events: the death of George V and accession of Edward VIII, the Rhineland occupation, the fall of Addis Ababa, the Spanish Civil War outbreak, the Berlin Olympics (August), the Montreux Convention, the Rome-Berlin Axis declaration, and the Abdication crisis.
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1936
Literature (by J. Isaacs): Notable works included Margaret Mitchell’s Gone With the Wind, John Maynard Keynes’s General Theory of Employment, and poetry by W.H. Auden. Art (by W.T. Whitley): The Royal Academy and modern British art. Drama (by W.A. Darlington): The London stage with works by J.B. Priestley and the founding of the Old Vic Company. The Cinema (by Monica Ewer): Chaplin’s Modern Times and British documentary films. Music (by W. McNaught): The Proms, works by Vaughan Williams, the death of Elgar. Biological Sciences (by W.B. Brierley): Advances in genetics and vitamins. Physical Sciences: Nuclear physics progress.
Finance and Commerce in 1936
The economic year showed steady recovery: trade improved, unemployment fell from 1.8 million to 1.5 million. The Budget had a surplus. Building activity boomed. Agricultural prices rose. The Stock Exchange rallied. Defence spending increased. The Special Areas (depressed regions) received new assistance.
Law in 1936
Important legal decisions: the Public Order Act curbed political uniforms and paramilitary organisations; the Trunk Roads Act transferred major routes to central government; the Education Act raised the school leaving age; the Cotton Spinning Industry Act reorganised the industry; the Tithe Act commuted tithe rentcharge.
Public Documents
I. The Soviet Constitution (November 1936) — the “Stalin Constitution,” declaring the USSR a socialist state of workers and peasants, guaranteeing civil rights (in theory), and establishing the Supreme Soviet as the supreme legislative body.
II. Treaty of Alliance Between His Majesty, in Respect of the United Kingdom, and His Majesty the King of Egypt (August 26) — the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, regulating the status of the Sudan, British military basing in the Canal Zone, and Egyptian sovereignty; ratified by Parliament.
III. Guarantees by Britain to France and Belgium — staff talks and mutual assurances in response to the German remilitarisation of the Rhineland.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1936
Notable deaths included King George V, Rudyard Kipling (writer), G.K. Chesterton (writer and critic), A.E. Housman (poet and scholar), Sir Henry Newbolt (poet), Sir Robert Baden-Powell (founder of the Boy Scouts), Cardinal Bourne (Archbishop of Westminster), and Luigi Pirandello (Nobel Prize-winning playwright).

sources/annual-register-1937.title: Annual Register, 1937
sources/annual-register-1937.content:
The Annual Register for 1937 (Vol. 179)
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The Defence Loan
The year opened with the Spanish Civil War still threatening a European explosion. An Anglo-Italian “Gentlemen’s Agreement” (January 2) regulating Mediterranean positions was signed in Rome by Count Ciano and Sir Eric Drummond. However, German and Italian replies to the Franco-British proposals on banning volunteers to Spain proved evasive. A Defence Loan of £400 million was announced by the Chancellor (Mr. Chamberlain); the debate exposed deep divisions over the pace of rearmament. The Government published a White Paper on defence expenditure. Incidents of subversive activity in the Navy came to light. The New Regency Bill was introduced. The Special Areas received increased grants. Labour’s “Five-Year Programme” was launched.
Chapter II — The Coronation
Mr. Baldwin announced his impending retirement after the Coronation. The Ministers of the Crown Bill gave legal status to the Cabinet. The Budget brought increases in the National Defence Contribution (NDC) — a graduated tax on business profits that caused major alarm in the City and had to be revised. The Coronation of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth took place on May 12 with great ceremony, attended by Empire Ministers and foreign dignitaries. The Imperial Conference met (May-June), discussing foreign affairs, defence, and trade co-operation. A London bus strike and the Harworth colliery dispute were settled. Mr. Baldwin formally resigned and Mr. Neville Chamberlain became Prime Minister on May 28. The Basque children (refugees from the Spanish Civil War) arrived in England.
Chapter III — The Nyon Arrangement
Mussolini sent a conciliatory message to Mr. Chamberlain. Submarine “piracy” in the Mediterranean against merchant shipping (including British vessels) led to the Nyon Conference (September) where nine Powers agreed on a naval patrol system. Italy initially stayed out but later joined. The Non-Intervention Committee’s plan for control of volunteers in Spain reached deadlock. The Government responded to the Far Eastern crisis (Japan’s full-scale invasion of China, July) with protests against attacks on British nationals. The British Ambassador to China was shot by Japanese aircraft. The Nine-Power Conference met at Brussels but achieved nothing. The Trades Union Congress and Labour Party Conference debated arms, Spain, and the United Front campaign. The Conservative Conference endorsed the Government’s defence policy.
Chapter IV — Britain and the Far Eastern Conflict
Parliament opened on October 26 with the King’s Speech — for the first time in years there was no mention of the League of Nations. The Air-Raid Precautions Bill was introduced. The Coal Bill united coal royalties under national control. Reports from the Special Areas Commissioner showed recovery. The question of relations with Germany came to the fore with Lord Halifax’s visit to Hitler at Berchtesgaden (November). The French Premier and Foreign Minister visited London. Talks for a US trade pact continued. Mr. Chamberlain exchanged notes with Mussolini. The Irish Free State enacted a new Constitution (Bunreacht na hÉireann), establishing Eire as a sovereign state with an elected President, and Britain negotiated its implications for Northern Ireland. Persistent “slump talk” was countered by the Premier’s optimism; by-elections were mixed.
Part I — Imperial History
Chapter I — Ireland (Northern Ireland and the Irish Free State)
Northern Ireland’s notable event was the King and Queen’s visit to Belfast on July 28, a great success. Lord Craigavon continued as Prime Minister. The Irish Free State enacted a new Constitution in December, replacing the 1922 Constitution, renaming the state “Eire” (Ireland), and providing for a President elected by proportional representation. The special position of the Catholic Church was recognised. Mr. de Valera’s government held a general election and was returned. Anglo-Irish relations remained tense over partition and the land annuity question.
Chapter II — Canada
Canada under Mr. Mackenzie King continued economic recovery. The Dominion participated in the Imperial Conference. Trade negotiations with the United States progressed. Canada’s attitude towards European commitments remained cautious, with a focus on imperial co-operation without binding obligations. The Coronation was marked by strong Canadian representation.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa
General Hertzog’s government held a general election in May (United Party majority reduced). The Representation of Natives Act, abolishing the Cape native franchise, became law. The question of South Africa’s neutrality in the event of a European war was debated. The Government resisted pressure to leave the gold standard linkage. Racial legislation remained a central concern.
Chapter IV — Australasia: The Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand
Australia under Mr. Lyons saw a general election in October; the United Australia Party-Country Party coalition was returned. The Budget showed surpluses in most states. The Loan Council restricted borrowings. New Zealand continued its Labour programme under Mr. Savage: the forty-hour week, guaranteed prices for dairy produce, and state housing construction resumed. The Coronation was celebrated across both Dominions.
Chapter V — India and Burma
The Government of India Act came into force for provincial autonomy (April). Elections had been held in early 1937; the Congress Party won in six provinces and formed ministries. The Congress rejected the federal (central) provisions of the Act. Burma was separated from India under the new constitution. The year was on the whole peaceful.
Part II — Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League’s year was one of continued frustration. The Italo-Abyssinian aftermath lingered. The League failed to mediate effectively in Spain or in the Sino-Japanese conflict. The Nyon Conference’s anti-piracy patrol was not a League initiative. The League’s prestige continued to erode as the Great Powers bypassed Geneva. China appealed to the League against Japan; a resolution condemned bombing of civilians but had no effect. The League Council dealt with the Alexandretta (Hatay) dispute between France and Turkey, which was resolved peacefully.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France under the Popular Front (Léon Blum) faced economic crisis: the franc was in difficulty, the “pause” in reforms was announced, and Blum resigned in June. Chautemps formed a new Radical-Socialist government. Social reforms (forty-hour week, paid holidays) remained controversial. Italy after the Abyssinian war was committed in Spain and drew closer to Germany. The Anglo-Italian “Gentlemen’s Agreement” failed to stop propaganda interference, though diplomatic channels remained open. Italy joined the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Pact in November.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
Germany experienced radicalisation in both economic and Church policy. Dr. Schacht resigned as Minister of Economic Affairs; Goering took over the Four-Year Plan. The struggle against the Evangelical Church intensified. Church and youth movements were brought under party control. The Nuremberg Rally demonstrated Nazi power. In Austria, Schuschnigg’s government faced mounting Nazi pressure, isolated after the Rome-Berlin Axis shifted Italy’s protection to acceptance of German primacy. Hitler’s November speech at Berchtesgaden to Lord Halifax signalled German colonial demands and discomfort with the status quo. The Anti-Comintern Pact was signed with Japan (November) and Italy shortly after.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
The USSR was in the grip of the Great Purges. The trial of the “Parallel Anti-Soviet Trotskyite Centre” (Pyatakov, Radek) took place in January; executions and imprisonments followed. Marshal Tukhachevsky and other senior Red Army commanders were tried and executed in June on charges of conspiracy with Germany — devastating the military leadership. The new Soviet Constitution was formally adopted. In Eastern Europe, Poland balanced between Germany and the USSR. Czechoslovakia remained vulnerable, with Henlein’s Sudeten German Party gaining strength. Turkey secured full re-militarisation of the Straits under Montreux.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium maintained its independent neutrality policy (declared in 1936). The Netherlands and Switzerland remained neutral. The Spanish Civil War continued: Franco’s Nationalists advanced in the north (Bilbao fell in June, Santander in August). The International Brigades fought on the Republican side. Portugal under Salazar supported Franco. The Nordic states (Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland) held to neutrality and Scandinavian co-operation.
Chapter VI — The Middle East: Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Palestine, Syria
Palestine was the major crisis of the region. The Peel Commission (led by Lord Peel) published its report in July, recommending partition into separate Jewish and Arab states, with a British-controlled corridor including Jerusalem. The proposal was hailed by Zionists and rejected by Arabs, who launched renewed violence. The Royal Commission’s partition plan created intense debate. Iraq under King Ghazi I moved towards greater independence. Syria remained under French mandate with continuing nationalist unrest.
Chapter VII — The Far East: China, Japan, Netherlands Indies
The Sino-Japanese War began in earnest with the Marco Polo Bridge incident (July 7). Japan rapidly occupied Peking, Tientsin, Shanghai, and Nanking. The fall of Nanking (December) was followed by the Nanking Massacre. The United States and Britain protested but took no military action. The Nine-Power Conference (Brussels, November) failed to produce a collective response. Japan rejected all mediation. The Soviet Union and China signed a non-aggression pact.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
Morocco remained calm under French and Spanish control. Egypt under the 1936 Treaty functioned as a sovereign state, with the Capitulations régime being formally abolished by the Montreux Convention (May), granting Egypt full judicial sovereignty over foreigners. King Farouk’s reign continued. The question of the Sudan remained under condominium.
Chapter IX — America: The United States and Latin America
President Roosevelt faced the “Roosevelt Recession” (downturn after the New Deal recovery). The Neutrality Act of 1937 (May 1) continued the arms embargo, including a “cash-and-carry” provision. Roosevelt’s “Quarantine Speech” (October 5) hinted at collective action against aggressors but Congress remained isolationist. The Supreme Court “court-packing” plan was defeated. In Latin America, the Chaco settlement was implemented. The coup in Brazil established Vargas’s Estado Novo dictatorship (November).
Part II — Chronicle of Events in 1937
Day-by-day record: the Anglo-Italian Agreement (Jan 2), the bombing of Almeria (May), the Coronation (May 12), Mr. Baldwin’s resignation (May 28), the Hindenburg disaster (May 6), the Normandy dock fire (Feb), the Duke of Windsor’s marriage (June 3), the Sino-Japanese War outbreak (July 7), the fall of Nanking (Dec), the Nyon Conference (Sept), the Peel Commission report (July), the Irish Constitution (Dec).
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1937
Literature (by J. Isaacs): Major works included J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit, George Orwell’s The Road to Wigan Pier, John Steinbeck’s Of Mice and Men. Art (by W.T. Whitley): The Royal Academy summer exhibition. Drama (by W.A. Darlington): New plays by Priestley, Rattigan; the Old Vic season. The Cinema (by Monica Ewer): Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, The Life of Emile Zola. Music (by W. McNaught): Vaughan Williams’s Serenade to Music; the death of Ravel. Biological Sciences: Sulphonamide drugs (Prontosil). Physical Sciences: Nuclear fission research; the cyclotron.
Finance and Commerce in 1937
Trade improved in the first half but the “Roosevelt Recession” in America caused a downturn in the second. The National Defence Contribution was revised. The Stock Exchange faced a sharp fall (autumn). Building societies continued active. Unemployment fell below 1.5 million. Agriculture had mixed fortunes. The exchange equalisation fund was increased. The British shipping industry faced competition.
Law in 1937
Important legislation: the Air-Raid Precautions Bill, the Coal Bill (nationalisation of royalties), the Factories Act (consolidating and modernising factory law), the Films Bill (British film quota), the Physical Training and Recreation Act, the Population (Statistics) Bill, the Livestock Industry Act. The Matrimonial Causes Bill reform was debated. The Prevention of Fraud (Investments) Act regulated share-pushing.
Public Documents
I. The Constitution of Ireland (Bunreacht na hÉireann) (December 1937) — enacted by referendum in the Irish Free State, establishing Eire as a fully sovereign state with an elected President (Uachtarán na hÉireann), a prime minister (Taoiseach), and a bicameral Oireachtas. Recognised the special position of the Catholic Church and claimed jurisdiction over the whole island of Ireland — the cause of continued tension with the United Kingdom over Northern Ireland.
II. The U.S. Neutrality Act (May 1, 1937) — continuing the arms embargo and instituting a “cash-and-carry” policy for non-military goods to belligerents, reflecting American determination to stay out of overseas conflicts.
III. Non-aggression Treaty between the USSR and China (August 21, 1937) — the Soviet Union and Nationalist China agreed to mutual non-aggression, enabling Soviet material aid to China after Japan’s invasion.
IV. Convention regarding the Abolition of the Capitulations in Egypt (Montreux, May 8, 1937) — abolishing the mixed courts and special legal privileges for foreigners in Egypt, a major step in Egyptian sovereignty.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1937
Notable deaths included Ramsay MacDonald (former Prime Minister, aged 70), Baron Rutherford of Nelson (physicist, pioneer of the nuclear atom), Lord Tweedsmuir (John Buchan, Governor-General of Canada and novelist), Sir James Barrie (playwright, creator of Peter Pan), Maurice Ravel (composer), Gustav Holst (composer), Waldemar Bonsels (author), and Sir Antonin Sert (architect).

sources/annual-register-1938.title: Annual Register 1938
sources/annual-register-1938.content:
The Annual Register 1938 — Volume 180
Part I — English History
Chapter I — Mr. Eden’s Resignation
The year opened with the National Government under Chamberlain still strongly entrenched, but a fundamental difference over policy toward Italy led to the resignation of Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden in February. Eden distrusted Mussolini and objected to opening conversations while Italy remained embroiled in Spain; Chamberlain overrode him, and Lord Halifax succeeded at the Foreign Office. The chapter also covers the Non-Intervention Committee’s work over Spain, the Commons debate on Czechoslovakia (the Government refusing a pledge to defend it), a Defence White Paper, and domestic legislation including the Coal Bill, Films Bill, and Housing Bill.
Chapter II — The Anglo-Italian Agreement
The Easter negotiations at Rome between Lord Perth and Count Ciano produced a conditional Anglo-Italian Agreement (April 16) that would come into effect only after a settlement in Spain. The Budget was introduced by Sir John Simon with increased defence expenditure; an Essential Commodities Reserves Bill was passed for wartime stockpiling. The Eire Agreements settled the land annuity and financial disputes. French Ministers visited London for talks. The chapter also records the “Sandys case” — a controversy over the Official Secrets Act when M.P. Duncan Sandys (Churchill’s son-in-law) was questioned by the Attorney-General about his defence sources.
Chapter III — The Munich Agreement
The central crisis of the year: Lord Runciman’s mediation mission to Prague failed to reconcile the Sudeten Germans and the Czechoslovak Government. As German military manoeuvres intensified, Chamberlain made three dramatic flights to Germany — Berchtesgaden (September 15), Godesberg (September 22), and finally Munich (September 29), where Hitler, Mussolini, Daladier, and Chamberlain agreed to the cession of the Sudetenland. The Anglo-German Declaration was signed. Duff Cooper resigned as First Lord of the Admiralty in protest. Parliament debated the settlement amid deep division; Labour moved an amendment of censure, but the Government won a large majority.
Chapter IV — More Rearmament
Parliament met in November for a new session. The King’s Speech announced a royal visit to Canada and the United States. The Government announced a Ministry of Supply to accelerate rearmament, though critics demanded a fuller inquiry into defence preparedness. The Criminal Justice Bill was introduced, an Anglo-American Trade Agreement negotiated, and Lord Baldwin was honoured with a fund. The Voluntary National Register was announced for air-raid precautions. Domestic measures included the Milk Industry Bill, Export Guarantees Bill, and a Cancer Bill. By the year’s end the “appeasement” policy was under growing attack, with by-elections showing a swing against the Government.

Part I — Imperial History
Chapter I — Ireland
Northern Ireland’s financial position was made more secure following the United Kingdom-Eire Agreement. The year saw continuing consolidation of the constitutional separation, with the Southern Irish Parliament functioning under the new Constitution of Eire.
Chapter II — Canada
The year opened hopefully with economic conditions improving outside the drought areas. The royal visit to Canada was announced for 1939. Domestically, Canadian politics grappled with trade questions and the lingering effects of depression in the prairie provinces.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa
Repercussions of the European crisis were felt throughout the Union. South African opinion was divided over the international situation, with General Hertzog’s Government maintaining a cautious line between British sentiment and Afrikaner neutralism.
Chapter IV — Australasia
Australian politics centred on efforts to revise the Ottawa Agreement in favour of local primary producers. New Zealand under its Labour Government continued its social reform programme, with growing attention to defence questions as the international situation deteriorated.
Chapter V — India and Burma
The first year of provincial autonomy under the Government of India Act, 1936, stood the test of a full budget cycle. Congress ministries consolidated their position in the provinces. Tension between Congress and the Muslim League increased. Burma was administered separately under its new constitution.

Part I — Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
The League played only a minor role in international politics during 1938, a year full of strife and discord. The succession of crises accelerated the League’s marginalisation, as great powers increasingly acted outside its framework.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France: The Chautemps Government struggled with strikes and budget difficulties. The fall of the Popular Front gave way to Daladier’s ministry, which secured emergency powers by decree. The Munich settlement divided French opinion bitterly. Italy: Mussolini drew closer to Germany, endorsing the Anschluss and adopting anti-Semitic racial laws modelled on the Nuremberg decrees.
Chapter III — Germany and Austria
Germany: Scarcity of foodstuffs and raw materials persisted. Hitler purged the army command (Blomberg-Fritsch affair) and in March carried out the Anschluss — the annexation of Austria — after forcing Chancellor Schuschnigg to cancel a plebiscite. The Kristallnacht pogrom (November 9–10) saw coordinated violence against Jews throughout Germany. Austria: After the Anschluss, Austrian institutions were rapidly Nazified and the country dissolved into German administrative districts.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
Soviet Union: The year witnessed a marked change in relations with Czechoslovakia and France as the Western powers abandoned collective security. The Great Purge continued with the trial of Bukharin and Rykov (March). Soviet policy turned increasingly suspicious of the West. Eastern Europe: Poland and Hungary took advantage of the Munich settlement to press territorial claims against Czechoslovakia; the First Vienna Award (November) transferred southern Slovakia and Subcarpathian Ruthenia to Hungary.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium faced budget deficits and reaffirmed its policy of independence. Spain: The year was dominated by the Republican offensive on the Ebro (July–November), Franco’s conquest of Catalonia, and the agonising debate over the Non-Intervention Committee’s plan for foreign troop withdrawal. Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland: The Scandinavian states maintained neutrality while strengthening their defences.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
Iran completed the Trans-Iranian Railway (808 miles from the Caspian to the Persian Gulf). Palestine: The Woodhead Commission reported that partition was impractical; the Government summoned a London Round Table Conference of Arabs and Jews. Arab revolt continued. Trans-Iranian railway completed. Iraq and Syria remained in political flux.
Chapter VII — The Far East: China and Japan
The Japanese invasion of China continued with the fall of Hankow (October) and Canton (October). Chinese forces suffered serious reverses, but the Nationalist Government retreated to Chungking and continued resistance. Japan proclaimed a “New Order in East Asia” and declared that the Open Door policy was obsolete.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
Morocco: French Morocco remained quiet; anti-French agitation did not revive. Egypt: The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936 continued to shape relations, with negotiations over the Sudan and the status of foreigners in Egypt.
Chapter IX — America
United States: President Roosevelt faced a severe recession (“Roosevelt recession”) after the 1937 economic downturn. His New Deal recovery programme struggled; he failed to “purge” conservative Democrats in the primaries. Foreign policy moved toward rearmament and the President’s “quarantine” concept, though isolationism remained strong. Pan-American Conference at Lima affirmed continental solidarity (Declaration of Lima). Latin American states continued to be affected by European trade disruption.

Part II — Chronicle of Events in 1938
Day-by-day record of the year’s events: January (Roosevelt’s rearmament message, Nuffield viscountcy, Eden resignation), February (Anschluss crisis intensifies, Austro-German agreement), March (German invasion of Austria, British protest, Bukharin trial in Moscow), April (Anglo-Italian Agreement signed, Eire agreements), May (Hitler’s Rome visit, Czech crisis — May weekend mobilisation), June (Non-Intervention Committee plan, Japan-UK tension over China), July (Runciman mission to Prague, Roosevelt’s appeal to Hitler), August (German army manoeuvres, Soviet-Japanese border clash at Lake Khasan), September (Chamberlain’s three flights to Germany, Munich Agreement, Czech mobilisation, Polish ultimatum to Teschen), October (German occupation of Sudetenland, Fall of Canton and Hankow to Japan, First Vienna Award), November (Kristallnacht pogrom, Duff Cooper resignation debate, Ministry of Supply created), December (Anglo-German trade talks, Imperial Airways expansion, Balkan Entente-Bulgaria Treaty).

Part II — Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1938
Literature: Notable publications included Jean-Paul Sartre’s La Nausée and Graham Greene’s Brighton Rock. Drama saw the continued success of J.B. Priestley and G.B. Shaw. Art: The year saw the International Surrealist Exhibition in Paris and the closing of the Bauhaus in Berlin. Drama: Emlyn Williams’s The Corn is Green and Terence Rattigan’s work. Cinema: Major releases included Walt Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (continuing its run), The Adventures of Robin Hood with Errol Flynn, Alexander Nevsky by Eisenstein. Music: Béla Bartók’s violin concerto, Shostakovich’s fifth symphony. Science: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann achieved nuclear fission in Berlin (December), though the full implications were only dimly perceived. The biological sciences section covers genetics and cytology advances.

Part II — Finance and Commerce in 1938
The year marked the turning-point in the economic progress that had begun with the suspension of gold payments in 1931; it witnessed a serious deterioration in trade and industrial activity. Britain’s export trade declined under the impact of international uncertainty and mounting tariff barriers. Rearmament expenditure began to stimulate heavy industry, but unemployment rose in the first half of the year. The Anglo-American Trade Agreement, negotiated but not yet ratified, aimed at reciprocal tariff reductions.

Part II — Law in 1938
Important legal developments included the Criminal Justice Bill, which sought to reform penal policy and restrict corporal punishment. The Sandys Case raised constitutional questions about parliamentary privilege and the Official Secrets Act. The year also saw legislation on hire-purchase, coal royalties, and food reserves.

Part II — Public Documents
I. Agreement between the United Kingdom and Italy (Rome, April 16, 1938): A protocol with annexes covering the Mediterranean, Middle East, Spanish withdrawal, and recognition of the Italian Empire in Abyssinia. Conditional upon a Spanish settlement.
II. Agreement Concluded at Munich (September 29, 1938): The Four-Power Agreement providing for the cession of the Sudetenland to Germany, with an international guarantee of the remainder of Czechoslovakia.
III. Treaty between the Members of the Balkan Entente and Bulgaria (July 31, 1938): An agreement removing the demilitarised zones and recognising Bulgaria’s equality of armaments.

Part II — Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1938
Notable figures who died in 1938 included Sir Austen Chamberlain (former Foreign Secretary, Nobel Peace Prize winner), Edmund Husserl (philosopher), Gabriele d’Annunzio (Italian poet and war hero), C.G. Jung’s colleague and various literary figures. The most prominent political loss was Sir Austen Chamberlain, who had shaped the League of Nations policy and the Locarno Treaties.

sources/annual-register-1939.title: Annual Register 1939
sources/annual-register-1939.content:
Sources

Full text of the 1939 Annual Register, extracted from the Internet Archive digitised copy (Digital Library of India collection). OCR quality is good and readable throughout.


Part I — English History
Chapter I — The End of “Appeasement”
Covers January to March 1939. The Munich settlement visibly collapses as Germany occupies the rump Czecho-Slovak state (March 15) and establishes the Protectorate of Bohemia-Moravia. Britain reacts by abandoning appeasement: conscription is introduced for the first time in peacetime, guarantees are offered to Poland, and the Government’s attitude hardens decisively. The chapter also covers the Anglo-Italian Agreement coming into force and the recognition of Franco’s government in Spain.
Chapter II — The New Peace Front
Covers April to August 1939. Italy invades Albania on Good Friday (April 7). Britain extends a unilateral guarantee to Poland (March 31, formalised April 6), followed by guarantees to Greece, Romania, and Turkey. The chapter details the lengthy and ultimately fruitless Anglo-French negotiations with the Soviet Union for a military alliance, the summer crisis over Danzig, and the final descent toward war in the last days of August as the Nazi-Soviet Pact is signed.
Chapter III — The Outbreak of War
Covers September to early October 1939. Germany invades Poland on September 1; Britain and France declare war on September 3. The chapter describes the sinking of the Athenia, the establishment of the War Cabinet, Churchill’s return to the Admiralty, the evacuation of children from London, the creation of the British Expeditionary Force in France, and the rapid conquest of Poland by German and Soviet forces.
Chapter IV — The Intensified Blockade
Covers October to December 1939 — the opening phase of the “Phoney War.” Britain and France reject Hitler’s “peace offer” of October 6. The chapter covers the sinking of HMS Royal Oak at Scapa Flow, the Graf Spee and the Battle of the River Plate, the mining of British waters, the first RAF bombing raids on German naval bases, the organisation of the blockade, and the beginnings of economic warfare.

The Empire
Chapter I — Ireland
Northern Ireland had a prosperous year with declining unemployment and a sound budget. In the South, the Dáil passed the Offences Against the State Act to deal with IRA activity. As war approached, de Valera announced Irish neutrality; Northern Ireland, as part of the United Kingdom, entered the war alongside Britain. The British government introduced the Military Training Act without extending conscription to Northern Ireland.
Chapter II — Canada
The fourth session of the 18th Parliament opened in January with Mackenzie King’s Liberals holding the largest majority in Canadian history. The budget reduced taxes, and the government promoted imperial trade through the Ottawa agreements. When war came, Canada’s Parliament debated participation and declared war independently on September 10, a week after Britain’s declaration. Mobilisation and the creation of a Canadian war effort began rapidly.
Chapter III — The Union of South Africa — South-West Protectorate — Southern Rhodesia — Mozambique
General Hertzog’s government was divided over the European crisis. On the outbreak of war, Hertzog moved for neutrality but was defeated in the House of Assembly (September 4) by 80 votes to 67. Smuts formed a new government and declared war on Germany. Southern Rhodesia offered military assistance and introduced compulsory military training.
Chapter IV — Australasia
Australia: the Duke of Kent’s planned appointment as Governor-General was postponed by the war. Robert Menzies became Prime Minister on the death of J. A. Lyons in April. Australia declared war on September 3, and the government introduced national registration, military conscription for home defence, and economic controls. New Zealand also declared war immediately and raised an expeditionary force.
Chapter V — India and Burma
Indian opinion was united in condemning Hitlerism, but the Viceroy’s declaration that India was at war without consulting Indian leaders provoked a crisis. Congress ministries in the provinces resigned in protest. The British government attempted conciliation with the Viceroy’s declaration of October 17 outlining Dominion status as a post-war goal, which Congress rejected. Burma was separated from India administration.

Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
World events in 1939 further mutilated the League as an instrument for international peace. The Council met in January and May but was increasingly sidelined. Finland, having been elected to a Council seat, appealed against Soviet aggression in December, leading to the Soviet Union’s expulsion from the League — the last significant act of the organisation before the war.
Chapter II — France and Italy
France lived in a war atmosphere from the beginning of the year. Daladier assumed dictatorial powers by decree and pursued rearmament. The French accepted the guarantee to Poland and prepared for war. Italy invaded Albania in April, and Mussolini signed the Pact of Steel with Germany in May. Italian relations with France deteriorated sharply, though Italy remained neutral when war broke out.
Chapter III — Germany
Nazi Germany threw off the mask of a peace-loving power. Hitler occupied Prague (March 15), demanded Danzig and the Corridor from Poland, denounced the Anglo-German Naval Agreement and the German-Polish Non-Aggression Pact. The chapter details the Hossbach-style decision-making, the secret military preparations for Fall Weiss, and the astonishing volte-face of the Nazi-Soviet Pact (August 23) which cleared the way for the invasion of Poland.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia — Estonia — Latvia — Lithuania — Poland — Danzig — Czechoslovakia — Hungary — Romania — Yugoslavia — Turkey — Greece — Bulgaria — Albania
The most striking feature of 1939 was the Soviet Union’s dramatic change in international orientation. After the failure of Anglo-French-Soviet military talks, Stalin signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact with Germany on August 23, with its secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence. The USSR invaded Poland on September 17, then forced mutual assistance pacts on Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Finland refused similar demands, leading to the Soviet attack (the Winter War) on November 30. The chapter also covers the destruction of Czechoslovakia, Hungary’s alignment with the Axis, and Turkey’s alliance with Britain and France.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium reaffirmed its policy of “independent neutrality” under Premier Spaak. The Spanish Civil War ended in March with Franco’s victory; Spain immediately withdrew from the League and signed the Anti-Comintern Pact. Finland resisted Soviet demands and was invaded. Portugal, under Salazar, renewed the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance. Sweden, Norway, and Denmark declared neutrality but feared German expansion.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
Iran: the Shah protested a minor press slight, leading to diplomatic tensions with France. Iraq: the government of Nuri es-Said pursued pro-British policies. Palestine: the MacDonald White Paper (May 1939) restricted Jewish immigration and land purchases, aiming for an independent Palestine within ten years — rejected by both Arabs and Jews. Syria and Lebanon remained under French mandate.
Chapter VII — The Far East: China — Japan
China’s National Government under Chiang Kai-shek maintained itself in Chungking, supplied overland from French Indo-China. The Sino-Japanese war continued with Japanese advances in Kwangsi and the capture of Nanning. Japan tightened its blockade of China and established a puppet regime in Nanking under Wang Ching-wei. Relations between Japan and the Western powers deteriorated, though the US maintained trade with Japan pending revision of the Neutrality Act.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
Spanish Morocco was transferred to Nationalist administration after the Civil War. Egypt remained nominally neutral but co-operated with Britain under the terms of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty. The Egyptian government severed diplomatic relations with Germany.
Chapter IX — America: The United States — Latin America
The United States: President Roosevelt remained dominant but was on the defensive before a conservative Congress. The Neutrality Act of 1937 was revised (November 4) to allow “cash-and-carry” arms sales to belligerents — benefiting Britain and France. Roosevelt’s “Quarantine the aggressors” speech and the Pan-American Declaration establishing a 300-mile maritime safety zone around the Americas (October). Latin American countries maintained neutrality, with Argentina proposing hemispheric solidarity.

Part II
Chronicle of Events in 1939
A month-by-month diary of events: January (New Year Honours, Beaverbrook’s National Trust gift), February (National Service Handbook issued), March (Prague occupation, British guarantee to Poland), April (Albania invasion, conscription introduced), May (Pact of Steel, Roosevelt’s peace message), June (Thetis submarine disaster, 99 lives lost), July (Anglo-Japanese Tientsin crisis), August (Nazi-Soviet Pact, Polish mobilisation), September (invasion of Poland, Britain declares war, Athenia sunk, Graf Spee commerce raiding begins), October (Hitler’s peace offer rejected, Royal Oak sunk), November (mine-laying operations, Finland invaded), December (Battle of the River Plate, Graf Spee scuttled).
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science in 1939
Literature — The year opened with the end of The London Mercury and The Criterion, but Horizon and New Writing began publication. Notable books: James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake (published May), John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath, Aldous Huxley’s After Many a Summer, Ernest Hemingway’s The Fifth Column and the First Forty-Nine Stories, Christopher Isherwood’s Goodbye to Berlin, W. H. Auden and Isherwood’s Journey to a War, J. B. Priestley’s Let the People Sing, Sir Hugh Walpole’s The Sea Tower, T. S. Eliot’s The Idea of a Christian Society. Non-fiction: Lord Elton’s Life of James Ramsay MacDonald, Sir Philip Magnus’s Edmund Burke, E. H. Carr’s The Twenty Years’ Crisis.
Art, Drama, Cinema, and Music — Theatre: J. B. Priestley’s Johnson Over Jordan (February) and Music at Night, T. S. Eliot’s The Family Reunion (March), Steinbeck’s Of Mice and Men adaptation (May). Music: Paul Hindemith’s Mathis der Maler at the BBC Proms, Bartók’s Music for Strings and Percussion, the first London performance of Shostakovich’s Fifth Symphony. Cinema: major films included Goodbye, Mr. Chips, The Wizard of Oz, and British productions preparing for war conditions. Art: exhibitions at the Royal Academy included works by Picasso, and a comprehensive survey of theatre costume and set design.
Science — In biology, a living coelacanth was discovered off South Africa, a fish of a type believed extinct since the Mesozoic. Nuclear fission research advanced: Hahn and Strassmann’s discovery was confirmed and extended; the concept of a chain reaction was increasingly discussed. Chemotherapy advanced with the development of sulfapyridine. Physics: the measurement of specific heats at ultra-low temperatures, and advances in spectroscopy.
Finance and Commerce in 1939
The year opened with little economic promise. Commodity prices were relatively steady and employment was increasing. The pre-war Budget closed with a manageable deficit. With the outbreak of war, emergency budgets introduced income tax increases, a National Defence Contribution, exchange controls, and a drastic expansion of government borrowing. The Board of Trade index of production reached 1937 levels. Imports fell sharply as the blockade tightened, and exports were restricted to essential war materials. Sterling came under pressure and the Exchange Equalisation Account was used extensively.
Law in 1939
The law reflected the momentous events of the year. The Administration of Justice (Emergency Provisions) Act gave the Lord Chancellor sweeping powers. The Prize Court was created. Emergency legislation included the Defence Regulations under the Emergency Powers (Defence) Act. Military conscription (Military Training Act) raised novel legal questions. Notable cases included the challenge to the internment of enemy aliens and the legal status of the German-Polish conflict under international law.
Public Documents
The volume prints nine major documents:

Agreement of Mutual Assistance between the United Kingdom and Poland (London, August 25, 1939) — The formal treaty implementing the British guarantee of March 31.
Treaty of Mutual Assistance between the United Kingdom, France, and Turkey (October 19, 1939).
Russo-German Pact (Moscow, August 23, 1939) — The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, including the secret protocol (not published at the time).
German-Soviet Treaty of Amity and Frontier (September 28, 1939) — The re-drawing of the partition line in Poland.
Soviet-Estonian Pact (September 28, 1939) — Mutual assistance allowing Soviet bases in Estonia.
Soviet-Latvian Pact (October 5, 1939) — Same terms, extending Soviet influence across the Baltic.
Soviet-Lithuanian Pact (October 10, 1939) — Including the transfer of Vilna to Lithuania.
German Government Memorandum to the Polish Government (April 28, 1939) — Denouncing the German-Polish Non-Aggression Declaration of 1934 and demanding Danzig.
Polish Government Memorandum to Germany (May 5, 1939) — Rejecting the German demands and upholding Polish rights in Danzig.

Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1939
Notable figures whose deaths are recorded, with biographical sketches:

W. B. Yeats (January 28) — Irish poet and dramatist, Nobel laureate, leading figure of the Irish Literary Revival.
Sir Henri Deterding (February 4) — Dutch oil magnate, head of Royal Dutch-Shell.
Sir Philip Sassoon (June 3) — British politician, aviator, and patron of the arts.
Lord Duveen (May 25) — Art dealer and benefactor of the National Gallery and Tate.
Sir Frank Dyson (May 25) — Astronomer Royal, 1910–33, key figure in the 1919 eclipse expedition that confirmed Einstein’s relativity.
Dr. Charles Horace Mayo (May 26) — American surgeon, co-founder of the Mayo Clinic.
Lord Howard of Penrith (August 1) — Distinguished British diplomatist (Ambassador to Spain, Washington).
Sir Francis Benson (December 31) — Eminent Shakespearean actor and actor-manager.
Admiral of the Fleet Sir Roger Backhouse (July 15) — First Sea Lord, 1938–39.
Dr. Edwin R. A. Seligman (July 20) — American economist, leading authority on public finance.
Professor Sigmund Freud (September 23) — Originator of psycho-analysis, Viennese neurologist who died in exile in London.
Professor Harvey Cushing (October 7) — Pioneering American neurological surgeon.
Sir Henry Simpson Lunn (March 18) — Founder of Lunn’s travel agency.
Lord Sanderson (May 25) — Principal of the Working Men’s College.
Lord Brabourne (February 23) — Governor of Bombay whose service saw the rise of Congress ministries in India.
Lord Allen of Hurtwood (March 3) — Pacifist peer, key figure in the appeasement movement.

sources/annual-register-1942.title: Annual Register 1942
sources/annual-register-1942.content:
The Annual Register for 1942
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The Fall of Singapore
Mr. Churchill’s visit to Washington at the end of 1941 continued into the first weeks of the new year, where his conversations with Mr. Roosevelt were directed to co-ordinating more closely the war efforts of Great Britain and the United States. On January 2 the two countries, along with China and the Soviet Union, signed the Declaration of the United Nations. The War Cabinet was reconstructed following the fall of Singapore to the Japanese on February 15 — the greatest military disaster in British history. The escape of the Scharnhorst and Gneisenau through the Channel added to public exasperation. Sir Stafford Cripps was sent to India with a new offer of Dominion status. The Japanese invasion of Burma led to the fall of Rangoon. In Libya, the British were driven back. Mr. Churchill demanded and received a vote of confidence.
Chapter II — The Anglo-Russian Treaty
At the beginning of April, Mr. Harry Hopkins and General Marshall came to London to discuss the military situation. The India Offer was rejected by Congress leaders. The Budget was presented, with massive increases in taxation. The Anglo-Russian Treaty of Alliance was signed in London on May 26 by Mr. Eden and Mr. Molotov. Rommel attacked in Libya, driving the British back; Tobruk fell on June 21, causing consternation in England. Mr. Churchill was again in Washington. The Eighth Army withdrew to El Alamein. A vote of censure was moved in the Commons but the Government won. The Beveridge fuel rationing plan was introduced.
Chapter III — The Demand for a Second Front
The Eighth Army made its stand at El Alamein. German advances in Russia continued, and a demand for a second front in Europe grew vociferous. An American mission arrived in England. The raid on Dieppe on August 19 cost heavy Canadian casualties but provided vital lessons. Mr. Churchill visited Moscow to inform Stalin that no second front could be opened in 1942. The King’s brother, the Duke of Kent, was killed in an air crash. The Trades Union Congress debated education policy and the second front. The Uthwatt Report on land development was published.
Chapter IV — The Allied Victory in North Africa
Parliament reassembled on September 29. A Bill for prolonging its own life for an eighth year was considered. General Montgomery’s plan of operations culminated in the decisive victory of El Alamein on October 23–24, with the pursuit of Rommel’s forces across Cyrenaica. On November 8, the Anglo-American expedition landed in North Africa (Operation Torch), changing the whole war situation. Rommel was driven from Cyrenaica and British forces entered Tunisia. The Beveridge Report on Social Insurance was published on December 1, receiving a favourable reception. The Commons condemned anti-Jewish atrocities. Rommel was further pursued, and fighting continued in Tunisia. A Minister-Resident was appointed in North-West Africa.
The Empire
Ireland
As a result of representations by Mr. de Valera, Northern Ireland was exempted from conscription at an early stage in the war. It therefore enjoyed all the economic advantages of the war industries boom while free from compulsory national service, resulting in an “unemployed roll of 17,000” despite the working class being fully employed.
Canada
Canada’s determination to marshal her total resources for the more vigorous prosecution of the war dominated all her activities throughout the year. The Speech from the Throne delivered on January 22 outlined a programme of total mobilisation.
The Union of South Africa
The year opened with a note of high hope sounded by Field-Marshal Smuts in his New Year broadcast. He reminded his listeners that the past year had been one of failures as well as great achievements, and appealed to his fellow South Africans for continued effort.
Australasia
Australia’s work for the Allied cause won high tribute from General MacArthur, the United States Commander-in-Chief in the Southern Pacific. Australia’s political history during 1942 was inextricably mingled with the general course of the World War.
India and Burma
Burma, after stubborn fighting, came under Japanese occupation. India was directly threatened with invasion and suffered air raids along her eastern shores. India’s accelerating contribution to the war effort and the fresh renown of her sons in far-flung battlefields marked the year.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
Throughout another difficult year of war, the League of Nations and the International Labour Organisation continued a wide range of activities, partly from Geneva and partly from war-time centres established in the United States, Canada, and elsewhere.
Chapter II — France and Italy
At the opening of 1942 the Darlan Ministry faced a new situation through the entry of the United States into the war. France remained under German occupation in the north, with the Vichy government in the south. In Italy, Mussolini’s regime continued the war alongside Germany.
Chapter III — Germany
Germany had not yet recovered from the excitement caused by the military reverses in Russia. For the first time the Army of the Third Reich had retreated, and the “final victory” over the Russians, announced in October 1941, was seen to be propaganda. The war on the Eastern Front consumed German resources at an unprecedented rate.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia — The Baltic States — Poland — Czechoslovakia — Hungary — Rumania — Yugoslavia — Turkey — Greece — Bulgaria
Throughout 1942 the Soviet Union continued to bear the main brunt of the war of the United Nations against Nazi Germany. The German summer offensive pushed deep into the Caucasus and towards Stalingrad. Poland, Czechoslovakia, and the Balkan states suffered under Axis occupation or pressure. Turkey remained neutral. Greece was under Axis occupation.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Finland each navigated the pressures of war. Belgium and the Netherlands steadfastly refused participation in the German “New Order.” Switzerland maintained its neutrality. Finland continued its “Continuation War” alongside Germany against the Soviet Union. Sweden remained neutral.
Chapter VI — The Middle East
