On January 29 a treaty was signed at Teheran between Iran on the one side and Great Britain and the Soviet Union on the other. Iraq, Palestine, Transjordan, Syria and Lebanon, and Arabia each faced the pressures of war, with Palestine remaining a centre of tension.
Chapter VII — The Far East
The year opened with a brilliant military success for China, as the Japanese advance on Changsha was repelled. Japan consolidated its conquests in Malaya, Burma, and the Philippines, establishing the so-called “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.” Thailand aligned itself with Japan.
Chapter VIII — Morocco and Egypt
On February 6 a bomb exploded on the quay at Tangier. Egypt, though nominally independent, was the base for the British Eighth Army and the scene of the decisive battles of El Alamein.
Chapter IX — America
The year 1942 opened in a very unpromising fashion for the United States. The Japanese lightning offensive in the Pacific had devastated American naval power at Pearl Harbor. However, the American war economy rapidly mobilised, and the tide began to turn with the naval victories of the Coral Sea and Midway. The United States became the “arsenal of democracy,” and the first American forces landed in North Africa in November.
Part II
Chronicle of Events in 1942
A day-by-day record of events from January to December, covering the war and home front in Britain and abroad.
Retrospect of Literature, Art, and Science
Literature, Art, Drama, the Cinema, Music, and the Biological and Physical Sciences were surveyed. Notable works included the continuing literary output under war conditions. The cinema saw the release of Mrs. Miniver and other wartime classics.
Finance and Commerce in 1942
A survey of the war economy, including war finance, taxation, industrial production, and trade under the conditions of total war.
Law in 1942
Legal developments including war-related legislation, prize court decisions, and emergency regulation cases.
Public Documents
I. India — Statement by the Prime Minister on the Indian constitutional offer.
II. India — Draft Declaration for Discussion with Indian Leaders (the Cripps Offer).
III. India — Text of Communiqué issued by the Governor-General.
IV. Declaration by United Nations (January 1, 1942).
V. Treaty with Iran (January 29, 1942).
VI. Treaty of Alliance between Great Britain and the U.S.S.R. (May 26, 1942).
VII. Nazi Crimes — Allied declaration on the punishment of war crimes.
VIII. Pact between Greece and Yugoslavia.
IX. Pact between Poland and Czechoslovakia.
Obituary of Eminent Persons Deceased in 1942
Notable figures who died during the year, including statesmen, soldiers, scientists, and artists.

sources/annual-register-1943.title: Annual Register 1943
sources/annual-register-1943.content:
The Annual Register for 1943
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The Casablanca Conference
When the year 1943 opened the British Eighth Army under General Montgomery was at Wadi el Kebir, two hundred miles east of Tripoli, pursuing Rommel’s Afrika Korps. By January 23 Tripoli was taken; the Casablanca Conference in mid-January produced the doctrine of unconditional surrender and co-ordinated Allied strategy for the Mediterranean. The chapter covers the Eighth Army’s advance into Tunisia, the political situation in North Africa, Chinese extra-territoriality renounced, the Beveridge Report debate, compulsory arbitration in mining, and the establishment of the Ministry of Town and Country Planning.
Chapter II — The Conquest of Tunisia and Sicily
The Budget for 1943-44 introduced pay-as-you-earn income tax and addressed external costs and price control. By May the Axis surrendered in Tunisia, yielding nearly 250,000 prisoners. In July the Allies invaded Sicily; Messina fell in August, opening the straits and securing the central Mediterranean. Churchill visited Washington. The chapter also covers the Bermuda Conference on refugees, the new Planning Bill, civil aviation policy, and the Conservative Party Conference.
Chapter III — The Invasion of Italy
The capture of Catania on August 5 opened new possibilities in the eastern Mediterranean. The Quebec Conference (Quadrant) in August set strategy for the Italian campaign and the cross-Channel invasion. Italy surrendered on September 3, the Badoglio government declared war on Germany, and Allied forces landed at Salerno. The Italian fleet surrendered at Malta. The chapter covers the TUC conference, trade union relations with the government, and the King’s Speech opening the new session.
Chapter IV — The Moscow, Cairo, and Teheran Conferences
In October General Smuts came to London for War Cabinet consultations, speaking of victory being in sight. The Moscow Conference of Foreign Ministers (Molotov, Eden, Hull) in October issued a declaration on post-war security and established the European Advisory Council. At Cairo and Teheran in November-December, Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin met for the first time, agreeing on the cross-Channel invasion (Overlord), the partition of Germany, and the post-war treatment of Poland.
The Empire
Chapter I — Ireland
In Northern Ireland a change of premiership brought Sir Basil Brooke to office in place of J. M. Andrews, forming a new Cabinet.
Chapter II — Canada
The year was one of historic achievement in Canada’s total war effort, marking the Dominion’s growing status as a world power, though political developments in Ontario and Quebec showed a trend towards lower taxation and resistance to conscription.
Chapter III — South Africa
Field-Marshal Smuts dominated the year with important utterances on the war and post-war world. He was returned with a decisive majority in the July general election. The chapter also covers Southern Rhodesia.
Chapter IV — Australasia
Australia’s Labour government, with equal Government and Opposition strength in the House at the start of the year, consolidated its position. New Zealand continued its war contribution alongside Australian forces in the Pacific theatre.
Chapter V — India and Burma
Neither the flowing tide of war in favour of the United Nations nor the arrival of the new Viceroy, Lord Wavell, brought any marked change in the obstinate Indian political situation. The policy of non-co-operation remained unrenounced; Burma remained under Japanese occupation.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
Against a background of conferences under United Nations auspices, the League continued to survive and render services, particularly in economic and social fields, refugee work, and the maintenance of international law.
Chapter II — France and Italy
French resistance to German occupation grew substantially. The Committee of National Liberation under General de Gaulle was recognised by the Allies. In Italy the fall of Mussolini, the Badoglio armistice, and the declaration of war on Germany marked the year.
Chapter III — Germany
For Germany 1943 was a black year. Unparalleled defeats began with the disaster at Stalingrad. German armies were driven from Africa with shame. At home conditions for the civilian population deteriorated badly as Allied bombing intensified.
Chapter IV — Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
Nineteen forty-three was a significant year on the Russian Front. The Stalingrad victory was followed by the liberation of the Caucasus, the great tank battle at Kursk, the crossing of the Dnieper, and the recapture of Kiev. Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Rumania, Yugoslavia, Turkey, Greece, Bulgaria, and Albania each experienced the shifting tides of war and diplomacy.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
Belgium remained under German occupation with intensified resistance. The Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Finland each navigated the pressures of war, occupation, blockade, and neutrality.
Chapter VI — The Middle East and North Africa
Egypt saw conversations on post-war independence. Palestine and Transjordan experienced continued tension. The Lebanon and Syria moved towards greater self-government. Iraq, Arabia, and the Arab Federation question occupied diplomatic attention. Persia and Morocco faced strategic pressures.
Chapter VII — The Far East
The military situation in China underwent little change; the initiative remained with the Japanese. China’s international position was strengthened by the renunciation of extra-territorial rights. Japan consolidated its occupied territories.
Chapter VIII — America
The United States accelerated war production towards the arsenal of democracy. A press interview by Mr. Wendell Willkie in December 1942 shaped early 1943’s political debates. Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, and Uruguay each dealt with the pressures of hemispheric solidarity, Axis influence, and alignment with the United Nations.
Part II
Chronicle of Events in 1943
Retrospect of Literature, Art, Drama, Cinema, Music, and Science in 1943
Covering literature, art (by Hilda F. Finberg), drama (by W. A. Darlington), the cinema (by Monica Ewer), music (by W. McN. Naught), biological sciences (by W. B. Brierley), and the physical sciences.
Finance and Commerce in 1943
Law in 1943
Public Documents

Treaty of Friendship between Soviet Russia and Czechoslovakia
Post-war Relief Agreement (UNRRA)
United Nations and Iran — Agreement

sources/annual-register-1944.title: Annual Register 1944
sources/annual-register-1944.content:
The Annual Register for 1944
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The Education Bill
At the opening of 1944 preparations were being actively made for the invasion of the Continent. The Teheran Conference had proclaimed the undertaking approaching; Eisenhower, Montgomery, and Tedder transferred headquarters from North Africa to Great Britain. The chapter covers the British air offensive, the Anzio landing and its disappointing results, the fight at Cassino, the Education Bill’s second reading and committee stage with the Government defeat and subsequent concessions, by-election surprises, the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Bill, Lord Beaverbrook on civil aviation, the British contribution to UNRRA, the National Health Service White Paper, the Royal Commission on Population, increased bombing of Germany, and the reorganisation of the Army.
Chapter II — The Invasion of Normandy
The invasion of the Continent had been timed for the beginning of June. The Budget for 1944-45 introduced the White Paper on Monetary Policy with Lord Keynes’s defence, the White Paper on Full Employment, electoral reform, and the coal industry agreement. The chapter covers the Wolfram agreements with Spain and Portugal, the Fleming Report on public schools, the Town and Country Planning Bill, D-Day (June 6), the capture of Bayeux, the fighting round Caen, the American capture of Cherbourg, the commencement of flying-bomb raids on London and the exodus from the capital, and the progress in Italy with the capture of Rome on June 4.
Chapter III — The Liberation of France and Belgium
The American breakout at Avranches proved the turning-point in the battle of Normandy. The Canadian offensive towards Falaise destroyed the German Seventh Army. A second Allied landing in Southern France followed. Belgium was liberated, Brussels and Antwerp fell to the British. The flying-bomb assault on London ended, though rocket bombs (V-2) began. The chapter covers the airborne attack on Holland, the British advance to Nijmegen, the attack on Arnhem, the securing of the Nijmegen salient, the clearing of the Scheldt estuary, the Quebec Conference (Octagon), the change in European political alignments, and the TUC congress.
Chapter IV — The Reconstruction Programme
The opening of the port of Antwerp heralded final victory in the near future. The chapter covers the expectation of a general election, Churchill’s Moscow visit in October, recognition of the Provisional French Government, the Dumbarton Oaks proposals for a new international organisation, the new Social Insurance scheme, the demobilisation plans, the redistribution of seats, the housing crisis and temporary housing, the Greek crisis and the clash between British troops and E.A.M., the Labour Party conference’s decision to remain in the Coalition, the Polish question, the disbandment of the Home Guard, and the fixing of agricultural prices.
The Empire
Chapter I — Ireland
In Northern Ireland the issue of a White Paper on Education was the most important event in a politically uneasy year. A measure to restore powers to Belfast Corporation caused internal differences. The suspension of travel between Great Britain and Eire continued.
Chapter II — Canada
Canada’s national war effort was vigorously maintained throughout the year. Political divisions from the continuous strain on man-power and economic conditions became more marked. Provincial general elections revealed divergent trends, and the Federal Government faced a Cabinet crisis at the close of the year.
Chapter III — South Africa and Southern Rhodesia
The year revealed more clearly the importance of South Africa’s productive contributions to the war effort. The Union astonished itself at its economic adaptability and five years of achievement, looking forward with confidence to solving post-war problems and contributing to the establishment of a stable world order.
Chapter IV — Australasia
A conference at Canberra of Australia and New Zealand representatives discussed problems of mutual interest arising from the war. The Australian government under Curtin consolidated its position. New Zealand continued its war contribution alongside Australian forces in the Pacific.
Chapter V — India and Burma
India’s contribution to the Allied war effort was brought more clearly to view by the exploits of her soldiers in Western theatres and the change on her Eastern flank from the defensive to the offensive. The year saw the enemy driven from her frontiers and from great parts of Northern and Central Burma. The Cripps offer’s rejection left the political question unresolved.
Foreign History
Chapter I — The League of Nations
More noticeably than in any previous war year, the League carried out its work in a disturbing atmosphere of uncertainty regarding its future status. Forty-five sovereign States maintained membership. The organisation continued to discharge duties connected with international co-operation while members discussed post-war international organisation elsewhere.
Chapter II — France and Italy
In France further changes made the Vichy Government a more reliable instrument of Nazi policy. Philippe Henriot replaced Paul Marion, presenting the Vichy case with force. General de Gaulle’s Committee of National Liberation gained recognition. In Italy, the Allied advance continued through the year, with the fall of Rome in June followed by further progress northward.
Chapter III — Germany
Four outstanding events marked the year for Germany: decisive military defeats in the East and the West, the attempt on Hitler’s life (July 20), the domination of the Army by the Nazi Party, and the slow but sure disintegration of the home front. The liberation of Italy and France and the advance of the Red Army towards German soil forced Germany onto the defensive.
Chapter IV — Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
At the beginning of the year the failure of the Western Powers to open a second front caused irritation in Russia. Leningrad was finally relieved in January. The Red Army advanced across the Dnieper into Poland, reaching the Vistula by August and the frontiers of East Prussia. The Warsaw uprising and its destruction, the Baltic States, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Rumania, Yugoslavia (Tito’s partisans), Turkey, Greece (the civil conflict), Bulgaria, and Albania each experienced the shifting tides of war and diplomacy.
Chapter V — Lesser States of Western and Northern Europe
For three-quarters of the year Belgium continued to experience the miseries of Nazi occupation — loss of liberty, forced labour, deportations, and mass arrests. The Netherlands endured the Hongerwinter. Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Iceland, Sweden, Norway, and Finland each navigated the pressures of war, blockade, and neutrality.
Chapter VI — The Middle East and North Africa
The sudden dismissal by the King of the Nahas Pasha Wafd Ministry and the Conference of Arab States at Alexandria in September were the two outstanding events in Egypt. Palestine and Transjordan experienced continued tension. Syria and the Lebanon moved towards independence. The Alexandria Protocol laid the foundation for the Arab League. Iraq and Iran faced strategic pressures.
Chapter VII — The Far East
Foreign and especially American observers in China grew highly critical of the Chiang Kai-shek regime and the Kuomintang, citing inefficiency and corruption. The Japanese offensive in China continued with the capture of Changsha, Hengyang, and advancing on Kweilin. The Allied counter-offensive in the Pacific gathered pace. Japan’s position deteriorated under mounting naval and air losses.
Chapter VIII — America
The United States’ course in 1944 reproduced the rhythm of the total Allied war effort. The first half was a period of preparation and tactical manoeuvre in the Presidential contest. The Republicans nominated Mr. Dewey; the Democrats renominated President Roosevelt for a fourth term. The Bretton Woods Conference established the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The Dumbarton Oaks Conference drafted proposals for the United Nations organisation. Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, and other Latin American states dealt with pressures of hemispheric solidarity and alignment with the United Nations.
Part II
Chronicle of Events in 1944
Retrospect of Literature, Art, Drama, Cinema, Music, and Science in 1944
Covering literature, art (by Hilda F. Finberg), drama (by W. A. Darlington), the cinema (by Monica Ewer), music (by W. McN. Naught), biological sciences (by W. B. Brierley), and the physical sciences.

sources/cabinet-office-to-1945.title: The Cabinet Office to 1945
sources/cabinet-office-to-1945.content:
The Cabinet Office to 1945
A structural and procedural history of the Cabinet Office from its origins in the Committee of Imperial Defence before 1914 through its formal creation in December 1916 to the end of the Churchill administration in July 1945, with a guide to the classification of its surviving records in the Public Record Office. Written by S.S. Wilson, Keeper of Public Records 1960–1966 and later administrative head of the Cabinet Office Historical Section, as a companion to the PRO Handbooks series on Cabinet and CID papers.

Chapter 1 — Introduction
Sets out the constitutional context: the development of Cabinet government from feudal monarchy through to the modern system of collective ministerial responsibility. Explains the creation of the Cabinet Office in December 1916 as the secretarial equipment necessary to record and notify the decisions of Lloyd George’s small War Cabinet, drawing on the existing secretariat of the Committee of Imperial Defence. Describes the nature and value of the Cabinet records as the most valuable single collection of modern official source material for British political history, while noting their limitations (created for current administration, not for historians).

Chapter 2 — The General Procedures of the Cabinet Office 1917–1945
Outlines the standard operating procedures that governed the Office throughout its first three decades: the Instructions to the Secretary (first circulated by Hankey in January 1917 and periodically revised); the circulation of memoranda in locked boxes; the preparation of the agenda by the Prime Minister through the secretary; the conduct of meetings (timing, chairmanship, attendance); the recording of Conclusions (replacing the earlier fuller Minutes from August 1919); handling of dissent; confidential annexes for matters of special secrecy; the weekly report to the Sovereign; the committee system; security arrangements; document symbols and referencing; registered files; the arrangement of Cabinet records in the PRO; staff composition; and the physical location of the Office in 2 Whitehall Gardens and later Great George Street.

Chapter 3 — The Cabinet and Committee of Imperial Defence before 1917
Traces the pre-history of Cabinet procedure from the eighteenth century, when the Cabinet was an informal body of the Sovereign’s principal ministers meeting without agenda or secretary. Shows how the Prime Minister’s letters to the Sovereign served as the sole record. Examines the misunderstandings and constitutional frictions that arose from the lack of formal procedure, the emergence of defence questions as a distinct category requiring systematic attention, the Esher Report of 1904 and the creation of the Committee of Imperial Defence, and Maurice Hankey’s appointment as secretary of the CID in 1912, which built the secretarial staff that would become the nucleus of the Cabinet Office in 1916.

Chapter 4 — The War Cabinet 1916–1919 and the Lloyd George Administration to October 1922
Covers the creation of Lloyd George’s five-member War Cabinet in December 1916 and the rapid establishment of its secretariat, including the ‘Garden Suburb’ of the Prime Minister’s personal advisers. Describes the new ministries created in 1916–17 (Shipping, Labour, Food, Pensions, National Service, Air). Examines the proliferation of memoranda (the GT and early CP series), the elaborate committee structure (War Policy, War Priorities, Eastern Committee, Economic Defence and Development, Home Affairs, Demobilisation), the Imperial War Cabinet and War Conference, the Peace Conference of 1919, the transition to a peace-time Cabinet of twenty members in November 1919, the Haldane Report on the Machinery of Government, and the growing political criticism that culminated in the Conservative election pledge to abolish the Cabinet Secretariat in 1922.

Chapter 5 — The Cabinet November 1922–September 1939
Examines the survival of the Cabinet Office after the Conservative victory of 1922, when Bonar Law’s government ‘provisionally’ approved the Instructions to the Secretary despite the party’s election pledge to abolish the secretariat. Follows the Office through the interwar period: Warren Fisher’s Treasury minute on the propriety of the secretariat, the establishment of the five-day rule for circulation of memoranda, the introduction of press communiqués in 1924, leakage of information, the custody of and access to Cabinet papers, the evolution of the 50-year and later 30-year rules for public access, the growth of the Cabinet committee system, subjects considered in Cabinet, political landmarks of the period, staff changes, and Hankey’s retirement in 1938 with Edward Bridges as his successor. Assesses Hankey’s overall contribution.

Chapter 6 — The Committee of Imperial Defence 1918–1939
Describes the revival of the CID after the First World War, initially through a Standing Defence Sub-Committee in 1920–23, which discussed the Singapore base, the Washington Conference and the future of the RAF. Covers the CID’s monthly meetings through the 1920s and their decline in the early 1930s before a significant increase after 1935. Examines the CID’s work on the ‘ten-year assumption’ (the rule that no major war would occur within ten years), the organisation for defence planning, grand strategy, disarmament policy, the rearmament programme after 1935, the creation of the Minister for Co-ordination of Defence (Inskip, later Chatfield) in 1936, and the CID’s relations with the Dominions.

Chapter 7 — The Committee of Civil Research and the Economic Advisory Council
Covers the post-Haldane Report attempt to extend the CID model into civil policy. Traces the establishment of the Committee of Civil Research under Balfour in 1925, its investigation into the iron and steel industry and other economic questions through a score of expert sub-committees, and its gradual decline. Describes its replacement under MacDonald by the Economic Advisory Council in 1930, the work of the Committee of Economists (including Keynes), and the later standing committees on Scientific Research and on Economic Information that reported to the Cabinet during the rearmament period. Also covers the Cabinet Committee on Non-Intervention in Spain.

Chapter 8 — Imperial and International Conferences 1915–1939
Provides a comprehensive chronological list of the imperial and international conferences for which the Cabinet Office provided the secretariat for the United Kingdom delegation from 1915 to 1939. These include the Anglo-French and Allied conferences and Supreme War Council meetings of 1917–18, the Imperial War Cabinets and Conferences, the Peace Conference, the Washington Disarmament Conference (1921–22), the Genoa Conference (1922), the Imperial Conferences of 1923, 1926, 1930 and 1937, the London Naval Conference (1930), the Ottawa Imperial Economic Conference (1932), the Lausanne Conference (1932), and many others.

Chapter 9 — The War Cabinet 1939–1945
The longest and most detailed chapter, covering the supreme control machinery of the Second World War. Begins with Hankey’s 1928 and 1938 papers to the CID on the options for supreme control. Describes Chamberlain’s nine-member War Cabinet of September 1939, Churchill’s five-member coalition War Cabinet of May 1940, and the Caretaker Cabinet of May–July 1945. Examines general procedure (agenda, circulation of memoranda, meetings, minutes, conclusions and confidential annexes), the contrast between Chamberlain’s orderly administration and Churchill’s more erratic methods, ministerial appointments overseas, the elaborate committee structure (Defence Committee (Operations), Defence Committee (Supply), the Chiefs of Staff Committee and its 2,000+ meetings, the Military Co-ordination Committee, the Combined Chiefs of Staff, the Battle of the Atlantic Committee, Night Air Defence, the Tank Parliament, the Lord President’s Committee, the Import Executive, the Production Executive, the Manpower Committee, the Economic Section, the Central Statistical Office, the Ministry of Reconstruction). Covers international meetings, staff complement, and closes with an assessment of Churchill’s impact and the Office’s achievement.

Chapter 10 — The Historical Section
Traces the origins of the Historical Section to Esher’s 1906 recommendation for a department to compile naval and military history under the CID, the completion of the history of the South African War and the Russo-Japanese War, and the decision of 1914 that the section should focus on wars involving Britain. Describes its transfer to the aegis of the Cabinet Office and its main work: the Official Histories of military operations in the First World War (the term ‘Official’ was dropped in the Second World War to avoid misunderstanding about the status of the accounts), and the civil and military histories series for the Second World War. Notes that authors were given free access to official documents and facilities for consulting participants, while respecting constitutional conventions on collective responsibility and civil service anonymity.

Annexes
The volume includes fourteen annexes providing documentary and statistical material:

Recollections of Cabinet Procedure before 1917 — Sir Herbert Creedy’s 1949 memoir of pre-war practice
The War Cabinet: Rules of Procedure, January 1917 — Hankey’s original rules of procedure
Cabinet Procedure, April 1936 — The codified instructions to the Secretary circulated as CP 88(36), with appendices covering Cabinet committees, CID procedure, and the Economic Advisory Council, plus the Treasury minute establishing the Committee of Civil Research
Notes on War Cabinet Procedure, May 1943 — The procedural rules for Churchill’s War Cabinet
Staff List, 1 January 1945 — Full establishment of the War Cabinet Office
List of Administrative Staff 1916–1945 — Names and tenures of senior staff
Notes to Tables in Annexes 7(a), 7(b), 8 and 9 — Explanatory notes
Meetings of Cabinet, CID and Committees, and Statistics of Staff 1916–1939 — Statistical tables
Meetings of War Cabinet and Committees, and Statistics of Staff 1939–1945 — Statistical tables
Ministers Originating Cabinet Business 1923–1945 — Analysis of papers by originating minister
Ministers Originating Papers to the Lord President’s Committee 1940–1945
Histories Sponsored by the Cabinet Office — List of published official histories
List of Committees (in three parts: before 1923, 1923–1939, 1939–1945)
List of Cabinet Office Posts — Classification and salary scales


Sources

Wilson, S.S. — The Cabinet Office to 1945 (Public Record Office Handbooks No. 17) — London: Her Majesty’s Stationery Office, 1975. ISBN 0 11 440034 2.
Digitised by the Internet Archive in 2022 with funding from Kahle/Austin Foundation.

sources/democratic-ideals-reality.title: Democratic Ideals and Reality
sources/democratic-ideals-reality.content:
Summary
Halford Mackinder’s Democratic Ideals and Reality is the founding text of modern geopolitics, introducing his famous Heartland thesis. Written in the final months of World War I and published in 1919, the book argues that the age of Columbian exploration is over and that the world has become a closed geopolitical system dominated by the vast Eurasian “World-Island.” Mackinder warns the democratic powers that the post-war settlement must prevent any single power — particularly Germany or Russia — from dominating the Heartland (roughly Eastern Europe and Central Asia), lest it build a world empire. His core dictum — “Who rules East Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island; who rules the World-Island commands the World” — became one of the most influential geopolitical axioms of the twentieth century.
Source
Mackinder, Halford John. Democratic Ideals and Reality: A Study in the Politics of Reconstruction. New York: Henry Holt and Company, 1919.
Full raw OCR text available at raw.txt
Chapters
Preface
Dated 1st February 1919. Mackinder explains that the book’s ideas were first developed in his 1904 paper “The Geographical Pivot of History” and in a 1905 article on “Man-power as a Measure of National and Imperial Strength.” The war has confirmed, not shaken, his earlier views.
Chapter I — Perspective (p. 3)
The future and peace; causes of past wars; growth of opposing interests; danger of merely juridical conceptions of the League of Nations; the possibility of a World-Tyranny; the problem stated.
Chapter II — Social Momentum (p. 8)
Democratic Idealism, its successive tragedies, and its relation to Reality; the Economic Reality of the “Going Concern”; the organizers of Going Concerns; the emergence of organizers from Revolution; the organizer and social discipline; the great Organizer is the great Realist; democratic prejudice against Experts; the organizer thinks strategically; Napoleon; Bismarck; the strategical mentality of Prussia; “Kultur” and strategy; the German war map; strategical thought in Economics; Democracy thinks ethically; “No annexations, no indemnities”; the necessity of reckoning with both geographical and economic Reality.
Chapter III — The Seaman’s Point of View (p. 38)
The Unity of the Ocean, the first geographical Reality; consequences not yet fully accepted; a historical view; contending river-powers in Egypt; the Nile “closed” by land-power; contending sea-powers in the Mediterranean; the Mediterranean “closed” by land-power; the Latin Peninsula as a sea-base; the encompassing of the World-Promontory by sea-power from the Latin peninsular base; division within the Latin European Peninsula; the opportunity for sea-power from the lesser but insular sea-base of Britain; of sea-bases in general; of sea-power in the Great War; the World-Island; the ultimate base of sea-power.
Chapter IV — The Landsman’s Point of View (p. 90)
The World-Island seen from within; the Heartland physically defined; the other Natural Regions; the Arabian Centerland; the mobile riders and the plowmen; the Arab bid for World Empire; the Steppes-belt; the Tartar invasions and their consequences; the Tibetan Heights and the N.W. entries to China and India; the open access from the Heartland to Arabia and to Europe; the Heartland strategically defined; the Black Sea basin included; the Baltic basin included; the Heartland as real a physical fact as the World-Island; the ultimate citadel of land-power.
Chapter V — The Rivalry of Empires (p. 141)
The Cossack advance over the Heartland; the Russian Homeland sharply delimited; the real Europe divided into East and West Europe; history of the relations of East and West Europe; their fundamental opposition and essential difference; German and Slav in East Europe; Trafalgar and the two streams of history; Britain and the Not-Europe; East Europe really within the Heartland; British and French policy in the Nineteenth Century; the Great War caused by the German attempt to control East Europe and the Heartland; the Economic Reality of organized man-power — the Going Concern; Political Economy and National Economy; the great Economic change of 1878; the German policy of stimulating growth of man-power to occupy the Heartland; Laissez-faire also a policy of Empire; the clash of the two policies as the inevitable consequence of two Going Concerns.
Chapter VI — The Freedom of Nations (p. 183)
We won the War but were nearly defeated; the hypothetical German Heartland Empire; the Heartland as the persistent geographical threat to world liberty; Germany’s mistake of the Western offensive; Hamburg and the man-power policy; the necessity of dividing East Europe and the Heartland into three, not two, State-systems; the peoples of the Middle Tier; feasibility of the League of Nations if this is done; no predominant partner; reckoning with Going Concerns; reasonable equality of power among members of the League; certain strategical positions of world importance; the Going Concern in the future and the unequal growth of Nations; the ideal of the Independent Nation of balanced economic development; tragedies of the Going Concern; the policy of truly free nations which makes for Peace.
Chapter VII — The Freedom of Men (p. 226)
Whether men and women will be more free in such free Nations; the need of basing organization within the Nation on localities; the alternative organization based on nation-wide classes and interests leads inevitably to international war of classes; the ideal of balanced provinces within balanced nations; such organization gives greatest opportunity to greatest number of men; the cause of the Nationality movement; opposed to undue centralization; fraternal nations must be balanced economically and formed of fraternal provinces; Fraternity depends on controlling the development of Going Concerns.
Postscript (p. 252)
The recent General Election, its meaning in a world setting; of the saving virtue of Neighborliness.
Appendix (p. 257)
Note on an Incident at the Quai d’Orsay, 25th January, 1919.
Index (p. 259)
Maps and Diagrams
