sources/economic-consequences-peace.title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
sources/economic-consequences-peace.content:
The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1920)
John Maynard Keynes’s devastating critique of the Versailles Treaty, arguing that the reparations and economic clauses would destroy the delicate fabric of European prosperity and lead to catastrophe.
Summary
Written in the summer of 1919 immediately after Keynes’s resignation from the British Treasury delegation at the Paris Peace Conference, The Economic Consequences of the Peace is a passionate polemic against the Treaty of Versailles. Keynes argues that the victors imposed a Carthaginian peace that ignored the Fourteen Points upon which Germany had surrendered, demanded reparations far beyond Germany’s capacity to pay, and destroyed the intricate economic organization upon which prewar European prosperity had depended. The book predicts that these policies will lead to economic collapse, social revolution, and ultimately another war — a prophecy widely seen as fulfilled by the rise of Nazism and the Second World War.
Source
Keynes, John Maynard. The Economic Consequences of the Peace. Introduction by Robert Lekachman. New York: Penguin Books (Penguin Twentieth-Century Classics), 1988.
First published in the United States by Harcourt, Brace and Howe, Inc., 1920. Reissued with an introduction by Robert Lekachman by Harper & Row, 1971. Published in Penguin Books 1988, reissued 1995.
eISBN: 978-1-101-16167-8
Full raw OCR text available at raw.txt (466,048 bytes)
Chapters
Preface (November 1919)
Keynes explains his position as British Treasury representative at the Paris Peace Conference until June 7, 1919, and his resignation when it became evident that no substantial modification of the draft terms could be hoped for. He states that his objections are of a public character based on facts known to the whole world.
Introduction — Robert Lekachman (1971)
Lekachman’s substantial introductory essay situates the book as a great polemic in the tradition of Malthus, Burke, and Marx. He examines Keynes’s portrayal of prewar Europe, his character sketches of the Council of Four, his analysis of reparations, and the subsequent history of the Dawes and Young Plans. Lekachman also discusses the critique by Etienne Mantoux in The Carthaginian Peace and assesses Keynes’s ultimate legacy.
Chapter I — Introductory
Keynes opens with his famous observation that few people realize the “intensely unusual, unstable, complicated, unreliable, temporary nature of the economic organization by which Western Europe has lived for the last half century.” He contrasts the obliviousness of England with the tremors felt in continental Europe, and describes the atmosphere of the Paris Conference as a nightmare of futility, smallness, and impending catastrophe. He warns that France and Italy, in abusing their victory to destroy Germany and Austria-Hungary, invite their own destruction through the deep economic and psychic bonds that tie Europe together.
Chapter II — Europe Before the War
A celebrated portrait of the pre-1914 European economic order: the free movement of goods, capital, and people; the gold standard; the security of property; and the social compact by which the rich accumulated capital and the poor accepted inequality. Keynes traces the demographic pressures of German, Austro-Hungarian, and Russian population growth, the organization of industry around coal, iron, and transport, and the psychological foundation of prewar stability. He warns that the war has “disclosed the possibility of consumption to all and the vanity of abstinence to many,” undermining the double bluff on which the capitalist system depended. The chapter concludes with an analysis of Europe’s deteriorating balance of trade, the loss of foreign investments, and the new dependence on American food supplies.
Chapter III — The Conference
Keynes’s famous character sketches of the Council of Four. Clemenceau is portrayed as the most formidable member — an old man with one illusion (France) and one disillusion (mankind), pursuing a Bismarckian policy of a Carthaginian peace to permanently weaken Germany. President Wilson is depicted as a “generously intentioned man” lacking the intellectual equipment to match Clemenceau and Lloyd George in face-to-face negotiations, whose moral authority evaporated in the morass of Paris. Lloyd George appears as brilliantly clever but inconstant and more concerned with electoral politics than with the reconstruction of Europe. Keynes traces how Clemenceau’s vision of permanent security through German destruction came to dominate the settlement.
Chapter IV — The Treaty
Keynes examines the legal basis of the peace, arguing that Germany surrendered in reliance on a solemn contract — the Fourteen Points and the Allied Note of November 5, 1918 — and that the Treaty constitutes a breach of this engagement. He then enumerates the economic provisions of the Treaty: the destruction of Germany’s overseas commerce (mercantile marine, colonies, foreign investments, and export connections); the seizure of her coal and iron resources (the Saar, Upper Silesia, and the delivery of coal to France, Belgium, and Italy); and the dismantling of her transport and tariff system. The chapter concludes that “little has been overlooked which might impoverish Germany now or obstruct her development in future.”
Chapter V — Reparation
The longest and most technically detailed chapter. Keynes examines the categories of damage claimable under the pre-Armistice contract, the vast expansion of claims to include war pensions and separation allowances (which multiplied the bill many times), and the actual figures set by the Treaty — a sum far beyond Germany’s capacity to pay. He estimates Germany’s maximum possible annual payment at 500 million (interest on a capital sum of 10 billion) and analyzes the sources from which Germany could pay: gold, foreign securities, shipping, and exports. He demonstrates that the transfer problem — Germany’s need to earn foreign currency through exports — was insuperable given Allied tariff barriers and the destruction of German productive capacity. He also critiques the Reparation Commission’s arbitrary powers and the lack of any fixed total sum in the Treaty.
Chapter VI — Europe After the Treaty
Keynes opens: “This chapter must be one of pessimism.” Keynes surveys the devastation wrought by the war and the Treaty across Europe: the breakdown of currency and credit, the inflation, the shortage of food and raw materials, the collapse of trade, and the disintegration of the transport system. He examines the plight of Germany, Austria, Hungary, and the new successor states. He notes that the Treaty makes no provision for the economic rehabilitation of Europe, the stabilization of new states, the reclamation of Russia, or any compact of economic solidarity among the Allies themselves. The chapter ends with a grim warning about the human cost of starvation and disease, citing medical reports on the tuberculosis and rickets epidemics in Central Europe.
Chapter VII — Remedies
Keynes proposes a four-part program for salvaging Europe from the consequences of the Treaty: (1) revision of the Treaty itself, including a fixed and reduced reparations total, the cancellation of inter-Allied war debts, and the return of Germany’s economic resources; (2) the settlement of inter-Ally indebtedness through a general cancellation; (3) an international loan and currency reform to stabilize the European exchanges and provide working capital for reconstruction; and (4) the opening of relations between Central Europe and Russia, including the rehabilitation of Russian production and trade. He argues that these measures require new leadership, as the Council of Four cannot undo its own work. The book concludes with a famous peroration on the “moral problem” of statesmanship and a plea for magnanimity.
Appendix — Notes
Keynes includes 173 numbered footnotes providing supporting data, calculations, and references for the arguments in the main text.

sources/hankey-man-of-secrets-vol1.title: [source] Hankey: Man of Secrets, Vol. I: 1877–1918 (Roskill, 1970)
sources/hankey-man-of-secrets-vol1.content:
Hankey: Man of Secrets, Vol. I: 1877–1918 (1970)
Stephen Roskill’s authorised biography of Maurice Hankey, the long-serving Secretary to the Committee of Imperial Defence and the War Cabinet — from his childhood and early naval career through his central role in British strategic decision-making during the First World War.
Source
Roskill, Stephen Wentworth. Hankey, Man of Secrets. Vol. I: 1877–1918. Annapolis, Md.: Naval Institute Press, 1970.
This is the first volume of a three-volume authorised biography of Maurice Hankey (1877–1963), based on his private papers, diaries, and official documents. Hankey served as Assistant Secretary and later Secretary of the Committee of Imperial Defence (1908–1914), and as Secretary to the War Cabinet (1914–1918) and the Imperial War Cabinet. He was present at nearly every major strategic decision of the war, from the Dardanelles expedition to the introduction of convoys.
Digital scan: Northwestern University Library copy.
Text
raw/hankey-vol1/raw.txt — 1,729,000 characters, OCR text from the 1970 edition (Chapters I–XX).
Contents
Chapter I — The Man and his Making
Hankey’s family background: the Hankey family tradition of public service, his father Robert Alers Hankey and his mother Helen Bakewell. His childhood in Adelaide and Brighton. Education at Rugby School. Early influences and the formation of his character. His decision to enter the Royal Marine Artillery.
Chapter II — In the Mediterranean Fleet, 1900–1901
Hankey’s service as a young Royal Marine officer in the Mediterranean Fleet. Life on the Mediterranean station. His first experience of naval routine, service politics, and the workings of the British Empire’s naval presence. His growing interest in strategy and administration.
Chapter III — From the Naval Intelligence Department to the Committee of Imperial Defence, 1902–1908
Hankey’s transfer to the Naval Intelligence Department at the Admiralty. The work of the NID under Prince Louis of Battenberg and Admiral Ottley. His first exposure to strategic planning. The origins of the Committee of Imperial Defence under Balfour. Hankey’s move to the C.I.D. as a staff officer.
Chapter IV — Assistant Secretary, Committee of Imperial Defence, 1908–1912
Hankey’s appointment as Assistant Secretary of the C.I.D. under Sir Charles Ottley. The structure and functioning of the C.I.D. The invasion scare debates. The Ballard-Hankey committee on economic pressure against Germany. Hankey’s evolving views on imperial defence. His growing reputation among ministers and service chiefs.
Chapter V — Secretary of the Committee of Imperial Defence, 1912–1914
Hankey succeeds Ottley as Secretary of the C.I.D. His work on the strategic planning for a European war. The development of the War Book. The Belgian neutrality question. The Agadir crisis and its aftermath. Hankey’s relationship with Asquith, Churchill, and Grey. The state of British preparedness in July 1914.
Chapter VI — The Test of War, August 1914–May 1915
The outbreak of war and the mobilisation of the C.I.D. machinery. Hankey’s role as the channel between the services and the Cabinet. The passage of the British Expeditionary Force. The first months of the war at sea. The escape of the Goeben and Breslau. Hankey’s growing frustration with the conduct of the war.
Chapter VII — Under the First Coalition, May–August 1915
The formation of the first Coalition government under Asquith. Hankey’s adjustment to the new political landscape. The Dardanelles campaign — the planning, the landings, and the developing stalemate. Hankey’s private doubts and his diary entries. The munitions crisis and the establishment of the Ministry of Munitions under Lloyd George.
Chapter VIII — Frustration and Disaster, August–December 1915
The failure at the Dardanelles. The decision to evacuate. Hankey’s role in the strategic debates. The Salonika expedition and the dispersion of Allied effort. The rising pressure on Asquith’s government. Hankey’s assessment of the military leadership.
Chapter IX — The Crumbling of the Coalition, January–May 1916
The Military Service Act and the introduction of conscription. The Easter Rising in Ireland and its effect on British politics. The Battle of Jutland (May 31–June 1, 1916) and its aftermath. Hankey’s observations on the naval battle and the command controversies. The ongoing crisis of confidence in Asquith’s leadership.
Chapter X — The Dardanelles Commission. The First Coalition under Pressure, June–October 1916
The Dardanelles Commission of inquiry. Hankey’s evidence and his private views on the campaign. The Somme offensive and the terrible casualties. The political manoeuvring against Asquith. The rising influence of Lloyd George. Hankey’s position as the permanent official at the centre.
Chapter XI — The Fall of the First Coalition, October–December 1916
The political crisis of December 1916. Lloyd George’s challenge to Asquith. Hankey’s role in the transition. The fall of the Asquith coalition and the formation of the Lloyd George War Cabinet. Hankey’s survival and his appointment as Secretary of the new War Cabinet.
Chapter XII — The War Cabinet in Action, December 1916–March 1917
The establishment of the War Cabinet. Hankey’s innovations in Cabinet procedure: the secretariat system, the circulation of conclusions, the control of agenda. The change in the direction of the war. The unrestricted U-boat campaign and the crisis of British shipping. The decision to adopt the convoy system.
Chapter XIII — The Darkening Scene, April–June 1917
The failure of the Nivelle offensive and the French mutinies. The Russian Revolution and its effect on Allied strategy. The entry of the United States into the war. Hankey’s assessment of the new strategic situation. The problems of co-ordination with the Allies. The Imperial War Cabinet.
Chapter XIV — Britain the Cornerstone, July–September 1917
The third battle of Ypres (Passchendaele). Hankey’s visits to the front and his impressions of Haig and the commanders. The growth of the Cabinet Secretariat. Hankey’s role in the co-ordination of Allied strategy. The reinforcement of the Italian front.
Chapter XV — Stalemate in Flanders: Disaster in Italy, October–December 1917
The conclusion of the Passchendaele offensive. The Italian disaster at Caporetto. The dispatch of British and French divisions to Italy. The Supreme War Council at Versailles. Hankey’s role in the creation of inter-Allied machinery. The war-weariness and the growing demand for a negotiated peace.
Chapter XVI — Calm before the Storm, January–March 1918
The preparation for the German spring offensives. Hankey’s work on the allocation of manpower. The debate over unity of command. The appointment of Foch as Allied Generalissimo. The state of British and Imperial forces on the eve of the great German attack.
Chapter XVII — Lloyd George and the Soldiers, April–May 1918
The German spring offensive (Operation Michael) and the crisis of March–April 1918. The political fallout: Lloyd George’s conflict with the military leadership. Hankey’s mediating role. The debate over extending the blockade. The mobilisation of imperial resources.
Chapter XVIII — The Crisis Overcome, May–July 1918
The turning of the tide. The second battle of the Marne. The Allied counter-offensive. Hankey’s role in the co-ordination of supply and transport. The planning for the final campaign. The growing confidence of the Allied leadership.
Chapter XIX — The Scent of Victory, July–August 1918
The Battle of Amiens (August 8) and the “hundred days.” The collapse of the German will to fight. Hankey’s diary entries on the final phase. The planning for the armistice. The question of the armistice terms.
Chapter XX — Victory at Last, September–November 1918
The final Allied offensives. The German request for an armistice. The negotiations and the signing of the Armistice on November 11, 1918. Hankey’s reflections on four years of war. The transition to peace. The demobilisation of the war machinery. Hankey’s position at the close of the war.
Appendix A — Specimen of Hankey’s Rough Notes for Minutes of a Cabinet Meeting
A facsimile and transcription of Hankey’s manuscript notes, showing his method of recording Cabinet discussions.
Appendix B — Administration Staff who Served in the Cabinet Office 1908–1918
A list of the administrative staff of the Cabinet Office from its origins in the C.I.D. through to the end of the war.

sources/hankey-man-of-secrets-vol2.title: [source] Hankey: Man of Secrets, Vol. II: 1919–1931 (Roskill, 1972)
sources/hankey-man-of-secrets-vol2.content:
Hankey: Man of Secrets, Vol. II: 1919–1931 (1972)
Stephen Roskill’s authorised biography of Maurice Hankey, from his work at the Paris Peace Conference through a decade of international conferences, the fall of the Coalition government, and the crisis of 1931 — the period of his greatest influence as Secretary to the Cabinet and the Committee of Imperial Defence.
Source
Roskill, Stephen Wentworth. Hankey, Man of Secrets. Vol. II: 1919–1931. Annapolis, Md.: Naval Institute Press, 1972.
This second volume of three covers Hankey’s central role in British government during the post-war decade. He served as Secretary to the War Cabinet (continuing from Vol. I) and then as the first Secretary to the peacetime Cabinet, Secretary to the Committee of Imperial Defence, Secretary-General to numerous international conferences, and Clerk to the Privy Council. His position gave him an unrivalled vantage point on every major question of British policy — the peace settlement, imperial relations, defence policy, the rise of Labour, and the economic collapse of 1931.
Digital scan: Northwestern University Library copy.
Text
raw/hankey-vol2/raw.txt — 1,584,000 characters, OCR text from the 1972 edition (Chapters I–XVIII).
Contents
Chapter I — The First Steps to Peace, November–December 1918
The immediate aftermath of the Armistice. Hankey’s recovery from influenza and his return to the Cabinet Office. The Imperial War Conference and the winding down of the war machinery. The planning for the Peace Conference. Hankey’s role in shaping British representation. The King’s commendation of the Cabinet Secretariat. The demobilisation crisis. Preliminary discussions on the shape of the peace.
Chapter II — The Hard Road to Peace, January–February 1919
The Paris Peace Conference opens. Hankey’s role as secretary to the British delegation and his relations with Lloyd George. The organisation of the conference machinery. The clash of personalities — Lloyd George, Clemenceau, Wilson, Orlando. The Council of Ten and the difficulty of managing the conference. The question of German reparations and war guilt. Hankey’s diary impressions of the key figures.
Chapter III — The Council of Four, March–May 1919
The delegation of business from the Council of Ten to the Council of Four (Lloyd George, Clemenceau, Wilson, Orlando). Hankey’s role as the sole secretary to the Four, recording their private discussions. The drafting of the Treaty of Versailles. Hankey’s observations on Wilson, the League of Nations, and the compromise on the Rhineland. The crisis over the French demand for security. The delivery of the peace terms to the Germans.
Chapter IV — The Treaties Signed, June–August 1919
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles (June 28, 1919). Hankey’s role in the subsequent conferences on the minor treaties — St. Germain, Neuilly, Trianon, Sèvres. The return to London and the resumption of normal Cabinet government. The King’s audience and the honours list. Hankey’s assessment of the peace settlement.
Chapter V — The End of the War Cabinet, September–December 1919
The transition from the War Cabinet to a peacetime Cabinet system. Hankey’s fight to preserve the Cabinet Secretariat against critics who saw it as Lloyd George’s instrument. The consolidation of the C.I.D. under the new structure. The Irish crisis and the beginning of the Anglo-Irish War. The financial retrenchment and the Geddes Axe.
Chapter VI — Europe in Disarray, January–April 1920
The continuing instability of post-war Europe. The conferences at San Remo, Hythe, and Boulogne. Hankey’s role as Secretary-General of these conferences. The problem of German reparations and the Spa Conference. The Russo-Polish War and the British response. The question of the Ottoman settlement and the growing crisis in the Middle East.
Chapter VII — The Era of Conferences I, May–December 1920
The Lympne conferences and the Anglo-French entente. Hankey’s method of managing international conferences — his mastery of procedure, drafting, and agenda control. The economic difficulties and the unemployment crisis at home. The mounting trouble in Ireland. The Government of Ireland Act and the escalation of violence.
Chapter VIII — The Era of Conferences II, January–October 1921
The continuation of the conference system. The London Conference on Reparations. The Upper Silesia dispute. Hankey’s role in the Anglo-Irish negotiations that led to the Treaty of December 1921. The Washington Naval Conference on disarmament and the limitation of naval armaments. The Chanak crisis and the beginnings of the Near Eastern emergency.
Chapter IX — The Washington and Genoa Conferences, November 1921–May 1922
The Washington Conference on Naval Disarmament: the Five-Power Treaty, the Four-Power Treaty, and the Nine-Power Treaty. Hankey’s attendance and his assessment of the results. The Genoa Economic Conference (April–May 1922) and the question of Russian debt. The collapse of the Genoa Conference and the separate Treaty of Rapallo between Germany and Russia.
Chapter X — The Near East Crisis and the Fall of Lloyd George, June–October 1922
The Chanak crisis: the Turkish nationalist advance under Kemal Ataturk, the burning of Smyrna, and the British threat of war. Hankey’s record of the Cabinet’s deliberations. The fall of Lloyd George’s Coalition government (October 1922). The Carlton Club meeting and the Conservative decision to leave the Coalition. Hankey’s assessment of Lloyd George’s fall.
Chapter XI — Under Bonar Law. The Fight for the Cabinet Secretariat, October–December 1922
Bonar Law forms a Conservative government. The attack on the Cabinet Secretariat as a Lloyd George inheritance. Hankey’s defence of his office and his survival. The reorganisation of the Cabinet Office. The continuation of the Irish settlement. The Lausanne Conference and the Turkish treaty.
Chapter XII — From Bonar Law to Baldwin, January–December 1923
Bonar Law’s resignation and the succession of Stanley Baldwin. Hankey’s adjustment to the new Prime Minister. The question of war debts and reparations — the Dawes Plan. The Ruhr occupation and the French-German crisis. Baldwin’s decision to go to the country on protection. The general election of December 1923 and the return of a hung parliament.
Chapter XIII — The First Labour Government, January–October 1924
The first Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald. Hankey’s relations with the new ministers — his assessment of MacDonald, Snowden, and Henderson. The continuation of the Dawes Plan negotiations. The London Conference on Reparations. The recognition of Soviet Russia. The Zinoviev letter affair and the fall of the Labour government. The general election of October 1924.
Chapter XIV — Back to Baldwin, November 1924–December 1925
Baldwin’s second government. Hankey’s work on the reorganisation of the C.I.D. The Locarno Treaties and the question of European security. The Geneva Protocol and the limitations of disarmament. The return to the gold standard. The Imperial Conference of 1925 and the question of dominion status. Hankey’s role in imperial relations.
Chapter XV — The Essentials of Defence, January 1926–May 1929
The General Strike of 1926 and Hankey’s role in the government’s emergency machinery. The C.I.D. sub-committees on imperial defence. The Ten-Year Rule and the debate over defence expenditure. Hankey’s growing concern about the state of British defences. The Washington Naval Treaty renewal and the naval arms race. Hankey’s work on the Singapore naval base. The Kellogg-Briand Pact.
Chapter XVI — The Second Labour Government, June–December 1929
MacDonald’s second Labour government. Hankey’s relationship with the new administration. The question of Indian constitutional reform — the Simon Commission and the Round Table Conference. The Wall Street Crash and the beginning of the Great Depression. The Young Plan on reparations. The London Naval Conference preparations.
Chapter XVII — A Year of Conferences, 1930
The London Naval Conference (January–April 1930). The Imperial Conference of 1930. Hankey’s role as Secretary-General. The Statute of Westminster and the evolution of Dominion autonomy. The economic deterioration. The May Committee on national expenditure. The rise of unemployment and the growing pressure on the pound.
Chapter XVIII — Crisis, 1931
The financial crisis of August 1931. The collapse of the Labour government. The formation of the National Government under MacDonald. Hankey’s diary record of the crisis. The bank rate, the gold standard, and the budget. The run on the pound and the decision to leave gold (September 21, 1931). Hankey’s draft “Manifesto” and his assessment of the political and economic situation. The general election of October 1931 and the overwhelming National Government victory. The end of an era.

sources/hankey-man-of-secrets-vol3.title: Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. III: 1931-1963
sources/hankey-man-of-secrets-vol3.content:
Summary
This third and final volume of Stephen Roskill’s biography of Maurice Hankey covers the period from 1931 to 1963, tracing Hankey’s career from his final years as Cabinet Secretary through the rearmament debates, his Empire tour, the Abyssinia crisis, his elevation to the peerage and appointment as Minister without Portfolio in Chamberlain’s war cabinet, his dismissal by Churchill in 1942, and his post-war years as a critic of government policy and elder statesman. The volume draws extensively on Hankey’s private papers and official documents to illuminate the inner workings of British defence policy and high-level decision-making across three decades of war and crisis.
Source
Roskill, Stephen Wentworth. Hankey, Man of Secrets. Vol. III: 1931-1963. London: Collins, 1974. ISBN 0 00 211332 5.
Full raw OCR text available at raw.txt
Chapters
Foreword and Acknowledgments (p. 1)
Roskill acknowledges the individuals and institutions who assisted with the research and preparation of the third and final volume, including Hankey’s family and the custodians of the relevant archives.
1. First Steps to Recovery. September 1931–December 1932 (p. 21)
Covers the immediate aftermath of the 1931 financial crisis and the formation of the National Government. Hankey continues as Cabinet Secretary, managing the machinery of government through a period of severe economic retrenchment while beginning to confront the emerging strategic challenges posed by Japan’s invasion of Manchuria and the growing threat from Germany.
2. The Fight for Rearmament. January 1933–August 1934 (p. 67)
Deals with Hankey’s central role in the rearmament debate following Hitler’s accession to power in Germany. As Secretary to the Committee of Imperial Defence (CID), Hankey works behind the scenes to build the case for British rearmament, navigating the tensions between the Treasury’s desire for economy and the service departments’ urgent needs, while the Defence Requirements Committee prepares its first report.
3. Empire Tour. August 1934–January 1937 (p. 121)
Covers Hankey’s extensive journey through the Empire — including Australia, New Zealand, and other dominions — to consult on defence coordination. This chapter details his observations on imperial defence problems, his meetings with dominion leaders, and the strategic conclusions he drew about the Empire’s capacity to support Britain in a future war.
4. The Darkening Scene. January–June 1935 (p. 148)
Describes the worsening international situation as Germany openly repudiates the Versailles Treaty and begins conscription, while Italy prepares for war against Abyssinia. Hankey’s growing influence on defence policy is evident as he works to strengthen the CID’s machinery and prepare Britain for the coming crisis.
5. Crisis with Italy. Hankey under Fire. July 1935–February 1936 (p. 176)
Covers the Abyssinian crisis and the imposition of League of Nations sanctions against Italy. Hankey comes under political fire as the Cabinet’s handling of the crisis is criticized. He is deeply involved in the strategic implications for British naval power in the Mediterranean and the damaging effect of the crisis on collective security and Anglo-Italian relations.
6. Germany, Italy and Japan. March–December 1936 (p. 220)
Examines the growing alignment between the three revisionist powers following the Abyssinian crisis. Hankey watches with alarm as Germany remilitarises the Rhineland, Italy draws closer to Germany, and Japan expands in the Far East. The chapter analyses the CID’s response to the multiplication of potential enemies.
7. The Triple Threat Grows. January–December 1937 (p. 255)
Continues the analysis of the three-power threat as the Axis takes shape. Hankey’s workload intensifies as rearmament finally accelerates under a new Defence Loans programme. The chapter covers the Imperial Conference of 1937 and Hankey’s efforts to coordinate dominion defence contributions.
8. ’… for on his choice depends / The safety and the health of the whole state.’ (p. 297)
The chapter title, taken from Kipling’s poem “The Chooser,” reflects the critical turning point as Hankey contemplates retirement from the post of Cabinet Secretary. This chapter covers the transition period as Hankey prepares to leave the office he helped to create and to which he had devoted nearly three decades of his career.
9. Interlude with Ellerman. 1937–1941 (p. 327)
Covers Hankey’s business activities during and after his retirement from the civil service, particularly his directorship with the Ellerman shipping lines. This interlude provides insight into Hankey’s private financial affairs and his continued interest in national affairs from outside Whitehall.
10. Retirement and a New Career. 1938 (p. 352)
Describes Hankey’s formal retirement as Cabinet Secretary and CID Secretary in 1938, his elevation to the peerage as Baron Hankey of The Chart, and his assumption of new public roles. The chapter charts his transition from civil servant to public figure and his continued involvement in defence debates during the Munich crisis.
11. The Last Months of Peace. August 1938–September 1939 (p. 377)
Covers the final year before the outbreak of the Second World War, including the Munich Agreement, the German occupation of Prague, and the frantic diplomacy of the summer of 1939. Hankey, now outside government, observes the slide to war with acute anxiety and offers his counsel to former colleagues.
12. In the War Cabinet and After. 3rd September 1939–10th May 1940 (p. 421)
Covers Hankey’s return to government service as Minister without Portfolio in Chamberlain’s War Cabinet at the outbreak of war. He takes on responsibilities for a range of home-front and economic-warfare matters, including petrol rationing, the Ministry of Information, and coordination of the war effort, serving through the period of the “Phoney War.”
13. Minister outside the War Cabinet. May 1940–July 1941 (p. 467)
Following Churchill’s appointment as Prime Minister in May 1940, Hankey is excluded from the five-member War Cabinet but continues to serve as a minister — first as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and later as Paymaster-General. This chapter covers his marginalisation from the inner circle of decision-making during the darkest period of the war.
14. Another Step Down. July–December 1941 (p. 497)
Describes Hankey’s further relegation to less important ministerial posts as Churchill consolidates his control over the war machine. Hankey’s influence wanes and his relationship with Churchill becomes increasingly strained, though he continues to work on a range of committee assignments.
15. Dismissal. January–July 1942 (p. 539)
Covers Hankey’s final break with Churchill and his dismissal from the government in the spring of 1942. The chapter analyses the reasons for Churchill’s decision — rooted in policy disagreements, personality clashes, and Churchill’s desire for a leaner administration — and Hankey’s bitter reaction to his exclusion.
16. Constructive Critic. August 1942–August 1945 (p. 562)
After his dismissal, Hankey becomes a vocal critic of government policy from the backbenches and through the press. He focuses on shipping policy, the convoy system, post-war planning, and the conduct of the war, maintaining a stream of memoranda and proposals to those still in power. The chapter covers his efforts to remain relevant until the war’s end.
17. The Last Phase. 1945–1963 (p. 601)
Covers Hankey’s final years, from the immediate post-war period to his death in 1963. He remains active as a writer, commentator, and elder statesman, publishing his memoirs and offering his perspective on the Cold War, the decline of the British Empire, and the nuclear deterrent. The chapter concludes with an assessment of Hankey’s place in British history.
Appendix A: British Defence Services. Annual Estimates 1929–1939 (p. 663)
Tabulated data on British defence expenditure across the three services in the decade before the Second World War.
Appendix B: German Air Strength 1934–1939
Data on the growth of the German Luftwaffe in the pre-war period.
Index (p. 669+)
Comprehensive index to the volume.
Notes

The actual Table of Contents in the published volume contains 17 chapters plus appendices and index (more detailed than the condensed 12-chapter structure sometimes cited in secondary references).
Chapter 5 page number (176) is estimated from the printed book; the OCR of that page number is garbled in the extracted text.
Chapter 11 page (377) and Chapter 12 page (421) are corrected from OCR artifacts (“3n” and “4.21” respectively).
Page numbers for the index and appendices are from the final pages of the volume.

sources/how-britain-is-governed.title: How Britain is Governed
sources/how-britain-is-governed.content:
How Britain is Governed: A Critical Analysis of Modern Developments in the British System of Government (1935)
Ramsay Muir’s searching critique of the British constitution as it actually worked in the interwar period — arguing that seven great changes since the nineteenth century had transformed the system into something dangerously different from the textbook ideal.
Summary
Written by a Liberal historian and former MP, How Britain is Governed is a sustained attack on the gap between the constitutional theory taught in the textbooks (still essentially Bagehot and Mill) and the reality of British government in the post-war era. Muir identifies seven transformative changes: the growth of uncontrolled bureaucracy; the rise of Cabinet dictatorship; the rigidity of party organisation that reduced the House of Commons to a registering machine; the distortion of the electoral system through organised parties in single-member constituencies; the House of Commons’s increasing incapacity to perform its work; the reduction of the House of Lords to impotence; and the emergence of extra-constitutional organised interests exerting direct pressure on government. The book was first published in 1929 and revised for a third edition in 1932, with a preface noting the deepening misgivings about parliamentary government under the strain of the world crisis and the wavering policy of democratic states.
Source
Muir, Ramsay. How Britain is Governed: A Critical Analysis of Modern Developments in the British System of Government. 3rd rev. ed. Boston & New York: Houghton Mifflin Company, 1935. Printed in Great Britain.
First edition 1929; second edition 1930; third revised edition, with a new preface dated October 1932, published 1935.
Full raw OCR text available at raw.txt (701,679 bytes)
Chapters
Introduction (pp. 1–17)
Muir opens by stating his purpose: to examine the actual working of representative democracy in post-war Britain. He argues that confidence in the system has been “seriously and progressively undermined” since the war. Representative democracy, which on the eve of the war had become the almost universal mark of a civilised state, is now regarded “at the best, with a sort of tepid acquiescence.” Even in Britain, its original home, the prestige of Parliament has strangely waned: newspapers have little space for its proceedings, and the mass of electors take their responsibilities lightly. Muir cites General Smuts on the declining importance of Parliament. He argues that the textbooks — still essentially those of Bagehot (1867) and Mill (1860) — describe a system that no longer exists, because the great enlargements of the franchise, the rise of rigid party organisations, and the emergence of Cabinet dictatorship have transformed everything.
Part I: THE GOVERNMENT
Chapter I — The Functions of ‘The Government’ (pp. 18–40)
Muir examines the doctrine of the “separation of powers” against the British principle of “concentration of responsibility” in the Cabinet. He analyses the real powers of the Government: legislative initiative, financial control, foreign policy, the prerogative of dissolution, and the growing range of delegated legislation. He asks what “the Government” really is — not a homogeneous body but a complex of Cabinet, ministers, departments, and the Prime Minister’s office, each with distinct and often conflicting interests.
Chapter II — The Professional Administrators and the Growth of Bureaucracy (pp. 41–80)
Muir traces the transformation from the old system of amateur administrators to the modern professional civil service. He catalogues the enormous growth of government functions since the nineteenth century and the corresponding expansion of bureaucratic power. He examines the powers of bureaucracy — delegated legislation, administrative discretion, control of information — and asks whether this growth is dangerous. He identifies the characteristic defects of bureaucracy: slowness, rigidity, secrecy, and the tendency to expand its own authority. The chapter concludes with an analysis of the machinery of control — ministerial responsibility, Treasury oversight, and parliamentary questions — and finds it inadequate.
Chapter III — The Prime Minister and the Cabinet (pp. 81–115)
Muir argues that the Cabinet has become a “party” body in the worst sense, and that it has arrogated to itself an omnipotence it cannot exercise efficiently. He describes how Cabinet business is actually transacted — the overload of business, the dominance of the Prime Minister, the neglect of long-term policy in favour of day-to-day crises. He argues that the most important functions of the Cabinet — strategic planning, coordination of policy, supervision of administration — are “almost or entirely neglected.” He proposes reforms: a smaller Cabinet, a Cabinet secretariat with real analytical capacity, and a clearer separation between ministerial responsibility for policy and departmental administration.
Chapter IV — Political Parties and the ‘Party System’ (pp. 116–152)
Muir examines the necessity of parties and the freedom of the old two-party system before the rise of rigid organisation. He traces the growth of party organisation from Joseph Chamberlain’s Birmingham caucus of 1877, through the rise of party funds, the Whips’ control over MPs, and the decline of the independent member. He argues that the two-party system has broken down in post-war conditions, as the rise of Labour created a three-party situation that the electoral system could not honestly represent. He examines party funds, party leadership, and whether the abuses of party can be rectified.
Part II: THE CONTROL ON BEHALF OF THE PEOPLE
Chapter V — The House of Commons: Its Election (pp. 153–196)
Muir analyses the existing method of election and its defects: the single-member constituency system, the distorting effects of organised parties, and the way general elections have become “a mere gamble” in which the result does not fairly reflect the mind of the nation. He examines proportional representation and its criticisms, and considers the conditions of government when no party has a clear majority — arguing that such a situation can work well given sensible conventions.
Chapter VI — The House of Commons: Its Work (pp. 197–244)
Muir examines the inefficiency of the House of Commons: excessive pressure of business, the effects of Cabinet dictatorship, faults of procedure, and the bewildering way in which national accounts are presented. He analyses the legislative work of the House, the control of finance and administration, and the discussion of general policy. He concludes that the House of Commons has no real control over the enormous and growing power of bureaucracy, or over the vast but inefficiently wielded powers of the Cabinet.
Chapter VII — The Second Chamber (pp. 245–278)
Muir surveys the House of Lords as it actually is — reduced by the Parliament Act 1911 and by wholesale creations of undistinguished peers for party-funding purposes to a position of “humiliating impotence.” He examines what work the Lords still perform, asks whether a Second Chamber is needed at all, and reviews projects of reform. He concludes that a properly constituted Second Chamber is necessary — not to prevent revolutionary change, but to revise over-hasty legislation from the Commons.
Chapter VIII — Other Methods of Control (pp. 279–320)
Muir examines devolution as a remedy for excessive centralisation: regional devolution (subordinate legislatures for the social services, as in America, Germany, Canada, Australia and South Africa) and “functional” devolution (ensuring industry is effectively consulted on government action affecting it). He also considers control by organised interests outside the constitution — trade unions, employers’ associations, the Bank of England — and the role of public opinion, the pulpit, the platform, and the Press. He argues that because Parliament is impotent to check bureaucracy, outside organisations are “almost unnoticed, taking up this task.”
Summary and Conclusions (pp. 321–328)
Muir restates his seven great changes and argues that they amount to a complete transformation of the system. The root cause of the evil is the two-party system: it worked well when parties were loosely organised, but elaborate party organisation has enabled Cabinet dictatorship and reduced Parliament to impotence. A two-party system is “essentially unnatural in modern conditions.” Muir proposes: a smaller and reorganised Cabinet; revised House of Commons procedure for real control over finance and legislation; a better Second Chamber; and both regional and functional devolution. He concludes with a warning: “If we cannot improve our methods of discussion, government by discussion will fall into disrepute; it is already doing so. … Representative government is on its trial.”
Index (pp. 329 ff.)

sources/rise-and-fall-british-naval-mast.title: The Rise and Fall of British Naval Mastery
sources/rise-and-fall-british-naval-mast.content:
The Rise and Fall of British Naval Mastery
Paul M. Kennedy
A comprehensive analytical history of British sea power from the Tudors to the late twentieth century, arguing that Britain’s naval predominance was fundamentally dependent upon economic strength, geographical position, and a favourable international balance of power — all of which eroded irreversibly after 1914.

Preface
Kennedy frames the work as the first detailed reconsideration of British sea power since Mahan’s The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890). The book analyses the reasons for Britain’s rise and fall as the predominant maritime nation, focusing on strategic, economic, and technological factors rather than simply recounting battles and admirals.
Introduction — The Elements of Sea Power
The analytical framework: sea power derives not merely from naval strength but from geographical position, national economic resources, a productive industrial base, a large merchant marine, and an appropriate national character. Britain’s peculiar combination of insularity, commercial aptitude, and industrial leadership gave it a unique advantage — and its loss of that advantage explains the decline.
Part One: RISE
Chapter One — The Early Years of English Sea Power (to 1603)
The foundation of English naval power from the medieval period through the Tudor era, covering the development of the Royal Navy under Henry VIII, the privateering of the Elizabethan age, and the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 as the first major demonstration of English maritime capability.
Chapter Two — The Stuart Navy and the Wars with the Dutch (1603–88)
The decline under the early Stuarts, followed by the Commonwealth’s naval build-up, the three Anglo-Dutch Wars (1652–54, 1665–67, 1672–74), and the Navigation Acts. The establishment of professional naval administration and the foundations of Britain’s commercial empire.
Chapter Three — The Struggle against France and Spain (1689–1756)
The long eighteenth-century struggle with France for maritime and colonial supremacy, including the Nine Years’ War, the War of Spanish Succession, the War of Jenkins’ Ear, and the early stages of the Seven Years’ War. Britain’s strategic and financial system proved more resilient than France’s.
Part Two: ZENITH
Chapter Four — Triumph and Check (1756–93)
The Seven Years’ War (1756–63) as the first truly global conflict, in which Britain expelled France from Canada and India — the zenith of eighteenth-century British naval power. The setbacks of the American War of Independence, when the Royal Navy lost command of the sea for the first time since the seventeenth century.
Chapter Five — The Struggle against France Renewed (1793–1815)
The Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, in which British sea power was decisive in containing French hegemony, maintaining the Continental blockade, and securing ultimate victory. Trafalgar (1805) established unassailable naval supremacy that lasted for a century.
Chapter Six — Pax Britannica (1815–59)
The period of uncontested British naval mastery. The Royal Navy policed the oceans, suppressed the slave trade, enforced free trade, opened China, and projected power globally with minimal challenge. The transition from sail to steam and the technological challenges this posed to British supremacy.
Chapter Seven — Mahan versus Mackinder (1859–97)
The late-Victorian navy: the strategic debate between Mahan’s sea-power thesis and Mackinder’s land-power thesis. The naval arms race with France and Russia, the shift from wooden ships to ironclads and Dreadnoughts, the challenge of maintaining global naval supremacy while rivals industrialised and expanded their own fleets.
Part Three: FALL
Chapter Eight — The End of Pax Britannica (1897–1914)
The Diamond Jubilee naval review of 1897, the greatest demonstration of British naval power ever assembled, masked the underlying erosion of Britain’s industrial and commercial predominance. The rise of the United States and Germany as naval powers, the German naval challenge and the Anglo-German naval race, the concentration of the fleet in home waters at the expense of imperial stations. By 1914 the Royal Navy was still the world’s largest but no longer able to maintain a two-power standard, and the strategic environment had shifted fundamentally against Britain.
Chapter Nine — Stalemate and Strain (1914–18)
The First World War demonstrated the limitations of sea power in a continental war. Jutland was indecisive; the submarine campaign came close to strangling Britain; the blockade of Germany required American co-operation to be effective. The war transformed the international power balance: Britain emerged with its naval position relatively weaker, its economy strained, and the United States now a formidable naval competitor. The war confirmed Mackinder’s thesis that land-power was beginning to eclipse sea-power.
Chapter Ten — The Years of Decay (1919–39) ← Key for 1919–45
The inter-war period saw the progressive deterioration of British naval strength. The Washington Naval Treaty (1922) ended the Anglo-American-Japanese naval race but also enshrined the end of British global naval supremacy. Economic depression and public pressure for disarmament forced savage cuts in naval expenditure — the Ten-Year Rule presumed no major war for a decade, repeatedly renewed until 1932. The Royal Navy’s capital-ship strength declined dramatically while Japan and the United States built up to treaty limits. Britain’s strategic dilemma — the need to defend interests in Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Far East simultaneously with inadequate forces — was never resolved. The ‘Singapore strategy’ for defending the Far East relied upon a main fleet deployment that could not be made in time. By 1939 the Royal Navy lacked the anti-submarine escorts, naval air arm (Fleet Air Arm was starved of modern aircraft), and modern radar that would be essential for the coming conflict. The chapter argues that the decay was structural and economic, not merely the result of pacifism or appeasement, and that Britain’s underlying industrial decline made sustained naval rearmament impossible.
Chapter Eleven — The Illusory Victory (1939–45) ← Key for 1919–45
The Royal Navy fought the Second World War with great tactical skill — the Battle of the Atlantic was won, the Italian battle fleet was neutralised at Taranto and Matapan, the convoys to Russia were fought through, and the Normandy landings were the greatest amphibious operation in history. Yet Kennedy argues the victory was ‘illusory’ in strategic terms. The navy’s fundamental task — protecting the sea lanes — was only possible with massive American assistance. By 1943-44 the United States Navy had become the dominant naval power in both the Atlantic and Pacific. The Royal Navy was increasingly relegated to a supporting role. The war accelerated every trend undermining British naval power: economic exhaustion, imperial dissolution, the rise of the superpowers, and the strategic obsolescence of traditional sea power in the age of air power and nuclear weapons. Britain emerged on the winning side but as a power that could no longer sustain its global naval commitments.
Chapter Twelve — The End of the Road: British Sea Power in the Post-war World
The post-1945 withdrawal from empire and the progressive reduction of the Royal Navy from a global to a regional force within the NATO framework. The 1947 Indian independence and the 1956 Suez crisis demonstrated the end of independent British power projection. The transition to nuclear submarines and Polaris, the end of the carrier fleet, the withdrawal from East of Suez, and the Falklands conflict as a final echo of imperial naval capability. Britain by the late twentieth century ranked as a middle-ranking naval power, alongside France, no longer able to exercise global maritime predominance.
Epilogue
Kennedy draws on the parallels with earlier declining maritime empires — Spain, the Netherlands — and reflects on the six Mahanian preconditions for sea power (geographical position, physical conformation, extent of territory, population, national character, and character of government), showing how each had turned against Britain. The book concludes that the decline of British naval mastery was the inevitable consequence of relative economic decline and the shift of the world’s centre of gravity away from Western Europe.

Relevance to United Kingdom 1919–45
Chapters 8 through 11 provide the essential strategic and analytical framework for understanding Britain’s position during the period covered by this wiki. Kennedy’s central argument — that British naval power was a function of underlying economic strength, and that its erosion after 1914 was structural and irreversible — is fundamental to any assessment of British foreign and defence policy between the wars and during the Second World War.

sources/road-to-wigan-pier.title: The Road to Wigan Pier
sources/road-to-wigan-pier.content:
The Road to Wigan Pier (1937)
George Orwell’s report from the depressed industrial North of England, combined with a searching examination of English class feeling and of why Socialism — which he treats as the only real way out of the mess — so often repels the very people who ought to support it.
Summary
Commissioned in the mid-1930s and published by Victor Gollancz for the Left Book Club in 1937, The Road to Wigan Pier falls into two clearly marked parts. Part One is a first-hand account of living conditions among miners and the unemployed in Lancashire and Yorkshire: lodging-houses, the coal face, housing shortage, the Means Test and the dole, diet, coal-picking, and the landscape of industrialism. Part Two turns autobiographical and polemical. Orwell situates himself as a product of the lower-upper-middle class, traces the formation of class smell and class prejudice from public school through service in the Burma police to tramping among the destitute, and argues that the failure of Socialism in England is less a matter of economics than of manners, snobbery, crankishness, and the identification of Socialism with a machine-worshipping cult of “progress.” He closes with a call to strip Socialism back to justice and liberty and to win the sinking middle class before Fascism does. The book is a primary witness to the social and political atmosphere of interwar industrial England on the eve of rearmament and war.
Source
Orwell, George. The Road to Wigan Pier. London: Victor Gollancz Ltd, 1937. Issued for the Left Book Club.
Full raw text extracted from the local Anna’s Archive epub available at raw.txt (397,960 bytes).
Note: The local digital file is a plain-text epub (“publisher: aaa”) without edition apparatus; bibliographic details above follow the standard first Left Book Club / Gollancz publication of 1937. Chapter divisions in the text are numbered 1–13 under PART ONE and PART TWO; the chapters themselves carry no separate titles in this edition.
Chapters
Part One
Chapter 1
Orwell opens in a crowded Wigan lodging-house run by the Brookers, describing the shared bedroom, the stench, the tripe shop downstairs, commercial travellers, old-age pensioners, and the landlady’s endless grievances. The chapter is a close portrait of petty commercial decay and domestic squalor among people living on the edge of the Means Test, and it ends as Orwell leaves Wigan by train, watching snow and slag-heaps give way to another industrial town and reflecting that even in the heart of industrialism patches of green remain.
Chapter 2
“Our civilization, pace Chesterton, is founded on coal.” Orwell describes going down a mine to the coal face while the fillers are at work: heat, noise, dust, the yard-high gallery, and the exhausting “travelling” to and from the face that is not even counted as the miner’s real work. He treats the miner as the type of the invisible manual worker on whose labour “superior persons” depend, recalling that women once dragged coal underground in harness and arguing that modern comfort rests on work the rest of society prefers to forget.
Chapter 3
Above ground, Orwell watches a shift leave the pit — pale faces under coal dust, blue scars from dust under healed cuts, the ritual of washing after tea — and turns to wages, output, and accident rates. He cites production figures (around 280 tons a year for the average mine-worker) and the “death stoppage” rubber stamp on pay-checks, noting that roughly one miner in nine hundred is killed each year and one in six injured. The chapter closes on the broader indignity of working-class life: waiting on other people’s convenience, the sense that “they” will never allow anything, and the social ease with which the “educated” still step forward as leaders.
Chapter 4
A survey of housing in the industrial towns: smoke-blackened rows without hot water, shared yards and w.c.s, houses unfit for habitation but kept tenanted because there are no others, caravan colonies and single rooms of extreme overcrowding, and Corporation estates that are only marginally better. Orwell records inspections of many houses and the courtesy of unemployed guides, and ends with a personal note on Wigan itself — liking the people, not the scenery — and the joke that the celebrated Wigan Pier has been demolished.
Chapter 5
Orwell attacks the habit of reading “two millions unemployed” as if only those two million suffered. Dependants, low-paid full-time workers, pensioners, and the unregistered push the underfed population far higher (he cites Sir John Orr and multiplies Labour Exchange figures). He describes the Means Test, P.A.C. allowances, occupational centres, and the National Unemployed Workers’ Movement, and argues that cheap luxuries — fish-and-chips, the radio, cinema, football pools, tinned salmon — have mitigated surface misery and helped avert revolution without any conscious “bread and circuses” design by the governing class.
Chapter 6
Food first: Napoleon’s maxim and the claim that diet shapes history more than dynasties. On about thirty shillings a week with rent taking a quarter, the unemployed diet is white bread, margarine, sugar, tea, potatoes, and the occasional scrap of meat — filling but deficient. Orwell links industrial substitutes and tinned food to a decline in physique, describes wasteful English cookery even among the poor, and closes with the Lancashire scene of unemployed men and women risking injury to pick coal and “carmel” from dirt trains for a few pence worth of fuel.
Chapter 7
Travelling north, Orwell marks the passage from southern villa-civilisation into the “real ugliness of industrialism”: burning slag-heaps, sulphur flames, canals, and the lunar landscape around Wigan. He digresses on the English North–South myth (cold climate, Nordic virtue, the cult of Scotland) and on how industrialisation twisted that antithesis. The chapter ends with a working-class interior — coal fire, kippers, strong tea — as a moment in time, contrasting it both with a hygienic Utopian future and with medieval squalor, and treating that interior as evidence that the age has not been altogether a bad one to live in.
Part Two
Chapter 8
“The road from Mandalay to Wigan is a long one.” Orwell explains why he went north — to see mass unemployment and the working class at close quarters as part of his approach to Socialism — and turns to autobiography. Born into the lower-upper-middle class (roughly £300–£2,000 a year, with a caste element as well as money), he analyses English class as a shadowy system of habits and smells, not income alone. He discusses the physical repugnance that divides classes in the West, quotes Somerset Maugham on smell, and exposes the bourgeois Socialist who idealises the proletariat while keeping bourgeois table manners and marrying inside his own class.
Chapter 9
Public-school snobbery, a scholarship boy among richer boys, and the wave of revolutionary feeling in England during and just after the Great War form the opening. Orwell recounts service in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma — the dirty work of Empire at close quarters, guilt shared with another official on a night train, the missionary who would not care to have his job — and his decision to resign. He then describes deliberately going among the destitute: a common lodging-house as “baptism,” tramping with an Irish tramp, and the sense that the class-bar was down among “the lowest of the low” (material already used in Down and Out in Paris and London).
Chapter 10
Making friends with tramps does not solve the class problem: outcasts are no more typical of the working class than literary intellectuals are of the bourgeoisie. Orwell argues that real intimacy with ordinary respectable working people is extremely hard, that abolishing class distinctions means abandoning middle-class ideology rather than attending summer schools or “levelling up” with fruit-juice and hygiene, and that forced class-breaking often intensifies antagonism. The middle-class Socialist who recoils in middle age may flee as far as Fascism once he sees that a classless society might mean the death of his own codes and tastes.
Chapter 11
“Meanwhile what about Socialism?” The country is in a serious mess: insecurity, mass underfeeding, a pinched middle class, and worse horrors possibly coming. Socialism as a world system is elementary common sense — the raft has provisions enough if shared — yet intelligent people often reject it. Orwell catalogues the unattractiveness of many Socialists (cranks, fruit-juice drinkers, Marx-quoting cocksure types) and the barrenness of Socialist literary culture, arguing that ordinary people’s recoil from individual Socialists, however childish, is a political fact that must be faced.
Chapter 12
A deeper objection: people fear not that Socialism will fail, but that it will succeed too well — a spiritually empty, machine-dominated future. Orwell links the word “Socialism” to aeroplanes, tractors, glass factories, and also to vegetarians, commissars, and the cult of Russia; he discusses machine-worship, the alienation of anyone with feeling for tradition, and comparisons of Wells’s The Sleeper Awakes with Huxley’s Brave New World. Fascism he reads as a possible stable slave-world with a small ruling caste. Against both machine-prig Socialism and Fascism he insists the only combinable ideal is justice and liberty — words that must ring again if Fascism is not to win.
Chapter 13
Is there anything one can do? The urgent task is to capture “normal decent” people for Socialism before Fascism plays its trump card. Orwell urges dropping the smell of crankishness and machine-worship, recognising that class is cultural as well as economic (the sinking middle class still thinks in bourgeois terms), and avoiding muscular efforts at instant class-breaking. He hopes that a real Socialist party, if formed in time, may soften class prejudice through common struggle; otherwise he foresees “a slimy Anglicized form of Fascism.” The book ends with the sinking middle class — schoolmasters, journalists, clerks, bankrupt drapers — invited to sink into the working class: “we have nothing to lose but our aitches.”
Sources

Orwell, George. The Road to Wigan Pier. London: Victor Gollancz Ltd (Left Book Club), 1937.
