sources/survey-of-international-affairs-.title: Survey of International Affairs, 1936
sources/survey-of-international-affairs-.content:
Survey of International Affairs, 1936 (Toynbee, 1937)
Toynbee’s annual survey of world politics for the calendar year 1936, compiled for the Royal Institute of International Affairs — the year in which the German military reoccupation of the Rhineland dealt the second great stroke against the post-war order, world rearmament became the steadiest and most widespread movement in the international field, and the forces supporting a collective system of international relations retreated almost into rout.
Summary
The central theme, stated in Toynbee’s Preface, is a retreat — “which at times and places almost quickened into a rout” — of the forces that since the peace settlement of 1920–1 had been supporting a collective system of international relations. The revulsion from a policy based on the theory that “union is strength” to a movement of sauve qui peut was the effect of the dismay caused by two strokes against the post-war order struck with apparent impunity: the Italian attack upon Abyssinia (dealt with in the Survey for 1935, vol. ii) and the German military reoccupation of the Rhineland (a principal subject of this volume). Negatively, the new policy took the form of an endeavour to escape from commitments to other states. The survey is organised in seven parts covering world affairs, world economic affairs, Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, the American continent, and the Far East, with a chronology of events for 1936 in an appendix. Contributors include H. V. Hodson (World Economic Affairs), D. A. Routh (the Montreux Convention), H. Beeley (Palestine), Katharine Duff (the American continent), and G. E. Hubbard (the Far East).
Source
Toynbee, Arnold J., assisted by V. M. Boulter. Survey of International Affairs 1936. London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, for the Royal Institute of International Affairs, 1937. Produced under the auspices of the Royal Institute of International Affairs, Chatham House.
Source scan: Internet Archive (archive.org/details/surveyofinternat0000arno_w6i9).
Full raw OCR text available at raw.txt (3,175,895 bytes; 48,230 lines).
Contents
Preface
Toynbee frames the year around the retreat from collective security, naming the Abyssinian and Rhineland strokes as the causes of the general dismay. The countries that went farthest in escaping from commitments, he notes, were also the most sensitive to the imputation that they were repudiating their social obligations. He quotes President Roosevelt’s Chicago speech (5 October 1937) on the “ninety per cent. of the population of the world” who wanted only to live and let live in peace.
PART I — WORLD AFFAIRS
(i) Introduction
The international spectacle of 1936 was “more chaotic, and perhaps also more enigmatic” than in 1935, when the field had been dominated by the Italian aggression against Abyssinia and the rearmament of Germany. In 1936 rearmament was both the steadiest and the most widespread of all movements in the international field — “no longer confined to countries of any one kind or calibre or locality,” in full swing in democratic as well as totalitarian states, in small countries as well as Great Powers, and in Africa and America as well as Europe and the Far East. Toynbee identifies the main cause as the anxiety excited by the apparent weakness of the forces that had counted for peace and order. Two Additional Notes follow: (i) The Post-War Ideologies in Belgium and in Great Britain; (ii) Reichsdeutsch Propaganda abroad under the National-Socialist Régime.
(ii) The London Naval Conference, 1935–6
A detailed account of the London Naval Conference (9 December 1935 – 25 March 1936) and its preliminaries: the position in the first half of 1934, the preliminary conversations of June–December 1934, the Japanese denunciation of the Washington Treaty, building programmes and exchanges of views in 1935, the conference itself, building programmes in 1936, and the negotiation of bilateral naval agreements and the ratification of the London Treaty — the framework within which Britain’s interwar naval position was recast.
(iii) The Development of Rearmament in 1936
An account of world rearmament through the year: the position to the end of March, the British White Paper on Defence of 3 March 1936 and the British Defence Estimates, the period from April to the French Decree of 11 August 1936 lowering the age for military service, and the course from the Russian decrees to the end of the year. A bird’s-eye view of world rearmament, of which a detailed country-by-country account “would far exceed the limits of space to which this Survey is confined.”
PART II — WORLD ECONOMIC AFFAIRS (by H. V. Hodson)
(i) The End of the Gold Bloc
Hodson opens with a British economist’s verdict that the monetary declarations of 26 September 1936 by the United States, French, and British Governments, as a prelude to the devaluation of the franc, “constitute the greatest economic event of 1936.” Their significance lay less in their content than as “a gesture of international co-operation” and a dividing point between phases of world economic development. The sections trace the weakness of the franc — between 29 May and 5 June the Bank of France lost 1,500,000,000 francs net, nearly £20,000,000 — Monsieur Blum’s “New Deal,” the Three-Power Currency Declaration, the end of the gold bloc, the realignment of the European currencies, exchanges after the realignment, and the consequences of devaluation.
(ii) The Rise in Prices and the Armaments Boom
The rise in prices and the boom in armaments: commodities and restriction and revival (wheat, rubber, tin, copper, oil, tea, sugar, cocoa, wool, lead and zinc, nickel), armaments and self-sufficiency, and a conclusion on the economics of rearmament.
PART III — EUROPE
(i) The German Military Reoccupation of the Rhineland and the Subsequent Negotiations between the Locarno Powers
The centrepiece of the volume. The section opens with the antecedents of 7 March 1936: the Franco-Russian Treaty of Mutual Assistance of 2 May 1935, Germany’s contention that it was incompatible with the Treaty of Locarno, and the French and British staff conversations which began at the end of October 1935. Hitler had declared in his Reichstag speech of 21 May 1935 that his Government would “scrupulously maintain every treaty voluntarily signed,” subject to the reservation “so long as the other partners are on their side ready to stand by that pact” — which in German eyes brought the denunciation of 7 March 1936 within that reservation. Toynbee notes that “right up to the 7th March, 1936, the general impression, at any rate in England — and this apparently in official circles as well as among the public — was that Herr Hitler was unlikely to commit an open breach of a treaty whose validity he had so recently reaffirmed.” The subsequent sections trace: the motives for the stroke; the events of 7 March and the reactions in other countries; the negotiations between the Locarno Powers in Paris and London (10–19 March); the meeting of the League Council in London (14–24 March); negotiations on the British plan of proposals of 19 March and the German counter-proposals of 31 March; the French Memorandum of 6 April and the Four-Power conversations at Geneva on 10 April; the British Questionnaire of 7 May and the German reaction; the policy of the new French Government and the Locarno Powers’ meeting in London on 23 July; the change in Belgian foreign policy; and the negotiations between the Locarno Powers and the attempt to assemble a Five-Power Conference (August to December 1936).
(ii) Relations between Germany and the Soviet Union since Herr Hitler’s Advent to Power
(iii) Poland’s Inclination towards Detachment
(iv) South-Eastern Europe
(a) Austria and Hungary between Italy and Germany (1935–6) — the problem of the “viability” of Austria; internal developments in Austria, the maintenance of the ascendancy of the Vaterländische Front over the Social Democrats and the National Socialists, and the struggle for power among the parties and personalities represented on the Front and the triumph of the Right wing of the Christian Social Party and Dr. von Schuschnigg; the maintenance of the Italo-Austro-Hungarian group; relations between Italy and Germany and the conclusion of the Agreement of 11 July 1936; and relations between Hungary and Germany.
(b) Czechoslovakia between Russia and Germany — the growth of tension, incidents and rumours, and the treatment and conduct of the German minority in Czechoslovakia.
(c) The Loosening of the Balkan and the Little Entente — old pacts and new facts; the Little Entente vis-à-vis Italy and Austria; the rapprochement between Jugoslavia and Bulgaria and the signature of the Jugoslav-Bulgarian Pact of 24 January 1937; and the inclination towards isolation in Greece and in Rumania.
(d) Germany’s Economic Drang nach Südosten.
(v) The Balticum between Russia and Germany
(vi) Danzig and the League of Nations (1936–7)
(vii) Relations between Germany and Italy
PART IV — THE MEDITERRANEAN
(i) The Montreux Convention regarding the Regime of the Black Sea Straits (20 July 1936) (by D. A. Routh)
Introduction; the historical background; from the signature of the Treaty of Lausanne to the dispatch of the Turkish Note of 10 April 1936; the Turkish Note and the negotiations leading up to the Montreux Conference; the Montreux Conference (22 June – 20 July 1936); and reactions to the signature of the Montreux Convention and subsequent negotiations for the adherence of the Italian Government.
(ii) The Anglo-Italian Declaration of 2 January 1937 concerning Assurances with regard to the Mediterranean
PART V — THE MIDDLE EAST
(i) Anglo-Egyptian Relations from the Breakdown of Treaty Negotiations in London on 5 May 1930 to the Signature of a Treaty in London on 26 August 1936
The long road to the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936, from the breakdown of negotiations in 1930 through to signature in London on 26 August 1936.
(ii) The Administration of the British Mandate for Palestine, 1935–6 (by H. Beeley)
Introductory; economic and social background; the Arab rising of 1936; and the report of the Royal Commission.
(iii) The Signature of the Franco-Syrian Treaty of 9 September 1936 and the Franco-Lebanese Treaty of 13 November 1936
(iv) The Franco-Turkish Dispute over the Sanjaq of Alexandretta (1936–7)
(v) Sa’udi Arabia and Her Neighbours
(vi) The Controversies over the Frontier between Iran (Persia) on the One Side and Turkey and ‘Iraq on the Other; and the Four-Power Middle Eastern Pact of 8 July 1937
PART VI — THE AMERICAN CONTINENT (by Katharine Duff)
(i) The Inter-American Conference for the Maintenance of Peace, December 1936
(ii) The Dispute between Bolivia and Paraguay in the Chaco Boreal (1934–7)
(iii) The New Treaty between the United States and Panama
PART VII — THE FAR EAST (by G. E. Hubbard)
(i) Introduction
(ii) Internal Developments in China
(iii) Internal Developments in Japan
(iv) The Economic and Strategic Relationship of ‘Manchukuo’ to Japan
(v) Relations between China and Japan
(vi) Japan and Communism
(a) Introductory; (b) The German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Agreement; (c) Relations between Japan and the U.S.S.R.
APPENDIX — Chronology of Events, 1936
A day-by-day chronology of the year’s events, from the death of George V and accession of Edward VIII through the Rhineland occupation, the fall of Addis Ababa, the Spanish Civil War outbreak, the Montreux Convention, the Berlin-Rome Axis, and the Abdication crisis.
Index
The volume concludes with a full index (pp. 963 ff.) and maps: The Islamic World; Abyssinia and Arabia; The Far East; The World on Mollweide’s Projection.

sources/the-new-despotism.title: The New Despotism
sources/the-new-despotism.content:
The New Despotism (1929)
Lord Chief Justice Gordon Hewart’s landmark denunciation of the growing power of the executive government to legislate by departmental regulation, adjudicate disputes outside the courts, and undermine the rule of law — a text that became a rallying cry for opponents of “bureaucracy” and administrative discretion in interwar Britain.
Summary
The New Despotism is a polemic by the Lord Chief Justice of England, Lord Hewart of Bury, published in 1929, warning of a creeping “despotism” — the progressive transfer of legislative and judicial power from Parliament and the courts to government departments. Hewart argues that through a combination of delegated legislation (statutory instruments enabling ministers to make binding rules), the statutory exclusion of judicial review, and the vesting of judicial functions in officials rather than judges, the executive was quietly subverting the British constitution. He identifies this as a deliberate conspiracy, drawing on a mass of statutes from the preceding two decades to demonstrate the scale of the phenomenon. The book opens with the famous example of Section 67 of the Rating and Valuation Act 1925, which empowered the Minister of Health to “remove difficulties” by order and to “modify the provisions of this Act” — a power Hewart calls the “high-water mark of legislative provisions of this character.” The book became a cause célèbre, cited in legal and political debate throughout the 1930s, and contributed to the establishment of the Donoughmore Committee on Ministers’ Powers (1929–32).
Source
Hewart, Gordon Hewart, Baron. The New Despotism. London: Ernest Benn Limited, 1929.
Copyright 1929 by Lord Hewart of Bury. Printed in Great Britain by Billing and Sons Ltd., Guildford and Esher.
Full raw OCR text available at raw.txt
Note: This source page uses the British first edition (Ernest Benn, 316 pp.), which includes a full Index absent from the American edition (Cosmopolitan Book Corporation, 311 pp., no index). The scan is complete with all pages intact.
Chapters
Chapter I — The Nature of the Question (p. 3–15)
Hewart opens with the example of Section 67 of the Rating and Valuation Act 1925, which empowered the Minister of Health to “remove difficulties” arising under the Act by order, and to “modify the provisions of this Act” as he saw fit. He cites a judicial comment that this section represented “the high-water mark of legislative provisions of this character,” and observes that a government department could, by order, override the very statute that created its power. He reviews a series of similar statutory provisions giving ministers power to make binding orders, poses the question of how such a situation arose, and introduces his thesis: that a systematic and deliberate policy has been pursued by the executive to acquire despotic power.
Chapter II — The Rule of Law (p. 17–30)
Hewart examines the concept of the rule of law in the English constitutional tradition. He draws on Dicey’s formulation — the absolute supremacy of regular law as opposed to arbitrary power, the equality of all subjects before the ordinary courts, and the subordination of the executive to judicial control. He argues that the rule of law is the central principle of the English constitution and that the new executive practices are a direct assault upon it.
Chapter III — “Administrative Law” (p. 31–38)
Hewart distinguishes English jurisprudence from continental systems of droit administratif and the French Conseil d’État. He argues that what is called “administrative law” on the Continent — separate courts for disputes involving the state — is fundamentally incompatible with the English rule of law, under which all persons, including officials, are subject to the same ordinary courts. He warns that the new English practices amount to the introduction of administrative law by stealth, but without the safeguards of the continental systems.
Chapter IV — Administrative Lawlessness (p. 39–56)
A substantial chapter detailing the statutory provisions by which ministers and government departments are empowered to decide questions of a judicial nature to the exclusion of the courts. Hewart catalogues statutes vesting powers of decision in ministers under acts relating to housing, health insurance, pensions, town planning, unemployment insurance, agriculture, and other fields. He argues that this represents not administrative law but “administrative lawlessness” — the exercise of judicial power without the independence, procedure, or publicity of the courts.
Chapter V — The System at Work (p. 57–78)
Hewart examines how the system operates in practice. He discusses the growing practice whereby Parliament delegates to government departments wide powers of legislation on matters of local government, health, education, industry, and housing. He traces the origin of the practice to the pressure of parliamentary business and the technical complexity of modern legislation, but argues that the delegation has become indiscriminate and that departments exploit the practice to enlarge their own power.
Chapter VI — Department Legislation (p. 79–102)
Hewart distinguishes between two kinds of delegated legislation: prerogative legislation (based on the Crown’s prerogative) and statutory delegated legislation (based on an Act of Parliament). He examines the scope of each, the constitutional limits that ought to apply, and the ways in which these limits have been progressively eroded. He gives particular attention to the power of departments to modify Acts of Parliament themselves through ministerial orders.
Chapter VII — The Independence of the Judiciary (p. 103–145)
Hewart argues that the new system directly threatens the independence of the judiciary, which he calls one of the great historic achievements of English liberty. He traces the history of judicial independence from the Act of Settlement, and shows how the transfer of judicial functions from courts to departments undermines it. The chapter includes a review of cases in which courts have asserted their jurisdiction against executive encroachment.
Chapter VIII — What is to be Done? (p. 146–167)
Hewart opens with a Russian epigraph — Что делать? (What is to be done?) — and reviews judicial opinions on the necessity of a right of appeal from decisions of official persons. He quotes Lord Justice Bowen, Lord Justice Scrutton, and others on the dangers of executive justice, and discusses the crown proceedings bill and the reform of the law relating to the Crown as litigant. The chapter argues for restoring the authority of the courts and restricting departmental adjudication.
Chapter IX — Some Leading Cases (p. 168–240)
Hewart reproduces substantial extracts from the judgments in key cases illustrating the courts’ struggle against executive encroachment. Cases examined include Scott v. Scott (publicity in judicial proceedings), Local Government Board v. Arlidge (the extent of natural justice in departmental inquiries), R. v. Minister of Health ex parte Wortley Rural District Council (ministerial power to remove difficulties), and others. Each case is analysed for its bearing on the constitutional question.
Chapter X — Examples from Statutes (p. 241–311)
The final chapter is a compendium of statutory provisions culled from the statute book, arranged as a reference resource. Hewart reproduces the text of sections from a wide range of Acts — including the Patents, Designs and Trade Marks Act 1883, the Rating and Valuation Act 1925, the Fertilizers and Feeding Stuffs Act 1926, the Sale of Food (Weights and Measures) Act 1926, the Poor Law Act 1927, and the Road Transport Lighting Act 1927 — each conferring legislative or judicial powers on ministers or government departments. The book is followed by a full Index.
